Protons = atomic number (Z).
Electrons = Z in a neutral atom (for an ion, subtract the charge: Na⁺ has 11 − 1 = 10 electrons).

Traditional English grammar names eight parts of speech:
1. Noun - names a person, place, thing, or idea (teacher, Ohio, pencil, freedom).
2. Pronoun - takes the place of a noun (she, it, they, who).
3. Verb - shows action or a state of being (run, think, is).
4. Adjective - describes a noun or pronoun (tall, blue, three).
5. Adverb - describes a verb, adjective, or another adverb (quickly, very, never).
6. Preposition - shows a relationship to a noun or pronoun (in, on, under, after).
7. Conjunction - joins words, phrases, or clauses (and, but, because).
8. Interjection - shows sudden feeling (wow, oh, hey).
A word's part of speech depends on how it is used: "run" is a verb in "I run" but a noun in "a long run."

A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea.
Common noun: a general name (city, dog). Proper noun: a specific name, capitalized (Chicago, Rover).
Concrete noun: can be sensed (apple, music). Abstract noun: an idea or feeling (courage, justice).
Collective noun: names a group (team, flock, jury).
Countable nouns have plurals (one book, two books); uncountable nouns usually do not (water, information).
Example: The team showed courage in Denver. (team = collective, courage = abstract, Denver = proper)

A pronoun replaces a noun. The noun it replaces is its antecedent.
Personal subject pronouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
Personal object pronouns: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
Possessive pronouns: mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs.
Reflexive: myself, yourself, themselves. Relative: who, whom, whose, which, that.
Demonstrative: this, that, these, those. Interrogative: who, what, which. Indefinite: someone, each, everybody, none.
Rule: a pronoun should agree with its antecedent in number. Example: The students packed their bags.

A verb expresses an action or a state of being and is the core of the predicate.
Action verb: shows something done (jump, write, decide).
Linking verb: connects the subject to a word that renames or describes it (is, am, are, was, were, seem, become). Example: The soup smells good.
Helping (auxiliary) verb: works with a main verb (has, have, had, do, does, did, will, can, should, might). Example: She has finished.
Transitive verbs take a direct object (She kicked the ball). Intransitive verbs do not (He slept).

An adjective describes or limits a noun or pronoun. It answers which one, what kind, or how many.
Example: three old maps (three = how many, old = what kind).
Degrees of comparison:
Positive: tall, good. Comparative (two things): taller, better. Superlative (three or more): tallest, best.
Longer adjectives usually use more and most: more careful, most careful.
Articles (a, an, the) are often classed as adjectives or as determiners.
Predicate adjectives follow a linking verb: The sky is gray.

An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. It answers how, when, where, how often, or to what extent.
Verb: She spoke softly. Adjective: a very bright light. Adverb: He ran quite fast.
Many adverbs end in -ly (quickly, happily), but many do not (soon, here, never, often, very, well).
Not every -ly word is an adverb: friendly and lovely are adjectives.

A preposition shows how a noun or pronoun (its object) relates to another word in the sentence, often in place or time.
Common prepositions: about, above, across, after, against, along, among, around, at, before, behind, below, beneath, beside, between, by, during, for, from, in, inside, into, near, of, off, on, over, since, through, to, toward, under, until, up, with, without.
A prepositional phrase = preposition + its object + any modifiers: under the old bridge.
The subject of a sentence is never inside a prepositional phrase: One of the dogs is barking (subject = One).

A conjunction joins words, phrases, or clauses.
Coordinating conjunctions join equal parts; remember FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
Subordinating conjunctions begin a dependent clause: because, although, since, unless, when, while, if, after, before.
Example: I stayed inside because it was raining.
Correlative conjunctions come in pairs: either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also, whether/or.

An interjection is a word or short phrase that expresses sudden emotion and is grammatically separate from the rest of the sentence.
Examples: Wow! Ouch! Hey, wait for me. Oh, I forgot.
A strong interjection is followed by an exclamation point; a mild one is followed by a comma.

Every complete sentence has a subject (who or what the sentence is about) and a predicate (what the subject does or is).
Example: The tired hikers | reached the summit.
Simple subject: the key noun or pronoun (hikers). Simple predicate: the main verb (reached).
A clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb.
Independent clause: can stand alone as a sentence. Dependent (subordinate) clause: cannot stand alone (because they started early).

Simple: one independent clause. The bell rang.
Compound: two or more independent clauses joined by a comma + FANBOYS conjunction or by a semicolon. The bell rang, and students left.
Complex: one independent clause + at least one dependent clause. When the bell rang, students left.
Compound-complex: at least two independent clauses + at least one dependent clause. When the bell rang, students left, but the teacher stayed.
By purpose: declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command), exclamatory (strong feeling).

English combines three times (past, present, future) with four aspects (simple, progressive, perfect, perfect progressive), giving 12 tenses. Example verb: walk.
Simple: walked / walk(s) / will walk
Progressive: was/were walking / am/is/are walking / will be walking
Perfect: had walked / has/have walked / will have walked
Perfect progressive: had been walking / has/have been walking / will have been walking
Keep tense consistent within a passage unless the time actually changes. Literary analysis is usually written in the present tense.

Form: base verb; add -s or -es for he, she, it. (I walk, she walks.)
Use for habits, general truths, schedules, and literary analysis.
Examples: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level. She practices piano every day. In the novel, Scout learns about prejudice.
Negative: do/does not + base verb (He does not walk).

Form: base verb + -ed for regular verbs (walked, played); irregular verbs change form (go/went, see/saw, write/wrote, buy/bought).
Use for a completed action at a definite time in the past.
Examples: We visited Boston last summer. She wrote the letter yesterday.
Negative: did not + base verb (They did not go).

Form: will + base verb (I will walk). "Be going to + base verb" also expresses the future (I am going to walk).
Use for predictions, promises, decisions, and planned future actions.
Examples: The train will arrive at noon. I am going to study tonight.
Negative: will not (won't) + base verb.

Form: am/is/are + verb-ing (I am walking, they are walking).
Use for an action happening right now, a temporary situation, or a planned near-future event.
Examples: She is reading right now. We are leaving tomorrow morning.
Stative verbs such as know, believe, and own are usually not used in progressive forms (say "I know," not "I am knowing").

Form: was/were + verb-ing (I was walking, they were walking).
Use for an action in progress at a past moment, often interrupted by another action in the simple past.
Examples: I was eating dinner when the phone rang. At 8 p.m. they were watching a movie.

Form: will be + verb-ing (I will be walking).
Use for an action that will be in progress at a specific future time.
Examples: At noon tomorrow, I will be taking my exam. This time next week, we will be flying to Texas.

Form: has/have + past participle (I have walked, she has eaten).
Use for past actions connected to now: experiences at an unspecified time, actions that began in the past and continue, or recent actions with present results.
Examples: I have visited Mexico twice. She has lived here since 2019. They have already finished.
Do not use it with a specific finished time: say "I saw it yesterday," not "I have seen it yesterday."

Form: had + past participle (I had walked).
Use for an action completed before another past action or time.
Examples: By the time we arrived, the movie had started. She had never seen snow before she moved to Maine.

Form: will have + past participle (I will have walked).
Use for an action that will be completed before a certain future time.
Examples: By June, I will have finished the course. They will have left before you get there.

Form: has/have been + verb-ing (I have been walking).
Use for an action that began in the past and is still continuing, often with for or since, stressing duration.
Examples: She has been studying for three hours. It has been raining since Monday.

Form: had been + verb-ing (I had been walking).
Use for an ongoing action that continued up to another point in the past.
Examples: They had been waiting for an hour when the bus finally came. He was tired because he had been running.

Form: will have been + verb-ing (I will have been walking).
Use for an action that will have continued for a length of time by a future point.
Example: By December, she will have been working here for ten years.

A verb must agree with its subject in number: singular subject + singular verb, plural subject + plural verb.
The dog barks. The dogs bark.
Ignore words between the subject and verb: The box of crayons is on the desk. (subject = box)
Subjects joined by and are usually plural: Sam and Ana are here.
With or / nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the coach nor the players were ready. Either the players or the coach was ready.
In sentences starting with there or here, find the subject after the verb: There are two reasons.

Always singular: each, every, either, neither, one, everyone, everybody, someone, anyone, nobody, everything. Everyone is invited.
Always plural: both, few, many, several. Several were missing.
Depend on the noun that follows (some, any, none, all, most, more): All of the pie is gone. All of the cookies are gone. (With none, both singular and plural are accepted.)
Collective nouns (team, family, jury) usually take a singular verb in American English when acting as one unit: The team is winning.
Titles and amounts treated as one unit are singular: Ten dollars is enough. "The Outsiders" is a novel.
Some nouns ending in -s are singular: news, mathematics, physics. The news is good.

A pronoun must agree with its antecedent (the noun it refers to) in number and person.
Correct: The students turned in their essays. The bird built its nest.
Unclear: When Maria met Jen, she was nervous. (who was nervous?) Fix: Maria was nervous when she met Jen.
Singular "they" for a person whose gender is unknown or not specified is accepted by the MLA and APA style guides: Someone left their umbrella. Some teachers still prefer "his or her," so follow your teacher's guidance.

t: Comma rule: before a conjunction joining two sentences
x:
Put a comma before a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) when it joins two independent clauses.
Correct: The storm ended, but the roads were still flooded.
No comma when the second part is not a full clause: The storm ended and moved east. (no new subject, so no comma)
Very short clauses may skip the comma in informal writing, but using it is never wrong.

t: Comma rule: after an introductory element
x:
Use a comma after an introductory word, phrase, or dependent clause that comes before the main clause.
Word: However, the plan failed.
Phrase: After the long meeting, we went home.
Clause: Because it was late, the store had closed.
If the dependent clause comes after the main clause, usually no comma is needed: The store had closed because it was late.
A very short introductory phrase (two or three words) may omit the comma: In 1990 the law changed.

t: Comma rule: items in a series (Oxford comma)
x:
Use commas to separate three or more items in a series.
Example: We bought apples, pears, and grapes.
The comma before the final "and" or "or" is called the Oxford or serial comma. MLA, APA, and Chicago styles use it; AP style (used by many newspapers) usually omits it. Whichever you choose, be consistent.
The Oxford comma can prevent confusion: I thanked my parents, the coach, and the principal.
Do not put a comma after the last item before the verb: Apples, pears, and grapes are fruit.

Set off with commas any word group that adds extra information but could be removed without changing the core meaning.
Nonessential: My brother, who lives in Ohio, is a nurse. (I have one brother; the clause is extra.)
Essential (no commas): The student who won the prize is my cousin. (the clause tells which student)
In American usage, "which" usually begins nonessential clauses (with commas) and "that" begins essential clauses (no commas).
Example: The car, which is red, needs gas. The car that is red needs gas.

An appositive is a noun or noun phrase that renames the noun right before it.
Nonessential appositives are set off with commas: Ms. Lee, our science teacher, coached the team.
Essential appositives, which identify which one, take no commas: The poet Langston Hughes wrote about Harlem. (there are many poets, so the name is essential)

Use a comma between two or more adjectives that each describe the noun equally (coordinate adjectives).
Test: if you can reverse them or put "and" between them, use a comma.
Comma: a long, boring lecture (a boring, long lecture / a long and boring lecture both work).
No comma: three red apples (you would not say "red three apples" or "three and red apples").

t: Comma rule: direct address, yes/no, and interjections
x:
Use commas to set off the name of a person being spoken to.
Examples: Sam, please close the door. Thank you, Dr. Kim, for your help.
Compare: Let's eat, Grandma. (speaking to Grandma) vs. Let's eat Grandma. (a very different meaning)
Also set off yes, no, and mild interjections: Yes, I finished. Well, that was surprising.

t: Comma rule: dates, addresses, and numbers
x:
Dates: put a comma between the day and year, and after the year if the sentence continues. On July 4, 1776, the declaration was adopted.
No comma with month and year only: in July 1776.
Places: separate city and state or country, and add a comma after the state if the sentence continues. She moved to Austin, Texas, in May.
Numbers: commas separate groups of three digits in numbers of five or more digits: 10,000 and 2,500,000. (Four-digit numbers may be written 4,500 or 4500.)

Use a comma to separate a speaker tag (he said, she asked) from a direct quotation.
Examples: Maya said, "The bus is late." / "The bus is late," Maya said. / "The bus," Maya said, "is late."
In American English, commas and periods go inside closing quotation marks. Question marks and exclamation points go inside only if they belong to the quotation.
Do not use a comma before a quotation introduced by "that": She said that the bus was "late again."

1. Join two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction: I studied all night; I still felt unprepared.
2. Before a conjunctive adverb or transition (however, therefore, moreover, otherwise) that joins two independent clauses, with a comma after it: The road was icy; however, the bus arrived on time.
3. Separate items in a list when the items already contain commas: We visited Dallas, Texas; Denver, Colorado; and Reno, Nevada.
Do not use a semicolon between a clause and a fragment. Wrong: Because it rained; we stayed home.

A colon introduces something that explains, lists, or completes what came before. The words before a colon should be a complete sentence.
List: Bring three things: a pencil, a ruler, and a calculator.
Explanation: She had one goal: to finish the race.
Long or formal quotation: The sign gave one warning: "Keep out."
Wrong: The supplies are: pencils and paper. (no colon directly after a verb or preposition)
Other uses: time (10:30), ratios (3:1), titles and subtitles (Book: A Subtitle), business-letter greetings (Dear Ms. Ruiz:).

Singular noun: add 's. the dog's bowl, the teacher's desk.
Singular noun ending in s: most styles (MLA, Chicago) still add 's: James's book, the bus's tires. (AP style uses only an apostrophe for names: James' book.)
Plural noun ending in s: add only an apostrophe. the dogs' bowls, the teachers' lounge.
Plural noun not ending in s: add 's. the children's toys, the women's team.
Joint ownership: Sam and Ana's project. Separate ownership: Sam's and Ana's projects.
Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: its, yours, hers, ours, theirs, whose.

An apostrophe marks missing letters in a contraction: do not = don't, it is = it's, they are = they're, will not = won't, I would = I'd.
Do not use an apostrophe to make an ordinary plural. Wrong: two apple's. Right: two apples.
Decades: the 1990s (no apostrophe before the s); '90s with the apostrophe replacing the missing 19.
Formal academic writing often avoids contractions; check your assignment.

a: how to write a book title
x:
Use quotation marks for a speaker's exact words and for words quoted from a source.
Titles in MLA style:
Italicize (or underline by hand) long or whole works: books, plays, films, TV series, albums, newspapers, magazines, websites.
Put in quotation marks short works or parts of a larger work: poems, short stories, essays, articles, songs, chapters, TV episodes.
Example: The poem "The Road Not Taken" appears in the book Mountain Interval (book title italicized).
Use single quotation marks for a quotation inside a quotation: "She told me, 'Wait here,' and left."

A fragment is a group of words punctuated as a sentence that is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.
Missing subject: Ran to the store. Fix: She ran to the store.
Missing verb: The dog in the yard. Fix: The dog in the yard barked.
Dependent clause alone: Because I was tired. Fix: I went to bed early because I was tired.
Fix a fragment by adding the missing part or attaching it to a nearby complete sentence.

a: what is a run on sentence
x:
A run-on (fused) sentence joins two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction.
Wrong: The game ended late we got home at midnight.
Fixes:
Period: The game ended late. We got home at midnight.
Semicolon: The game ended late; we got home at midnight.
Comma + coordinating conjunction: The game ended late, so we got home at midnight.
Subordinating conjunction: Because the game ended late, we got home at midnight.
A long sentence is not automatically a run-on; it is a run-on only when clauses are joined incorrectly.

A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma.
Wrong: I finished my essay, it took three hours.
Fixes: use a period (... essay. It took ...), a semicolon (... essay; it took ...), a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (... essay, and it took ...), or make one clause dependent (Although it took three hours, I finished my essay.)
A transition word such as however or therefore does not fix a splice by itself. Wrong: I studied, however, I failed. Right: I studied; however, I failed.

Active voice: the subject performs the action. The chef cooked the meal.
Passive voice: the subject receives the action; it uses a form of "be" + past participle, and the doer may appear after "by" or be left out. The meal was cooked (by the chef).
To change passive to active, find who did the action and make that the subject.
Active voice is usually clearer and more direct. Passive voice is useful when the doer is unknown or unimportant (The window was broken overnight) or in some scientific writing (The samples were heated).
Passive is not the same as past tense: "The meal is cooked daily" is passive in the present tense.

A modifier should sit next to the word it describes.
Misplaced: She served sandwiches to the kids on paper plates. (the kids are not on the plates) Fix: She served the kids sandwiches on paper plates.
Dangling: the word being described is missing. Walking to school, the rain started. (the rain was not walking) Fix: Walking to school, I got caught in the rain.
Check: after an introductory phrase, the subject of the main clause should be the one doing the action in the phrase.

Items in a list or comparison should share the same grammatical form.
Not parallel: She likes hiking, to swim, and riding bikes.
Parallel: She likes hiking, swimming, and biking. (all -ing) or She likes to hike, to swim, and to bike.
Pairs with correlative conjunctions need matching parts: He is not only smart but also kind. (adjective / adjective)
Parallelism makes writing clearer and is a common rhetorical device in speeches.

a: difference between their there and they're
x:
their = belonging to them (possessive). Their house is blue.
there = a place, or used to introduce a sentence. Put it over there. There are three cats.
they're = they are. They're coming at noon.
Test: if "they are" fits, write they're.

your = belonging to you (possessive). Is this your jacket?
you're = you are. You're going to love this book.
Test: if "you are" fits, write you're.

its = belonging to it (possessive; no apostrophe, like his and hers). The dog wagged its tail.
it's = it is or it has. It's raining. It's been a long day.
Test: if "it is" or "it has" fits, write it's. There is no word "its'".

a: difference between to too and two
x:
to = a preposition showing direction, or part of an infinitive. We walked to school. I like to read.
too = also, or excessively. I want to come too. The soup is too hot.
two = the number 2. I have two sisters.

affect is usually a verb meaning to influence. The weather affected our plans.
effect is usually a noun meaning a result. The weather had a big effect on our plans.
Memory trick: Affect = Action (verb); Effect = End result (noun).
Less common uses: effect as a verb means to bring about (to effect change); affect as a noun is a psychology term for displayed emotion.

than is used in comparisons. She is taller than her brother.
then refers to time or sequence, or means "in that case." We ate, and then we left. If you are ready, then let's go.
Memory trick: than and compare both have an "a"; then and when both have an "e".

accept is a verb meaning to receive or agree to. I accept your apology.
except is usually a preposition meaning excluding or but. Everyone came except Leo.
Memory trick: except and exclude both start with ex.

lose (one o) is a verb meaning to misplace or fail to win. Don't lose your keys. We might lose the game.
loose (two o's) is an adjective meaning not tight or not fastened. My shoelace is loose.
The -ing form is losing (I am losing my patience), not loosing, unless you mean setting something loose.

whose = possessive form of who. Whose backpack is this?
who's = who is or who has. Who's ready? Who's seen my phone?
Test: if "who is" or "who has" fits, write who's.

principal (noun) = the head of a school, or a sum of money; (adjective) = main or most important. The principal spoke. The principal reason was cost.
principle (noun only) = a basic truth, rule, or belief. She stood by her principles. the principles of physics.
Memory trick: the principal is your pal; a principle is a rule (both end in -le).

complement = something that completes or goes well with something else. The sauce complements the pasta.
compliment = praise. She complimented my drawing. Complimentary also means free of charge.
Memory trick: a complement completes; a compliment is something I like to hear.

stationary (adjective) = not moving. A stationary bike.
stationery (noun) = writing paper and envelopes.
Memory trick: stationEry goes with Envelopes; stationAry means stAnding still.

capital = a city that is the seat of government (Austin is the capital of Texas), an uppercase letter, or money for investment.
capitol = the building where a legislature meets. The Capitol in Washington, D.C., is home to Congress (capitalized when it means that building).
Memory trick: the capitOl building often has a dOme.

desert (DEZ-ert, noun) = a dry, sandy region. The Sahara is a desert.
desert (dih-ZURT, verb) = to abandon. The soldier did not desert his post.
dessert (dih-ZURT) = the sweet course after a meal.
Memory trick: dessert has two s's because you always want seconds.

weather = conditions of the atmosphere (rain, sun, wind). The weather is cold today.
whether = introduces alternatives or a condition, like "if." I don't know whether to stay or go.

fewer is used with countable nouns (things you can count one by one). fewer students, fewer cookies.
less is used with uncountable nouns (amounts). less water, less time, less homework.
Common exceptions: less is normally used with time, money, and distance treated as amounts (less than five dollars, less than ten miles).

who is a subject pronoun (like he). Who called? (He called.)
whom is an object pronoun (like him). Whom did you call? (You called him.) To whom should I write?
Test: answer the question with he or him. If him fits, use whom. (Remember: him = whom, both end in m.)
In casual speech many people use who in both cases, but formal writing keeps the distinction.

lie = to recline; takes no object. Forms: lie, lay, (has) lain, lying. I lie down. Yesterday I lay down.
lay = to put or place something; needs an object. Forms: lay, laid, (has) laid, laying. Lay the book on the table. She laid the book there.
Tricky point: the past tense of lie is lay. Last night the dog lay on the rug.
lie meaning "to tell an untruth" is regular: lie, lied, lied, lying.

advice (noun, ends in -ice, sounds like "ice") = a suggestion or recommendation. She gave me good advice.
advise (verb, ends in -ise, sounds like "eyes") = to give advice. I advise you to start early.

allusion = an indirect reference to something, often a well-known person, story, or event. Calling a strong friend "a Hercules" is an allusion.
illusion = a false perception or belief. The mirror created an illusion of space.
Allude (verb) means to refer indirectly; elude means to escape or avoid.

emigrate = to leave one country to live in another (Exit). She emigrated from Poland.
immigrate = to come Into a new country to live. She immigrated to Canada.
Same move, different viewpoint: she emigrated from Poland and immigrated to Canada.

farther is used for physical distance. The lake is farther than the park. (Memory trick: farther has "far" in it.)
further is used for figurative or abstract extent, or to mean "additional." Let's discuss this further. Further questions go to the office.
In everyday American usage further is sometimes used for distance too, but farther for distance is the traditional rule.

imply = to suggest something without saying it directly (done by the speaker or writer). Her smile implied she agreed.
infer = to conclude something from evidence or hints (done by the listener or reader). From her smile, I inferred she agreed.
The writer implies; the reader infers.

good is an adjective; it describes nouns. She is a good singer. The pizza tastes good (after a linking verb).
well is usually an adverb; it describes how something is done. She sings well.
well can also be an adjective meaning healthy: I don't feel well.
Wrong: He played good. Right: He played well.

breath (noun, short e sound, rhymes with death) = the air you take in or let out. Take a deep breath.
breathe (verb, long e sound, ends in -e) = to take air in and out. Remember to breathe slowly.

cite (verb) = to quote or name a source as evidence. Cite three sources in your essay.
site (noun) = a location, including a website. the construction site, a news site.
sight (noun) = the ability to see, or something seen. The sunset was a beautiful sight.

Introduction: a hook to grab attention, brief background, and a thesis statement (usually the last sentence) that states the main claim and often previews the points.
Body paragraphs (often three): each begins with a topic sentence that supports the thesis, then gives evidence (facts, examples, quotations), explains how the evidence supports the point (analysis), and ends with a concluding or transition sentence.
Conclusion: restates the thesis in new words, sums up the main points, and ends with a final thought (why it matters, a call to action, or a broader connection). Do not add brand-new evidence.
Longer essays follow the same pattern with more body paragraphs. A common body-paragraph pattern is claim, evidence, reasoning (CER).

a: how to write a thesis statement
x:
A thesis statement is one or two sentences, usually at the end of the introduction, that state the essay's main argument or point.
A strong thesis is specific, arguable (a reasonable person could disagree), and can be supported with evidence.
Weak: The Great Gatsby is a book about the 1920s. (a fact, not an argument)
Stronger: In The Great Gatsby, Fitzgerald uses Gatsby's failed pursuit of Daisy to show that wealth cannot buy the past or social acceptance.
Formula to start: In [text/topic], [author/subject] [shows/argues] [claim] because/through [reasons].
Avoid announcing ("In this essay I will...") unless your teacher allows it.

A topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph, usually as its first sentence. In an essay, each topic sentence should connect back to the thesis.
Example thesis: School should start later because teens need more sleep and learn better later in the day.
Example topic sentence: First, a later start time would let teenagers get the sleep their bodies need.
Every other sentence in the paragraph should support the topic sentence.

A hook is the opening sentence(s) of an essay, meant to catch the reader's interest. Common types:
1. A surprising fact or statistic (make sure it is accurate and cited).
2. A question that makes the reader think.
3. A brief anecdote or scene.
4. A relevant quotation (cited).
5. A bold statement or a common belief you will challenge.
After the hook, give context, then the thesis. Avoid dictionary definitions and very broad openers like "Since the beginning of time."

In an argumentative essay, a counterargument (counterclaim) is a reasonable opposing view; the rebuttal explains why your position is still stronger.
Pattern: Some people argue that [opposing view]. While [concede what is fair], [evidence and reasoning for your side].
Example: Some argue that later start times would make after-school sports end too late. However, schools that shifted schedules can adjust practice times, and the benefits of more sleep outweigh the inconvenience.
Addressing the other side fairly builds credibility (ethos).

Transitions show how ideas connect.
Adding: also, furthermore, moreover, in addition, additionally.
Contrasting: however, on the other hand, in contrast, nevertheless, although.
Cause and effect: therefore, as a result, consequently, thus, because.
Examples: for example, for instance, specifically, to illustrate.
Sequence: first, next, then, finally, meanwhile, afterward.
Concluding: in conclusion, overall, ultimately, in summary.
Punctuation: a transition that joins two independent clauses needs a semicolon before and a comma after it (I was tired; however, I kept going).

Quoting: copying a source's exact words inside quotation marks.
Paraphrasing: restating a specific passage completely in your own words and sentence structure, about the same length as the original.
Summarizing: stating only the main ideas of a source in your own words, much shorter than the original.
All three require a citation. Using someone else's words or ideas without credit is plagiarism.
Tip: to paraphrase, read the passage, look away, write it from memory, then check that you did not copy phrases.

MLA (9th edition) in-text citations usually give the author's last name and the page number in parentheses, with no comma and no "p." between them.
One author: (Morrison 45)
Two authors: (Smith and Lopez 112)
Three or more authors: (Nguyen et al. 30)
Author named in your sentence: Morrison argues that ... (45).
No author: use a shortened title in quotation marks or italics: ("Rising Seas" 4)
No page numbers (most websites): just the author: (Patel)
The period goes after the closing parenthesis. Every in-text citation must match an entry on the Works Cited page.

MLA 9 pattern for a book with one author:
Last name, First name. Title of Book. Publisher, Year.
Example (made-up book): Rivera, Ana. The Quiet River. Harbor Press, 2019.
The book title is italicized (underline it if handwriting).
Two authors: Rivera, Ana, and Sam Cole. Title. ...
Three or more: Rivera, Ana, et al. Title. ...
MLA 9 does not require the city of publication for most books.

MLA 9 pattern for a page on a website:
Last name, First name. "Title of Page or Article." Name of Website, Publisher (if different from the website name), Day Month Year published, URL.
Example (made-up page): Chen, Lily. "How Bees Communicate." Nature Notes, 12 Mar. 2021, www.naturenotes.example/bees.
The page title goes in quotation marks; the website name is italicized.
If there is no author, start with the title. If there is no date, add an access date at the end: Accessed 5 Oct. 2024.
MLA abbreviates months longer than four letters (Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec.). The http:// or https:// may be left off the URL.

t: MLA Works Cited page and paper format
x:
Works Cited page: starts on a new page at the end; the title Works Cited is centered (not bold or underlined); entries are double-spaced, alphabetized by the first word (usually the author's last name), with a hanging indent of 0.5 inch (the second and later lines are indented).
MLA paper basics: 1-inch margins; double-spaced throughout; a readable 12-point font such as Times New Roman.
First-page heading at the top left, each on its own line: your name, instructor's name, course, date (day month year, e.g., 4 May 2025). Then the title, centered.
Header: your last name and the page number in the top right corner of every page.

Aristotle described three main modes of persuasion:
Ethos: appeal to credibility or character. The speaker shows they are trustworthy or qualified. Example: "As a nurse for twenty years, I have seen..."
Pathos: appeal to emotion. The speaker makes the audience feel something (fear, pity, pride, hope). Example: a story about a lost puppy to encourage donations.
Logos: appeal to logic and evidence. The speaker uses facts, statistics, reasoning, and examples. Example: "Students who slept eight hours scored higher on average."
Strong arguments usually combine all three. Kairos, a related idea, means choosing the right moment or timing for an argument.

When analyzing a persuasive text, identify its rhetorical situation. One common acronym is SOAPSTone:
Speaker: who is writing or speaking, and their background.
Occasion: the time, place, and event that prompted it.
Audience: who it is intended for.
Purpose: what the speaker wants the audience to think or do.
Subject: the topic.
Tone: the speaker's attitude, shown through word choice.
A rhetorical analysis explains how the speaker's choices (appeals, diction, structure) work to achieve the purpose for that audience.

Ad hominem (Latin for "to the person") attacks the person making an argument instead of the argument itself.
Example: "Why should we listen to Jordan's idea for the budget? He can't even keep his locker clean."
Jordan's locker has nothing to do with whether the budget idea is good.

A straw man misrepresents or exaggerates someone's argument to make it easier to attack.
Example: Student: "We should have fewer homework assignments on weekends." Reply: "So you think students should never have to do any work at all?"
The reply attacks a position the student never took.

A slippery slope claims that one small step will inevitably lead to a chain of extreme consequences, without evidence for each step.
Example: "If we let students use phones at lunch, soon they'll use them in every class, nobody will learn anything, and the school will fail."
Each link in the chain needs its own support; the fallacy assumes them all.

A false dilemma presents only two options when more actually exist.
Example: "Either you join the soccer team or you don't care about school spirit."
Someone could show school spirit in many other ways.

A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from too little or unrepresentative evidence.
Example: "I met two rude people from that town, so everyone there must be rude."
Two people are not enough to judge a whole population.

This fallacy treats a claim as true just because someone famous or in authority says so, especially when that person is not an expert on the topic.
Example: "A famous basketball player says this cereal improves memory, so it must work."
Citing real experts in their own field is reasonable evidence; the fallacy is relying on authority alone or on irrelevant authority.

The bandwagon fallacy (appeal to popularity, or ad populum) argues that something is true or good because many people believe or do it.
Example: "Everyone at school has these sneakers, so they must be the best."
Popularity alone does not prove quality or truth.

Circular reasoning uses the conclusion as one of its own premises, so the argument goes in a circle.
Example: "This book is the best in the series because it is better than all the others."
The reason just restates the claim. The formal term is "begging the question."

A red herring brings up an irrelevant topic to distract from the real issue.
Example: When asked why her group's project was late, a student says, "Well, the cafeteria food has been terrible all week."
The cafeteria food has nothing to do with the deadline.

Post hoc ergo propter hoc (Latin: "after this, therefore because of this") assumes that because one event happened after another, the first caused the second.
Example: "I wore my lucky socks and we won the game, so the socks made us win."
Timing alone does not prove cause. A related error is assuming that correlation proves causation.

An appeal to ignorance argues that a claim is true because it has not been proven false, or false because it has not been proven true.
Example: "No one has proven that my plan won't work, so it will definitely work."
A lack of evidence against something is not evidence for it.

Tu quoque (Latin for "you too") dismisses a criticism by pointing out that the critic does the same thing, instead of answering the criticism.
Example: "You can't tell me to stop eating junk food; you ate chips yesterday."
Even if the critic is inconsistent, the original point may still be valid.

This fallacy tries to win an argument by stirring up emotions (pity, fear, anger) instead of giving relevant reasons.
Example: "You have to give me an A. If you don't, I'll be so upset, and my whole summer will be ruined."
Using pathos is not always a fallacy; it becomes one when emotion replaces evidence the argument actually needs.

A metaphor compares two unlike things by saying one thing IS another, without using "like" or "as."
Example: The classroom was a zoo after the bell rang.
An extended metaphor carries the comparison through several lines or a whole work.
Difference from a simile: a simile uses "like" or "as" (The classroom was like a zoo).

A simile compares two unlike things using "like" or "as."
Examples: Her voice was as soft as a feather. The runners scattered like startled pigeons.
A comparison of two similar things (My bike is like your bike) is not a simile, because a simile compares things that are basically different.

Personification gives human qualities, actions, or feelings to something that is not human (an animal, object, or idea).
Examples: The old car groaned up the hill. The wind whispered through the empty hallway.

Hyperbole is deliberate, extreme exaggeration for emphasis or humor; it is not meant to be taken literally.
Examples: This backpack weighs a ton. I have told you a million times to close the door.

Alliteration is the repetition of the same beginning consonant sound in words that are close together.
Example: Sixteen sleepy seals slid silently into the sea.
It is about sound, not spelling: "kind cats" alliterates (both start with a k sound).

Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words, usually inside the words.
Example: The rain in late May came again. (repeated long a sound)
It creates rhythm and musical effect without full rhyme.

Consonance is the repetition of consonant sounds in nearby words, especially at the ends or in the middle of words.
Example: Mike likes his bike and kite. (repeated k sound)
Alliteration is a special kind of consonance where the repeated sound is at the beginning of words.

Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates the sound it describes.
Examples: buzz, sizzle, crash, hiss, thump, meow, splash.
Sentence: The bacon sizzled while rain pattered on the window.

Imagery is descriptive language that appeals to the five senses: sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
Example: The kitchen smelled of warm cinnamon, and the crust crackled as I broke the cold, sticky bun in half.
Imagery helps readers picture a scene and often builds mood.

A symbol is a person, object, color, or event that stands for a larger idea beyond its literal meaning.
Example (original): In a story, a character keeps her late grandmother's broken watch; the stopped watch can symbolize her wish to stop time and hold on to the past.
Common symbols: a dove for peace, a journey for personal growth, winter for death or hardship. Meaning depends on context in the work.

Foreshadowing is a hint or clue about what will happen later in a story.
Example: Before the hikers set out, the ranger mentions that the old bridge "hasn't been checked in years." Later, the bridge collapses.
Foreshadowing builds suspense and makes later events feel connected.

A flashback interrupts the present action of a story to show an event that happened earlier.
Example: As Maya stands at the starting line, the story shifts back to the day years ago when she first fell trying to run.
Flashbacks give background and explain characters' motives. The opposite device, showing a future event, is a flash-forward.

Verbal irony is when a speaker says the opposite of, or something different from, what they actually mean.
Example: Stepping into a pouring storm, Leo says, "Lovely weather for a picnic."
Sarcasm is a harsh or mocking kind of verbal irony.

Situational irony is when the outcome of a situation is the opposite of what was expected.
Example: A fire station burns down. Or: a student spends all night writing a speech about the importance of sleep and falls asleep during the assembly.

Dramatic irony is when the audience or reader knows something that a character does not.
Example: Readers know the surprise party guests are hiding behind the couch, but the main character walks in complaining that everyone forgot her birthday.
It creates suspense or humor. It is common in drama; in Romeo and Juliet, the audience knows Juliet is not truly dead when Romeo finds her.

An allusion is a brief, indirect reference to a well-known person, place, event, or work of literature, art, history, or mythology.
Example: "Don't open that closet; it's a real Pandora's box." (alludes to the Greek myth of Pandora)
Allusions rely on the reader recognizing the reference.

An oxymoron places two contradictory words side by side.
Examples: deafening silence, jumbo shrimp, bittersweet, original copy, cruel kindness.
Compare paradox, which is a whole statement that seems contradictory.

A paradox is a statement that seems to contradict itself but reveals a deeper truth.
Example: "The more I learn, the less I realize I know."
An oxymoron is a two-word contradiction; a paradox is a contradictory idea or statement.

Juxtaposition places two contrasting things (characters, images, ideas, settings) side by side to highlight their differences.
Example: A story opens with a lavish wedding feast in a mansion, then cuts to a family sharing one loaf of bread outside its gates.

A motif is a recurring image, object, phrase, or idea in a work that helps develop its theme.
Example: In an original story about grief, rain falls in every scene where the main character remembers her brother.
A motif repeats; a symbol may appear only once. A motif supports a theme but is not the theme itself.

Theme is the central message or insight about life or human nature that a work expresses.
Topic vs. theme: a topic is one or two words (friendship); a theme is a complete statement (True friendship requires sacrifice).
To find a theme, ask what the main character learns, how conflicts are resolved, and what ideas repeat.
A work can have more than one theme, and themes are usually implied rather than stated directly.

Tone is the author's or speaker's attitude toward the subject or audience, shown through word choice (diction), details, and style.
Tone words: sarcastic, admiring, bitter, playful, formal, nostalgic, critical, hopeful, somber.
Example: "Oh, another meeting. How wonderful." has a sarcastic tone.
Tone is the writer's attitude; mood is the reader's feeling.

Mood (atmosphere) is the feeling a work creates in the reader.
Writers build mood through setting, imagery, and word choice.
Example: The hallway was silent except for a dripping pipe; one flickering bulb cast long shadows. (mood: tense, eerie)
Mood words: suspenseful, gloomy, peaceful, joyful, tense, mysterious, romantic.

Diction is an author's choice of words. It can be formal or informal, concrete or abstract, plain or ornate.
Connotation (feelings a word carries) matters: "thrifty" sounds positive, "stingy" sounds negative, though both mean careful with money (denotation = dictionary meaning).
Analyzing diction means explaining how specific word choices create tone, mood, or characterization.

A euphemism is a mild or indirect word or phrase used in place of one that seems harsh, blunt, or unpleasant.
Examples: "passed away" for died, "let go" for fired, "between jobs" for unemployed.

Understatement deliberately presents something as less important or serious than it is, often for humor or emphasis. It is the opposite of hyperbole.
Example: After a hurricane flattens his house, a man says, "Well, it's a bit drafty."
Litotes is a type of understatement that uses a negative to express a positive: "She's not a bad singer" (meaning she is good).

Anaphora is the repetition of the same word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses, sentences, or lines.
Example: We will study harder. We will practice longer. We will win this year.
It is common in speeches and poetry for emphasis and rhythm.

As a literary device, apostrophe is when a speaker directly addresses someone absent or dead, or something nonhuman, as if it could hear and answer.
Example: "Oh, stubborn alarm clock, why must you ring so early?"
It is different from the apostrophe punctuation mark.

Synecdoche uses a part to stand for the whole (or the whole for a part). Example: "All hands on deck" (hands = sailors); "nice wheels" (wheels = car).
Metonymy uses something closely associated with a thing to stand for it. Example: "The White House announced..." (meaning the president's administration); "The pen is mightier than the sword" (pen = writing, sword = force).

Characterization is how an author reveals a character's personality.
Direct characterization: the narrator tells us outright. "Tom was greedy."
Indirect characterization: the reader infers traits from evidence. A common acronym is STEAL:
Speech (what the character says), Thoughts, Effect on others (how others react), Actions, Looks (appearance).
Example of indirect: Tom grabbed the last three cookies before anyone else could reach the plate.

Protagonist: the main character, whose goals and conflict drive the story.
Antagonist: the character or force that opposes the protagonist. It can be a person, nature, society, or something inside the protagonist.
The protagonist is not always good, and the antagonist is not always evil; the terms describe roles in the conflict.

t: Round, flat, static, and dynamic characters
x:
Round character: complex, with many traits; seems like a real person.
Flat character: simple, with one or two traits.
Dynamic character: changes in an important way during the story (often the protagonist).
Static character: stays basically the same from beginning to end.
A character can be round and static, or flat and static; most dynamic characters are round.

A foil is a character whose traits contrast with another character's, usually the protagonist's, to highlight the other character's qualities.
Example: In an original story, a cautious, rule-following twin is a foil to her reckless, impulsive sister.
In Romeo and Juliet, Mercutio's joking cynicism about love is often seen as a foil to Romeo's intense romanticism.

An archetype is a character type, plot pattern, symbol, or theme that recurs across many cultures and time periods.
Character archetypes: the hero, the mentor, the trickster, the innocent, the villain.
Situational archetypes: the quest, the journey, the battle of good versus evil, the fall from innocence.
The "hero's journey" (monomyth) is a common pattern described by Joseph Campbell in The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949).

An allegory is a story in which characters, events, and settings stand for abstract ideas or real historical or political situations, so the whole story has a second meaning.
Example: George Orwell's Animal Farm is an allegory of the Russian Revolution and the rise of the Soviet Union under Stalin.
An allegory is like an extended symbol that runs through the whole work.

Satire uses humor, irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to criticize people, institutions, or society, usually to provoke change.
Classic example: Jonathan Swift's essay "A Modest Proposal" (1729) shockingly "suggests" that poor Irish families sell their children as food, to attack the cruel treatment of the poor in Ireland.
Parody, which imitates a specific work or style for comic effect, is often used as a tool of satire.

In medias res (Latin for "into the middle of things") means a story begins in the middle of the action, and earlier events are filled in later, often through flashbacks.
Classic example: Homer's Odyssey begins near the end of Odysseus's ten-year journey home, and he later recounts earlier adventures.

In first-person point of view, the narrator is a character in the story and uses "I" or "we."
The reader learns only what this narrator sees, thinks, and chooses to tell.
Example: I knew the moment I opened the door that something was wrong.
Example in literature: Scout Finch narrates To Kill a Mockingbird; Nick Carraway narrates The Great Gatsby.

In third-person limited point of view, a narrator outside the story uses "he," "she," or "they" and shares the thoughts and feelings of only one character (or one at a time).
Example: Ana glanced at the clock. She hoped no one could tell how nervous she was.

In third-person omniscient point of view, an all-knowing narrator outside the story uses "he," "she," or "they" and can reveal the thoughts and feelings of any character.
Example: Ana hoped no one noticed her shaking hands, but across the room, Marcus had already seen them and felt sorry for her.
Third-person objective is a variation in which the narrator reports only actions and dialogue, revealing no character's thoughts.

In second-person point of view, the narrator addresses the reader as "you," placing the reader in the story.
Example: You open the door and step into the cold. You know you should turn back.
It is rare in novels but common in instructions and choose-your-own-adventure books.

An unreliable narrator is a narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted, because they are lying, biased, confused, mentally unstable, or too young or naive to understand events.
Example: The narrator of Edgar Allan Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart" insists he is sane while describing a murder and his growing panic.
Readers must look for clues that the narrator's version differs from what really happened.

A sonnet is a 14-line poem, traditionally written in iambic pentameter.
The Shakespearean (English) sonnet has three quatrains (four-line groups) followed by a rhyming couplet.
Rhyme scheme: ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.
The quatrains usually develop an idea or problem, and the final couplet often gives a twist, conclusion, or resolution (the "turn" or volta often comes at line 13).
William Shakespeare's 154 sonnets were published in 1609.

The Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet, named for the Italian poet Petrarch (1304-1374), has 14 lines divided into an octave (8 lines) and a sestet (6 lines).
Octave rhyme scheme: ABBAABBA.
Sestet rhyme schemes vary, commonly CDECDE or CDCDCD.
The octave usually presents a problem or question; the sestet responds to it. The shift between them, at line 9, is called the volta (turn).

An iamb is a metrical foot of two syllables: unstressed, then stressed (da-DUM), as in "a-WAY" or "to-DAY."
Pentameter means five feet per line.
So iambic pentameter is a line of ten syllables in five iambs: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM.
Original example: The WIND / was COLD / and DARK / the WIN/ter NIGHT.
It is the most common meter in English poetry and drama; Shakespeare's plays and sonnets use it heavily. Unrhymed iambic pentameter is called blank verse.

Meter is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of poetry. Each unit is a foot.
Iamb: unstressed-stressed (da-DUM): be-LIEVE
Trochee: stressed-unstressed (DUM-da): GAR-den
Anapest: unstressed-unstressed-stressed (da-da-DUM): in-ter-RUPT
Dactyl: stressed-unstressed-unstressed (DUM-da-da): BEAU-ti-ful
Spondee: stressed-stressed (DUM-DUM): HEART-BREAK
Number of feet per line: monometer 1, dimeter 2, trimeter 3, tetrameter 4, pentameter 5, hexameter 6.

A rhyme scheme is the pattern of end rhymes in a poem, marked with letters.
Give the first line's end sound A. Every later line that rhymes with it is also A. The next new sound is B, then C, and so on.
Example: The sun went down (A) / behind the hill (B) / across the town (A) / the air grew still (B). Rhyme scheme: ABAB.
Common schemes: couplets AABB, alternate ABAB, enclosed ABBA.
Kinds of rhyme: end rhyme (at line ends), internal rhyme (within a line), slant/near rhyme (similar but not identical sounds, like "worm" and "swarm").

Free verse: poetry with no regular meter and no regular rhyme scheme. Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass (first published 1855) is a famous early example.
Blank verse: poetry with a regular meter, usually unrhymed iambic pentameter. Much of Shakespeare's dialogue and John Milton's Paradise Lost are in blank verse.
Memory trick: blank verse is "blank" only of rhyme; free verse is free of both rhyme and meter.

A stanza is a group of lines in a poem, separated by a space, similar to a paragraph in prose.
Couplet: 2 lines. Tercet: 3 lines. Quatrain: 4 lines. Quintain (cinquain): 5 lines. Sestet: 6 lines. Septet: 7 lines. Octave: 8 lines.
A heroic couplet is a pair of rhyming lines in iambic pentameter.

Enjambment: a sentence or phrase runs past the end of a line onto the next line without punctuation.
Example: I waited by the window for / the letter that never came.
End-stopped line: a line that ends with punctuation and a natural pause.
Caesura: a strong pause in the middle of a line, often shown by punctuation (comma, period, dash). Example: I waited, and waited. Nothing came.

t: Poetic forms: haiku, limerick, ode, elegy, ballad, villanelle
x:
Haiku: a Japanese form; in English usually three lines of 5, 7, and 5 syllables, often about nature or a season.
Limerick: a humorous five-line poem with rhyme scheme AABBA.
Ode: a formal lyric poem praising or addressing a person, object, or idea.
Elegy: a poem of mourning for someone who has died, or reflecting on loss.
Ballad: a narrative poem, often in quatrains, that tells a story and was traditionally sung.
Villanelle: 19 lines (five tercets and a quatrain) with two refrains and only two rhyme sounds; rhyme scheme ABA ABA ABA ABA ABA ABAA.
Lyric poem: a short poem expressing personal feelings. Narrative poem: tells a story. Epic: a long narrative poem about a hero.

The speaker is the voice that "talks" in a poem. The speaker is not automatically the poet; a poet may write as an invented character or persona.
When analyzing a poem, write "the speaker says..." rather than "the poet says...," unless the poem is clearly autobiographical.

a: what is a refrain in poetry
x:
A refrain is a line or group of lines repeated at intervals in a poem or song, often at the end of each stanza.
It emphasizes an idea and creates rhythm. Villanelles and ballads often use refrains.

A tragedy is a serious drama in which the main character (the tragic hero) suffers a downfall, often death, partly caused by their own flaw or error.
Tragedies were developed in ancient Greece (Sophocles, Aeschylus, Euripides) and later by playwrights such as Shakespeare (Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet, Macbeth, Othello, King Lear).
Aristotle's Poetics, the earliest surviving major work on drama theory, discusses tragedy, including the ideas of hamartia and catharsis.

Tragic hero: a main character, often of high status, who is admirable but flawed and falls from fortune to misfortune.
Hamartia: the tragic flaw or error in judgment that leads to the hero's downfall.
Hubris: excessive pride or self-confidence, a common tragic flaw.
Anagnorisis: the moment the hero recognizes the truth of their situation.
Catharsis: the release of emotions (pity and fear) the audience feels at the end of a tragedy.
Example: Macbeth's ambition is usually described as his tragic flaw.

In classic drama, a comedy is a play with a light tone that ends happily, often with a marriage or reunion, rather than necessarily being full of jokes.
Shakespearean comedies (A Midsummer Night's Dream, Much Ado About Nothing, Twelfth Night) often feature mistaken identities, misunderstandings, young lovers facing obstacles, and a happy resolution.

Soliloquy: a long speech in which a character, alone on stage (or believing they are alone), speaks thoughts aloud so the audience hears them. Hamlet's "To be, or not to be" speech is a famous soliloquy.
Monologue: a long speech by one character delivered to other characters.
Aside: a short remark spoken to the audience (or to one character) that the other characters on stage supposedly cannot hear.
All three reveal a character's thoughts; the difference is who is listening.

Act: a major division of a play. Shakespeare's plays are printed in five acts.
Scene: a smaller division within an act, usually one time and place.
Dialogue: conversation between characters, the main way a play tells its story.
Stage directions: instructions in a script (often in italics or brackets) describing setting, movement, and tone.
Cast of characters (dramatis personae): the list of characters at the start.
Playwright: the author of a play. Script: the written text.
Chorus: in Greek drama, a group that comments on the action; Romeo and Juliet opens with a Chorus speaking a sonnet prologue.

Plot is the sequence of events in a story. Gustav Freytag's pyramid divides it into five parts:
1. Exposition: introduces characters, setting, and background.
2. Rising action: the conflict begins (often with an inciting incident) and tension builds through complications.
3. Climax: the turning point and moment of highest tension.
4. Falling action: events after the climax as the conflict winds down.
5. Resolution (denouement): loose ends are tied up and the story ends.

Conflict is the struggle between opposing forces that drives a plot.
Internal conflict: a struggle inside a character's mind. Character vs. self: a girl must decide whether to tell the truth about a friend.
External conflicts:
Character vs. character: two characters oppose each other.
Character vs. nature: a character struggles against nature (a storm, wilderness, animals). Hatchet by Gary Paulsen is a classic example.
Character vs. society: a character opposes laws, customs, or a community. Fahrenheit 451 is a classic example.
Character vs. technology, and character vs. the supernatural or fate, are sometimes added.

Setting is where and when a story takes place: the location, time period, season, time of day, and social environment.
Setting can create mood, shape characters' choices, and even act as an antagonist (for example, a harsh winter in a survival story).

Main genres: fiction, nonfiction, poetry, and drama.
Fiction subgenres: realistic fiction, historical fiction, science fiction, fantasy, mystery, horror, dystopian fiction, myth, fable, folktale.
Nonfiction subgenres: biography (a life story written by someone else), autobiography and memoir (written by the person), essay, journalism, speeches.
A novel is a long work of prose fiction; a novella is shorter; a short story can be read in one sitting.
Dystopian fiction depicts a society that seems ideal or controlled but is oppressive, as in 1984 and The Giver.

t: Making inferences and citing textual evidence
x:
An inference is a logical conclusion based on clues in the text plus your own knowledge. Clues + what I know = inference.
Example: A character slams the door and won't make eye contact; you can infer she is angry or upset.
Textual evidence supports a claim with specific details or quotations from the text, cited with page or line numbers.
Pattern: make a claim, give evidence, then explain how the evidence supports the claim.

Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare. Published/written: c. 1595 (first printed 1597). Genre: tragedy (play).
In Verona, two teenagers from feuding families, the Montagues and the Capulets, fall in love and secretly marry. A street fight, Romeo's banishment, and a failed plan involving a sleeping potion lead to both lovers' deaths, which finally reconciles the two families.
Main themes: love and haste, fate, family hatred and conflict, youth versus age.

Macbeth by William Shakespeare. Published/written: c. 1606. Genre: tragedy (play).
After three witches prophesy that he will become king of Scotland, the general Macbeth, urged on by Lady Macbeth, murders King Duncan and takes the throne. Guilt and paranoia drive him to more murders, Lady Macbeth dies, and Macbeth is killed in battle by Macduff.
Main themes: ambition, guilt, fate versus free will, appearance versus reality, the corrupting effect of power.

Hamlet by William Shakespeare. Published/written: c. 1600. Genre: tragedy (play).
Prince Hamlet of Denmark learns from his father's ghost that his uncle Claudius murdered the king, took the throne, and married Hamlet's mother, Gertrude. Hamlet's delayed and uncertain revenge leads to many deaths, including those of Polonius, Ophelia, Gertrude, Claudius, Laertes, and Hamlet himself.
Main themes: revenge, action versus indecision, mortality, madness, corruption.

Julius Caesar by William Shakespeare. Published/written: 1599. Genre: tragedy (play).
Fearing that Julius Caesar will become a tyrant, Roman senators led by Brutus and Cassius assassinate him. Mark Antony's funeral speech turns the crowd against the conspirators, civil war follows, and Brutus and Cassius die after their defeat at Philippi.
Main themes: power and ambition, honor, loyalty and betrayal, the power of rhetoric, fate.

The Odyssey, attributed to Homer. Published/written: around the 8th century BCE (exact date debated). Genre: ancient Greek epic poem.
After the Trojan War, the Greek hero Odysseus spends ten years trying to return home to Ithaca, facing monsters, gods, and temptations such as the Cyclops, the Sirens, and Circe, while his wife Penelope holds off suitors. He finally returns in disguise and, with his son Telemachus, defeats the suitors.
Main themes: homecoming, loyalty, cleverness, hospitality (xenia), perseverance, pride.

Beowulf by an unknown Anglo-Saxon poet. Published/written: composed sometime between about 700 and 1000 CE; survives in one manuscript from around 1000 CE. Genre: Old English epic poem.
The warrior Beowulf travels to Denmark and kills the monster Grendel and then Grendel's mother, saving King Hrothgar's mead hall. Decades later, as king of the Geats, he fights a dragon to protect his people and dies of his wounds.
Main themes: heroism, loyalty, fame and reputation, mortality, good versus evil.

a: who wrote oedipus rex (oedipus the king)
x:
Oedipus Rex (Oedipus the King) by Sophocles. Published/written: probably first performed around 429 BCE (exact date uncertain). Genre: ancient Greek tragedy (play).
King Oedipus of Thebes investigates the cause of a plague and discovers that he has unknowingly fulfilled a prophecy by killing his father and marrying his mother, Jocasta. Jocasta takes her own life, and Oedipus blinds himself and goes into exile.
Main themes: fate versus free will, the search for truth, pride (hubris), sight versus blindness.

Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen. Published/written: 1813. Genre: novel (romantic comedy of manners).
Elizabeth Bennet, one of five sisters in an English gentry family that needs its daughters to marry well, clashes with the proud, wealthy Mr. Darcy. As both overcome their misjudgments of each other, they fall in love and marry.
Main themes: pride, prejudice and first impressions, marriage, social class, reputation.

Frankenstein by Mary Shelley. Published/written: 1818. Genre: Gothic novel, often called an early work of science fiction.
The young scientist Victor Frankenstein brings a creature to life from dead body parts, then abandons it in horror. Rejected by everyone, the creature takes revenge by killing people Victor loves, and creator and creature pursue each other to the Arctic.
Main themes: dangerous ambition and knowledge, responsibility, isolation, nature versus nurture, what it means to be human.

Jane Eyre by Charlotte Bronte (Brontë). Published/written: 1847. Genre: novel (Gothic and coming-of-age).
Orphaned Jane survives a harsh childhood, becomes a governess at Thornfield Hall, and falls in love with her employer, Mr. Rochester, but learns on their wedding day that he is already married to a woman confined in the attic. She leaves, builds an independent life, and later returns to marry Rochester after a fire kills his wife and leaves him blind.
Main themes: independence, morality and integrity, social class, love, gender roles.

The Scarlet Letter by Nathaniel Hawthorne. Published/written: 1850. Genre: novel (historical fiction, American Romanticism).
In 17th-century Puritan Boston, Hester Prynne is forced to wear a scarlet letter A as punishment for adultery after giving birth to her daughter, Pearl, and she refuses to name the father. The father, the respected minister Arthur Dimmesdale, is destroyed by hidden guilt while Hester's husband, Roger Chillingworth, secretly seeks revenge.
Main themes: sin and guilt, hypocrisy, public versus private identity, judgment and redemption.

t: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (Frederick Douglass)

narrative of the life of frederick douglass, an american slave themes

Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave by Frederick Douglass. Published/written: 1845. Genre: autobiography (slave narrative).
Douglass describes his life enslaved in Maryland, the cruelty of slavery, and how he secretly taught himself to read and write. He tells of his escape to freedom (leaving out the details to protect those who helped) and his work as an abolitionist.
Main themes: literacy as a path to freedom, the dehumanizing effects of slavery, hypocrisy, identity and self-determination.

A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens. Published/written: 1843. Genre: novella.
On Christmas Eve, the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge is visited by the ghost of his former partner, Jacob Marley, and then by the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present, and Yet to Come. After seeing his life and a possible lonely death, he becomes generous and kind.
Main themes: redemption, generosity, poverty and social responsibility, family.

Great Expectations by Charles Dickens. Published/written: 1861 (serialized 1860-1861). Genre: novel (coming-of-age).
Pip, an orphan raised by his sister and her blacksmith husband, Joe, receives a fortune from a secret benefactor and goes to London to become a gentleman. He learns that his benefactor is Magwitch, a convict he helped as a child, not the wealthy Miss Havisham, and he comes to value loyalty and kindness over social status.
Main themes: ambition and social class, loyalty, guilt, self-improvement, appearance versus reality.

t: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (Mark Twain (Samuel Clemens))
a: who wrote adventures of huckleberry finn
x:
Adventures of Huckleberry Finn by Mark Twain (Samuel Clemens). Published/written: 1884 in Britain, 1885 in the United States. Genre: novel (satire, picaresque).
Huck Finn fakes his own death to escape his abusive father and travels down the Mississippi River on a raft with Jim, a man escaping slavery. Huck struggles with what society has taught him and decides to help Jim gain his freedom. (The novel's racial slurs and stereotypes have made it a frequent subject of debate in schools.)
Main themes: freedom, slavery and racism, individual conscience versus society, friendship, hypocrisy.

Little Women by Louisa May Alcott. Published/written: 1868-1869 (two volumes). Genre: novel (coming-of-age).
The four March sisters, Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy, grow up in Massachusetts while their father serves in the Union Army during the Civil War. The novel follows them through poverty, ambition, love, and loss, including Beth's death and Jo's growth as a writer.
Main themes: family, gender roles, growing up, work and ambition, sacrifice.

The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald. Published/written: 1925. Genre: novel.
Narrator Nick Carraway describes his mysterious, newly rich neighbor Jay Gatsby, who throws lavish parties on Long Island in the summer of 1922 hoping to win back Daisy Buchanan. Gatsby's dream collapses after Daisy, driving his car, kills Myrtle Wilson, and Myrtle's husband shoots Gatsby.
Main themes: the American Dream, wealth and social class, the impossibility of repeating the past, illusion versus reality, moral decay.

t: Their Eyes Were Watching God (Zora Neale Hurston)

Their Eyes Were Watching God by Zora Neale Hurston. Published/written: 1937. Genre: novel.
Janie Crawford tells her friend Pheoby the story of her life and three marriages in early-20th-century Florida, including years in the all-Black town of Eatonville. With her third husband, Tea Cake, she finds love and her own voice, but after a hurricane he is bitten by a rabid dog, and she is forced to kill him in self-defense and is acquitted at trial.
Main themes: independence and self-discovery, love, finding one's voice, gender roles, race.

a: who wrote of mice and men
x:
Of Mice and Men by John Steinbeck. Published/written: 1937. Genre: novella.
During the Great Depression in California, migrant ranch workers George Milton and Lennie Small, a large, strong man with an intellectual disability, dream of owning a small farm together. After Lennie accidentally kills Curley's wife, George shoots Lennie himself to spare him from an angry mob.
Main themes: dreams, friendship, loneliness, the strong versus the weak.

a: who wrote the grapes of wrath
x:
The Grapes of Wrath by John Steinbeck. Published/written: 1939. Genre: novel (won the 1940 Pulitzer Prize).
Forced off their Oklahoma farm during the Dust Bowl and the Great Depression, the Joad family travels to California hoping for work. They find poverty and exploitation in migrant camps, but the novel stresses family, solidarity, and human dignity.
Main themes: economic injustice, family, dignity, collective action, migration.

Animal Farm by George Orwell. Published/written: 1945. Genre: novella (political allegory, satire).
The animals of Manor Farm overthrow their human farmer to create a society of equals, but the pigs, led by Napoleon, gradually seize power and become as oppressive as the humans. The story is an allegory of the Russian Revolution and the Soviet Union under Stalin.
Main themes: power and corruption, propaganda, totalitarianism, class and inequality.

1984 (Nineteen Eighty-Four) by George Orwell. Published/written: 1949. Genre: dystopian novel.
Winston Smith works at the Ministry of Truth in Oceania, a totalitarian state ruled by the Party and its figurehead, Big Brother, where constant surveillance and propaganda control what people think. His secret rebellion and love affair with Julia end when he is arrested and tortured until he betrays her and accepts the Party.
Main themes: totalitarianism, surveillance, manipulation of truth and language (Newspeak), individuality.

Brave New World by Aldous Huxley. Published/written: 1932. Genre: dystopian novel.
In the future World State, people are produced in laboratories, conditioned into fixed social castes, and kept content with entertainment and a drug called soma. Bernard Marx and John, called "the Savage," who was raised outside this society, challenge its values, with tragic results for John.
Main themes: technology and control, happiness versus freedom, individuality, consumerism.

The Hobbit by J. R. R. Tolkien. Published/written: 1937. Genre: fantasy novel.
Bilbo Baggins, a comfort-loving hobbit, is recruited by the wizard Gandalf and thirteen dwarves to help reclaim their homeland and treasure from the dragon Smaug. On the journey he finds a magic ring, gains courage and cleverness, and helps bring peace at the Battle of Five Armies.
Main themes: courage, personal growth, greed, home.

t: The Diary of a Young Girl (Anne Frank)

The Diary of a Young Girl by Anne Frank. Published/written: first published in Dutch in 1947; in English in 1952. Genre: diary (nonfiction).
A Jewish teenager records her thoughts and daily life while hiding with her family and four others in a secret annex in Amsterdam from 1942 to 1944, during the Nazi occupation. The group was discovered and arrested in August 1944, and Anne died in the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in early 1945; her father, Otto, the only one of the group to survive, had the diary published.
Main themes: identity and growing up, hope, fear and confinement, prejudice, the Holocaust.

t: The Catcher in the Rye (J. D. Salinger)

The Catcher in the Rye by J. D. Salinger. Published/written: 1951. Genre: novel (coming-of-age).
Sixteen-year-old Holden Caulfield, expelled from his prep school, spends several days wandering New York City before going home. He criticizes what he sees as the fakeness of the adult world and wants to protect the innocence of children, especially his younger sister, Phoebe.
Main themes: alienation, innocence, identity, grief (his younger brother Allie has died).

t: The Old Man and the Sea (Ernest Hemingway)

The Old Man and the Sea by Ernest Hemingway. Published/written: 1952. Genre: novella (won the 1953 Pulitzer Prize).
Santiago, an aging Cuban fisherman who has gone 84 days without a catch, battles a giant marlin for days far out at sea and finally kills it. On the way back, sharks eat the marlin, leaving only its skeleton, but Santiago returns with his dignity intact.
Main themes: perseverance, pride, dignity in defeat, humans versus nature.

Fahrenheit 451 by Ray Bradbury. Published/written: 1953. Genre: dystopian novel.
In a future American society where books are banned, fireman Guy Montag's job is to burn them. Influenced by his curious young neighbor Clarisse and shaken by a woman who chooses to die with her books, he begins reading, rebels, and escapes to join exiles who memorize books to preserve them. (The title refers to the temperature at which the novel says paper burns.)
Main themes: censorship, knowledge, conformity, technology and mass media.

a: who wrote lord of the flies
x:
Lord of the Flies by William Golding. Published/written: 1954. Genre: novel (allegorical).
After a plane crash, a group of British schoolboys stranded on an uninhabited island try to govern themselves under Ralph, with help from the thoughtful Piggy. Order collapses as Jack and his hunters turn violent, Simon and Piggy are killed, and the survivors are finally rescued by a naval officer.
Main themes: civilization versus savagery, loss of innocence, human nature, power.

Night by Elie Wiesel. Published/written: published in Yiddish in 1956, in French in 1958, and in English in 1960. Genre: memoir.
Wiesel recounts how, as a teenager in 1944, he and his family were deported from their hometown of Sighet to Auschwitz, and his struggle to survive in Auschwitz and Buchenwald. His mother and younger sister are killed on arrival, and his father dies in Buchenwald in early 1945, a few months before the camp is liberated.
Main themes: faith and doubt, father-son bonds, dehumanization, survival, silence and memory.

Things Fall Apart by Chinua Achebe. Published/written: 1958. Genre: novel.
Okonkwo, a proud and respected leader in the Igbo village of Umuofia in what is now Nigeria, is exiled for seven years after accidentally killing a clansman's son. When he returns, Christian missionaries and a British colonial government have changed the community, and his resistance ends in tragedy.
Main themes: tradition versus change, colonialism, masculinity and pride, fate.

t: A Raisin in the Sun (Lorraine Hansberry)

A Raisin in the Sun by Lorraine Hansberry. Published/written: 1959. Genre: drama (play).
The Youngers, an African American family living in a crowded apartment on Chicago's South Side, disagree about how to use a $10,000 life-insurance payment. They decide to buy a house in an all-white neighborhood despite pressure to stay out. (The title comes from Langston Hughes's poem "Harlem.")
Main themes: dreams deferred, family, racial discrimination, pride and dignity.

A Separate Peace by John Knowles. Published/written: 1959. Genre: novel (coming-of-age).
At a New Hampshire boarding school during World War II, Gene Forrester's envy of his athletic best friend, Finny, leads him to jounce a tree branch, causing Finny to fall and shatter his leg. Finny later dies during surgery after a second fall, and an adult Gene looks back on his guilt.
Main themes: friendship and rivalry, guilt, loss of innocence, war.

a: who wrote to kill a mockingbird

To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee. Published/written: 1960. Genre: novel (won the 1961 Pulitzer Prize).
In 1930s Maycomb, Alabama, Scout Finch narrates as her father, lawyer Atticus Finch, defends Tom Robinson, a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. Although Tom is convicted, Scout and her brother, Jem, learn about prejudice, courage, and empathy, partly through their reclusive neighbor, Boo Radley.
Main themes: racism and injustice, moral courage, empathy, loss of innocence, coming of age.

The Outsiders by S. E. Hinton. Published/written: 1967. Genre: young adult novel.
Fourteen-year-old Ponyboy Curtis, a "greaser" in an Oklahoma city, narrates the rivalry between his gang and the wealthier Socs. After his friend Johnny kills a Soc in self-defense, events lead to a church-fire rescue and the deaths of Johnny and Dally, and Ponyboy realizes that people on both sides share the same struggles. Hinton began writing it as a teenager.
Main themes: social class, belonging and loyalty, family, innocence.

t: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (Maya Angelou)
