I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings by Maya Angelou. Published/written: 1969. Genre: autobiography (memoir).
Angelou describes growing up in Stamps, Arkansas, with her grandmother and brother, and later in St. Louis and California, facing racism and trauma, including sexual abuse as a young child, after which she stops speaking for years. With the help of mentors and a love of literature, she regains her voice and confidence, and the book ends as she becomes a young mother.
Main themes: identity, racism, resilience, the power of words and voice.

t: The House on Mango Street (Sandra Cisneros)

The House on Mango Street by Sandra Cisneros. Published/written: 1984. Genre: novel in vignettes (coming-of-age).
In short vignettes, Esperanza Cordero, a young Mexican American girl in a Latino neighborhood of a big city (modeled on Chicago), describes her family, neighbors, and growing up. She dreams of a house of her own and of leaving, while promising to come back for those who cannot leave.
Main themes: identity, home and belonging, gender roles, poverty, community.

Beloved by Toni Morrison. Published/written: 1987. Genre: novel (won the 1988 Pulitzer Prize).
In Ohio after the Civil War, Sethe, who escaped slavery, lives in a house haunted by the ghost of her baby daughter, whom she killed rather than let her be taken back into slavery. A young woman calling herself Beloved, who seems to be that daughter, arrives and forces Sethe to confront her past.
Main themes: the trauma of slavery, memory, motherhood, freedom and community.

Hatchet by Gary Paulsen. Published/written: 1987. Genre: young adult survival novel.
Thirteen-year-old Brian Robeson is the only survivor when a small plane crashes in the Canadian wilderness, and he has only the hatchet his mother gave him. Over 54 days he learns to make fire, find food, and survive, while coming to terms with a family secret about his parents' divorce.
Main themes: survival, self-reliance, humans and nature, growing up.

Number the Stars by Lois Lowry. Published/written: 1989. Genre: historical fiction (won the 1990 Newbery Medal).
In Nazi-occupied Copenhagen in 1943, ten-year-old Annemarie Johansen and her family help her Jewish best friend, Ellen Rosen, hide and escape to Sweden. The story is based on the real rescue of most of Denmark's Jews by boat in 1943.
Main themes: courage, friendship, sacrifice, the Holocaust.

The Giver by Lois Lowry. Published/written: 1993. Genre: dystopian young adult novel (won the 1994 Newbery Medal).
Jonas lives in a community that has eliminated pain, choice, and even color; at the Ceremony of Twelve he is chosen to be the next Receiver of Memory. Learning true memories from the Giver, he discovers that "release" means killing, and he escapes with the infant Gabriel.

The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins. Published/written: 2008. Genre: dystopian young adult novel.
In the nation of Panem, sixteen-year-old Katniss Everdeen volunteers to take her younger sister's place in a televised fight to the death run by the ruling Capitol. With Peeta Mellark, the other tribute from District 12, she survives by outwitting the Games and openly defies the Capitol.

t: The three branches of the US government
x:
The US Constitution separates power among three branches (separation of powers):
Legislative (Article I): Congress, made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Makes the laws.
Executive (Article II): the President, Vice President, and the executive departments (the Cabinet) and agencies. Carries out and enforces the laws.
Judicial (Article III): the Supreme Court and lower federal courts. Interprets the laws and decides cases.
Each branch can limit the others through checks and balances.

The House has 435 voting members (set by federal law at 435 since 1913, apart from a temporary increase to 437 after Alaska and Hawaii became states), plus 6 non-voting delegates (Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands).
Seats are divided among the states by population, recalculated after each census every 10 years. Every state has at least one.
Term: 2 years, with no term limit; all seats are up for election every two years.
Requirements: at least 25 years old, a US citizen for at least 7 years, and a resident of the state represented.
Special powers: all bills for raising revenue (taxes) must start in the House; the House alone can impeach (formally charge) federal officials by majority vote; it chooses the President if no candidate wins an Electoral College majority.
It is led by the Speaker of the House, elected by its members.

The Senate has 100 members, two from each of the 50 states.
Term: 6 years, with no term limit. Terms are staggered so about one-third of the seats are up for election every two years.
Senators have been elected directly by voters since the 17th Amendment (1913); before that, state legislatures chose them.
Requirements: at least 30 years old, a US citizen for at least 9 years, and a resident of the state represented.
Special powers: approves treaties (two-thirds vote needed); confirms presidential appointments such as federal judges, Cabinet members, and ambassadors (majority vote); holds the trial after a House impeachment (two-thirds vote needed to convict and remove).
The Vice President is President of the Senate but votes only to break a tie.

a: how long is a president term
x:
Term: 4 years. Under the 22nd Amendment (1951), no one may be elected President more than twice.
Requirements (Article II): a natural-born US citizen, at least 35 years old, and a US resident for at least 14 years.
Main powers: commander in chief of the armed forces; signs or vetoes bills passed by Congress; makes treaties (with the approval of two-thirds of the Senate); appoints federal judges, ambassadors, and Cabinet officers (with Senate confirmation); grants pardons and reprieves for federal crimes (except in cases of impeachment); gives Congress information on the State of the Union; issues executive orders to direct the executive branch.
The Cabinet includes the Vice President and the heads of the 15 executive departments (such as State, Treasury, Defense, and Justice, whose head is the Attorney General).

t: Vice President and presidential line of succession
a: who becomes president if the president dies
x:
The Vice President has the same age and citizenship requirements as the President, serves a 4-year term, presides over the Senate (voting only to break ties), and becomes President if the President dies, resigns, or is removed.
Under the Presidential Succession Act of 1947, the order after the Vice President is:
1. Speaker of the House
2. President pro tempore of the Senate
3. Secretary of State
4. Secretary of the Treasury
5. Secretary of Defense
6. Attorney General
...then the other Cabinet secretaries in the order their departments were created.
The 25th Amendment (1967) covers presidential disability and filling a vacancy in the vice presidency.

t: The judicial branch and the Supreme Court
x:
Article III creates the Supreme Court and lets Congress create lower federal courts.
The Supreme Court has 9 justices (one Chief Justice and eight associate justices). The Constitution does not set the number; Congress fixed it at nine in 1869.
Federal judges are nominated by the President, confirmed by the Senate, and serve "during good behavior," which in practice means for life unless they retire, resign, or are impeached and removed.
Lower federal courts: 94 district courts (trial courts) and 13 courts of appeals (circuit courts).
Judicial review, the power to strike down laws or government actions that violate the Constitution, was established in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
Most cases reach the Supreme Court on appeal; it chooses to hear only a small fraction of the cases it is asked to review.

Checks and balances let each branch limit the others so no branch becomes too powerful.
Legislative checks: can override a presidential veto (two-thirds of both houses); Senate confirms appointments and ratifies treaties; controls the budget; can impeach and remove the President and federal judges; can propose constitutional amendments.
Executive checks: the President can veto bills; appoints federal judges; can grant pardons.
Judicial checks: courts can declare laws and executive actions unconstitutional (judicial review).
Example: Congress passes a bill, the President vetoes it, and Congress overrides the veto; later, the Supreme Court could still rule the law unconstitutional.

t: How a bill becomes a law
a: how a bill becomes a law
x:
1. A member of Congress introduces a bill in the House or Senate (bills to raise revenue must start in the House).
2. The bill is sent to a committee, which studies it, may hold hearings, amends it, and votes on whether to send it to the full chamber. Most bills die in committee.
3. The full chamber debates and votes; a simple majority passes it. (In the Senate, ending a filibuster on most bills requires 60 votes for cloture.)
4. The other chamber repeats the process. Both chambers must pass identical text; differences may be worked out in a conference committee.
5. The bill goes to the President, who can sign it into law or veto it.
6. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate.
If the President does nothing for 10 days (not counting Sundays) while Congress is in session, the bill becomes law without a signature. If Congress adjourns during those 10 days, the unsigned bill dies (a pocket veto).

The President and Vice President are chosen by the Electoral College, not directly by the national popular vote.
Each state gets electors equal to its number of Representatives plus its 2 Senators; Washington, D.C., gets 3 (23rd Amendment).
Total: 435 + 100 + 3 = 538 electors. A candidate needs a majority, at least 270, to win.
Voters in each state choose a slate of electors. Forty-eight states and D.C. give all their electors to the statewide popular-vote winner; Maine and Nebraska split electors by congressional district.
Electors cast their votes in December, and Congress counts them in a joint session in early January.
If no candidate gets 270, the House chooses the President (each state delegation casts one vote) and the Senate chooses the Vice President (12th Amendment).
Election Day is the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. Five times (1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016) the winner did not win the national popular vote.

Federalism divides power between the national (federal) government and the state governments.
Delegated (enumerated) powers belong to the federal government: printing money, declaring war, making treaties, regulating interstate and foreign trade.
Reserved powers belong to the states (10th Amendment): running elections, setting up schools and local governments, issuing driver's licenses, most police powers.
Concurrent powers are shared: taxing, borrowing money, making and enforcing laws, establishing courts.
The Supremacy Clause (Article VI) makes the Constitution and valid federal laws the "supreme Law of the Land," so they override conflicting state laws.

a: what does each article of the constitution do
x:
The Constitution has a Preamble, seven articles, and 27 amendments.
Preamble: begins "We the People of the United States" and states its goals, including to form a more perfect Union, establish justice, and secure the blessings of liberty.
Article I: the legislative branch (Congress).
Article II: the executive branch (the President).
Article III: the judicial branch (the courts).
Article IV: relations among the states (such as "full faith and credit" for other states' public acts and records) and admitting new states.
Article V: how to amend the Constitution.
Article VI: the Constitution as the supreme law of the land; national debts; oaths of office; no religious test for public office.
Article VII: ratification by nine states.

t: How the Constitution is amended (Article V)
x:
Step 1, proposal (two ways):
a two-thirds vote of both the House and the Senate (used for all 27 amendments), or
a national convention called by two-thirds of the state legislatures (never used).
Step 2, ratification (two ways):
approval by three-fourths of the state legislatures (38 of 50 states), or
approval by conventions in three-fourths of the states (used only for the 21st Amendment).
The President has no formal role in the amendment process.
More than 11,000 amendments have been proposed in Congress, but only 27 have been ratified; the first ten are the Bill of Rights.

Popular sovereignty: the government's power comes from the people.
Limited government: the government has only the powers the Constitution gives it; leaders must obey the law (rule of law).
Separation of powers: power is divided among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches.
Checks and balances: each branch can limit the others.
Federalism: power is shared between the national and state governments.
Republicanism: citizens elect representatives to make decisions for them.
Individual rights: protected especially by the Bill of Rights.

a: when was the declaration of independence signed
who wrote the declaration of independence
x:
Adopted by the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776. Congress voted for independence on July 2; most delegates signed the engrossed copy on August 2, 1776. There were 56 signers in all.
Thomas Jefferson wrote the first draft for a Committee of Five (Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, and Robert R. Livingston).
Structure: an introduction; a statement of principles (all men are created equal and have unalienable rights including "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness," and governments get their power from the consent of the governed); a list of grievances against King George III; and a conclusion declaring the colonies free and independent states.
Its ideas about natural rights and the right to alter or abolish a bad government were influenced by the philosopher John Locke.

a: weaknesses of the articles of confederation
x:
The first US constitution. Approved by the Continental Congress in 1777; in force after all 13 states ratified it on March 1, 1781 (Maryland was last). Replaced by the Constitution in 1789.
It created a weak central government, a "league of friendship" among sovereign states:
one-house Congress in which each state had one vote; no President (no executive branch) and no national court system;
Congress could not tax or regulate trade between the states and could not force states to provide money or troops;
important laws needed 9 of 13 states, and amendments needed all 13.
Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787), an armed uprising of indebted farmers in Massachusetts, convinced many leaders that a stronger government was needed.
A success: the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 set up a process for admitting new states.

Delegates met in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787, originally to revise the Articles of Confederation; they wrote a new constitution instead. George Washington presided. James Madison, who kept detailed notes, is called the "Father of the Constitution."
Great (Connecticut) Compromise: a two-house Congress, with the House based on population (Virginia Plan) and equal representation in the Senate (New Jersey Plan).
Three-Fifths Compromise: three-fifths of the enslaved population of a state would be counted for representation in the House and for direct taxes.
The Constitution was signed by 39 delegates on September 17, 1787 (now Constitution Day). It took effect when New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify, on June 21, 1788, and the new government began operating in 1789. Delaware ratified first (December 7, 1787) and Rhode Island last (May 29, 1790).

t: Federalists, Anti-Federalists, and the Federalist Papers
x:
During the ratification debate (1787-1788), Federalists supported the new Constitution and a stronger national government; Anti-Federalists feared it gave the national government too much power and demanded a bill of rights.
The Federalist Papers are 85 essays published in New York newspapers in 1787-1788 under the pen name "Publius," written by Alexander Hamilton (most of them), James Madison, and John Jay, to persuade New Yorkers to ratify.
Well-known essays: No. 10 (Madison, on controlling factions in a large republic), No. 51 (Madison, on checks and balances and separation of powers), No. 78 (Hamilton, on the judiciary).
Anti-Federalist leaders included Patrick Henry and George Mason. Their pressure led to the Bill of Rights.

The Mayflower Compact was an agreement signed in November 1620 aboard the Mayflower, before the passengers went ashore at what became Plymouth Colony in present-day Massachusetts.
Forty-one adult male passengers agreed to form a "civil body politic" and to make and obey just and equal laws for the general good of the colony.
It is an early example of self-government and government by consent of the governed in the English colonies.

a: what did the emancipation proclamation do
x:
Issued by President Abraham Lincoln, taking effect January 1, 1863, during the Civil War (a preliminary version was announced in September 1862 after the Battle of Antietam).
It declared that enslaved people in the Confederate states still in rebellion "are, and henceforward shall be free."
It did not apply to the slaveholding border states loyal to the Union (such as Kentucky and Maryland) or to Confederate areas already under Union control, and it could be enforced only as Union armies advanced.
It also allowed Black men to enlist in the Union Army and Navy; about 180,000 served in the Army.
Slavery was abolished throughout the United States by the 13th Amendment, ratified in December 1865.

a: what was the gettysburg address about
four score and seven years ago
x:
Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of a national cemetery for Union soldiers at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, about four months after the Battle of Gettysburg (July 1-3, 1863).
It is only about 270 words long and took about two minutes to deliver. It begins "Four score and seven years ago" (87 years, meaning 1776).
Lincoln described the war as a test of whether a nation founded on liberty and equality could survive and called for "a new birth of freedom" and a government "of the people, by the people, for the people."

a: when was the bill of rights ratified
x:
The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution. James Madison drafted them; Congress proposed twelve amendments in September 1789, and ten were ratified on December 15, 1791.
1st: freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition
2nd: right to keep and bear arms
3rd: no forced quartering of soldiers in homes
4th: no unreasonable searches and seizures; warrants need probable cause
5th: grand jury, no double jeopardy, no forced self-incrimination, due process, just compensation
6th: speedy and public trial, impartial jury, right to a lawyer
7th: jury trial in many civil cases
8th: no excessive bail or fines; no cruel and unusual punishment
9th: listing some rights does not deny others kept by the people
10th: powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people

t: 1st Amendment (1791): freedoms of religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition
x:
Ratified 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights.
Congress may make no law: respecting an establishment of religion (Establishment Clause) or prohibiting the free exercise of religion (Free Exercise Clause); abridging the freedom of speech or of the press; or limiting the right of the people peaceably to assemble and to petition the government for a redress of grievances.
Through the 14th Amendment, these limits also apply to state and local governments.
These rights are not unlimited; for example, the Supreme Court has allowed limits on true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, defamation, and obscenity.

t: 2nd Amendment (1791): right to keep and bear arms
x:
Ratified 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights.
Text: "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed."
In District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), the Supreme Court held that it protects an individual's right to keep a handgun at home for self-defense; McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010) applied it to the states.
The Court has said the right is not unlimited, and the scope of permissible regulation remains a subject of ongoing legal and political debate.

Ratified 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights.
No soldier may be housed (quartered) in any house in peacetime without the owner's consent, nor in wartime except as prescribed by law.
It responded to British laws such as the Quartering Acts before the American Revolution. It is one of the least-litigated amendments.

t: 4th Amendment (1791): no unreasonable searches and seizures
x:
Ratified 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights.
Protects people's persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures.
Warrants may be issued only upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, and must describe the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized.
Related cases: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) applied the exclusionary rule (illegally obtained evidence cannot be used at trial) to the states; New Jersey v. T.L.O. (1985) allowed school officials to search students with "reasonable suspicion."

t: 5th Amendment (1791): rights of the accused; due process; takings
7th Amendment (1791): jury trial in civil cases
x:
Ratified 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights.
In federal civil lawsuits at common law where the value in controversy exceeds twenty dollars, the right to a jury trial is preserved.
A fact decided by a jury cannot be re-examined by another federal court except according to the rules of common law.
The Supreme Court has not applied this amendment to the states.

t: 8th Amendment (1791): no excessive bail or cruel and unusual punishment
x:
Ratified 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights.
Excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted.
Courts interpret "cruel and unusual" using evolving standards; for example, the Supreme Court has ruled that the death penalty cannot be applied to people who were under 18 when they committed their crimes (Roper v. Simmons, 2005).

t: 9th Amendment (1791): rights retained by the people
x:
Ratified 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights.
The listing of certain rights in the Constitution shall not be interpreted to deny or weaken other rights kept by the people.
It answered the concern that a list of rights might be read as the complete list.

t: 10th Amendment (1791): powers reserved to the states or the people
x:
Ratified 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights.
Powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the states, are reserved to the states respectively, or to the people.
It is the constitutional basis for reserved powers in federalism (such as states running schools and elections).

t: 11th Amendment (1795): limits on lawsuits against states
x:
Ratified 1795.
Federal courts may not hear lawsuits against a state brought by citizens of another state or by citizens or subjects of a foreign country.
It overturned the Supreme Court's decision in Chisholm v. Georgia (1793), which had allowed such a suit.

t: 12th Amendment (1804): separate electoral votes for President and Vice President
x:
Ratified 1804.
Electors cast separate ballots for President and Vice President. Before this, the runner-up became Vice President, which produced the 1800 tie between Thomas Jefferson and Aaron Burr, who were running mates.
If no candidate wins a majority of electoral votes, the House of Representatives chooses the President from the top three, with each state delegation having one vote, and the Senate chooses the Vice President.

Ratified December 1865, after the Civil War. First of the three Reconstruction Amendments (13th, 14th, 15th).
Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime of which the person has been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States or any place subject to its jurisdiction.
Congress has the power to enforce it with legislation.

t: 14th Amendment (1868): citizenship, due process, and equal protection
x:
Ratified 1868 as a Reconstruction Amendment.
Section 1: all persons born or naturalized in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens of the United States and of the state where they live. No state may abridge the privileges or immunities of citizens, deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, or deny any person the equal protection of the laws.
Other sections dealt with counting population for House seats, barred certain former officials who joined the rebellion from office, and addressed Civil War debts.
It is one of the most cited parts of the Constitution: courts have used its Due Process Clause to apply most of the Bill of Rights to the states (incorporation), and its Equal Protection Clause in cases such as Brown v. Board of Education (1954).

t: 15th Amendment (1870): voting rights regardless of race
x:
Ratified 1870 as the last of the Reconstruction Amendments.
The right of citizens to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any state on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.
Many states later used poll taxes, literacy tests, and intimidation to keep Black citizens from voting; the Voting Rights Act of 1965 was passed to enforce the amendment more effectively.

Ratified 1913.
Congress has the power to lay and collect taxes on incomes, from whatever source derived, without dividing them among the states according to population.
It overcame the Supreme Court's 1895 ruling in Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co., which had struck down a federal income tax.

Ratified 1913.
US senators are elected directly by the voters of each state, instead of being chosen by state legislatures as Article I originally required.
It also allows a state's governor to make a temporary appointment to fill a vacancy if the state legislature permits.

Ratified January 1919; took effect in January 1920.
Banned the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors in the United States. The era is called Prohibition.
It was repealed by the 21st Amendment in 1933. It is the only amendment ever repealed.

Ratified August 1920.
The right of citizens to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any state on account of sex.
It followed decades of activism by the women's suffrage movement, including leaders such as Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton (both of whom died before it passed), and later Alice Paul and Carrie Chapman Catt. Tennessee was the 36th and deciding state to ratify.

t: 20th Amendment (1933): "Lame Duck" Amendment: start dates of terms
x:
Ratified January 1933.
Moved the start of the President's and Vice President's terms to noon on January 20, and the start of Congress's terms to noon on January 3, shortening the "lame duck" period after elections (terms formerly began on March 4).
It also covers what happens if a President-elect dies before taking office.

Ratified December 1933.
Repealed the 18th Amendment, ending national Prohibition, while allowing states to keep their own controls on alcohol.
It is the only amendment ratified by state ratifying conventions rather than by state legislatures, and the only one that repeals another amendment.

a: how many terms can a president serve
x:
Ratified 1951.
No person shall be elected President more than twice. A person who served more than two years of another President's term may be elected only once, so the maximum is about 10 years in office.
It followed Franklin D. Roosevelt's election to four terms (1932, 1936, 1940, 1944); before that, presidents had followed George Washington's two-term tradition.

t: 23rd Amendment (1961): electoral votes for Washington, D.C.
x:
Ratified 1961.
Gives the District of Columbia electors in presidential elections, as many as it would have if it were a state, but no more than the least populous state. In practice this is 3 electors.
It does not give D.C. voting representation in Congress.

t: 24th Amendment (1964): ban on poll taxes in federal elections
x:
Ratified 1964.
The right to vote in federal elections (for President, Vice President, and Congress) shall not be denied because of failure to pay a poll tax or any other tax.
Poll taxes had been used, especially in the South, to keep poor and Black citizens from voting. In 1966 (Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections) the Supreme Court ruled that poll taxes in state elections also violate the Equal Protection Clause.

Ratified 1967, after President John F. Kennedy's assassination.
If the President is removed, dies, or resigns, the Vice President becomes President.
If the vice presidency is vacant, the President nominates a Vice President, who takes office after confirmation by a majority of both houses of Congress (used for Gerald Ford in 1973 and Nelson Rockefeller in 1974).
The President can declare himself temporarily unable to serve, making the Vice President Acting President; the Vice President and a majority of the Cabinet can also declare the President unable to serve, with Congress deciding any dispute.

Ratified 1971, the fastest ratification of any amendment (just over three months).
The right of citizens who are 18 years of age or older to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any state on account of age.
Supporters argued that people old enough to be drafted to fight in the Vietnam War should be able to vote.

Ratified 1992, the most recent amendment.
Any law changing the salary of members of Congress cannot take effect until after the next election of Representatives.
It was first proposed by James Madison in 1789 as part of the original package of twelve amendments, but it was not ratified by enough states until 1992, more than 202 years later, helped by a campaign started by college student Gregory Watson in 1982.

Marbury v. Madison (1803)
Question: William Marbury, appointed a justice of the peace in the last days of John Adams's presidency, never received his commission and asked the Supreme Court to order Secretary of State James Madison to deliver it. Could the Court issue that order?
Holding: Unanimous; opinion by Chief Justice John Marshall. Marbury had a right to his commission, but the section of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that let him bring the case directly to the Supreme Court was unconstitutional, so the Court could not issue the order.
Significance: Established judicial review: the power of federal courts to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution.

McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
Question: Could Congress create a national bank (the Second Bank of the United States), and could Maryland tax it?
Holding: Unanimous; opinion by Chief Justice John Marshall. Yes, Congress could create the bank under its implied powers from the Necessary and Proper Clause. No, a state cannot tax a federal institution, because "the power to tax involves the power to destroy."
Significance: Strengthened federal power, implied powers, and the Supremacy Clause.

Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
Question: Could New York grant a monopoly on steamboat travel between New York and New Jersey, against a boat operator licensed under federal law?
Holding: Unanimous; opinion by Chief Justice John Marshall. Congress's power to regulate interstate commerce includes navigation, and the federal license overrode the conflicting New York monopoly.
Significance: Gave a broad reading to the Commerce Clause and established federal authority over interstate commerce.

Worcester v. Georgia (1832)
Question: Could Georgia enforce its laws inside the Cherokee Nation's territory?
Holding: Opinion by Chief Justice John Marshall: no. The Cherokee Nation was a distinct political community, and only the federal government could deal with it; Georgia's laws had no force there.
Significance: President Andrew Jackson and Georgia did not enforce the ruling, and the Cherokee were forcibly removed on the Trail of Tears (1838-1839).

Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
Question: Dred Scott, an enslaved man who had lived for years in a free state and a free territory, sued for his freedom. Could he sue in federal court, and could Congress ban slavery in the territories?
Holding: 7-2; opinion by Chief Justice Roger Taney. People of African descent, whether enslaved or free, were not US citizens and could not sue in federal court; Congress had no power to ban slavery in the territories, so the Missouri Compromise ban was unconstitutional.
Significance: Widely considered one of the worst decisions in the Court's history; it deepened the sectional crisis before the Civil War and was overturned by the 13th and 14th Amendments.

Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
Question: Homer Plessy challenged a Louisiana law requiring separate railway cars for white and Black passengers. Did state-required racial segregation violate the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause?
Holding: 7-1: no. The Court upheld segregation under the doctrine of "separate but equal." Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented, writing that the Constitution is color-blind.
Significance: Allowed legal segregation (Jim Crow laws) for decades; overturned for public education by Brown v. Board of Education (1954).

Schenck v. United States (1919)
Question: Charles Schenck was convicted under the Espionage Act for distributing leaflets urging men to resist the World War I draft. Did his conviction violate the First Amendment?
Holding: Unanimous: no. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that speech can be punished if it creates a "clear and present danger" of harms Congress may prevent, comparing it to falsely shouting fire in a crowded theater.
Significance: Showed that free speech has limits; the clear-and-present-danger test was later replaced by the stricter "imminent lawless action" test in Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969).

Korematsu v. United States (1944)
Question: Fred Korematsu, a Japanese American citizen, refused to leave a West Coast area under a World War II military exclusion order. Was the order, which led to the incarceration of Japanese Americans, constitutional?
Holding: 6-3: yes, the Court upheld the exclusion order as a wartime necessity.
Significance: Now widely condemned. Korematsu's conviction was vacated by a federal court in 1983, the US government formally apologized and paid reparations under the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, and in Trump v. Hawaii (2018) the Court's majority stated that Korematsu was wrongly decided.

Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka (1954)
Question: Does racial segregation of children in public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment, even if facilities are supposedly equal?
Holding: Unanimous (9-0); opinion by Chief Justice Earl Warren: yes. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.
Significance: Overturned Plessy v. Ferguson in public education and was a landmark of the civil rights movement. Thurgood Marshall argued the case for the NAACP. A follow-up ruling (1955) ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed."

Mapp v. Ohio (1961)
Question: Can evidence obtained through an illegal search be used in a state criminal trial?
Holding: 6-3: no. The exclusionary rule, which bars illegally obtained evidence, applies to the states through the 14th Amendment.
Significance: Applied Fourth Amendment protections to state courts and changed police search practices nationwide.

Engel v. Vitale (1962)
Question: Does a public school's official, state-written daily prayer violate the First Amendment, even if participation is voluntary and the prayer is nondenominational?
Holding: 6-1: yes. Government-written, school-sponsored prayer violates the Establishment Clause.
Significance: A landmark ruling on religion in public schools. Students remain free to pray privately and voluntarily.

Gideon v. Wainwright (1963)
Question: Clarence Earl Gideon was denied a free lawyer and convicted in Florida. Must states provide a lawyer to defendants in felony cases who cannot afford one?
Holding: Unanimous: yes. The Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies to the states through the 14th Amendment.
Significance: Led to public defender systems across the country. Gideon was retried with a lawyer and acquitted.

New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964)
Question: Can a public official win a libel lawsuit over false statements in a newspaper ad about civil rights protests without proving the paper acted with bad intent?
Holding: Unanimous: no. A public official must prove "actual malice," meaning the publisher knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for whether it was true.
Significance: Greatly strengthened freedom of the press and of criticism of public officials.

Miranda v. Arizona (1966)
Question: Ernesto Miranda confessed during police questioning without being told of his rights. Must police inform suspects of their rights before custodial interrogation?
Holding: 5-4: yes. Under the Fifth Amendment, suspects in custody must be told before questioning that they have the right to remain silent, that anything they say can be used against them, and that they have the right to an attorney (appointed if they cannot afford one).
Significance: Created the "Miranda warnings" police give today.

Loving v. Virginia (1967)
Question: Richard Loving, a white man, and Mildred Loving, a woman of Black and Native American descent, were convicted under Virginia's ban on interracial marriage. Do such laws violate the 14th Amendment?
Holding: Unanimous: yes. Bans on interracial marriage violate both the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses.
Significance: Struck down such laws in the 16 states that still had them.

New York Times Co. v. United States (1971)
Question: Could the federal government stop newspapers from publishing the Pentagon Papers, a classified history of US involvement in Vietnam?
Holding: 6-3: no. The government had not met the heavy burden needed to justify prior restraint (censorship before publication).
Significance: A major ruling for freedom of the press.

Roe v. Wade (1973)
Question: Does the Constitution protect a woman's decision to have an abortion?
Holding: 7-2: the Court held that the right to privacy under the 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause included a right to choose abortion, with limits that increased during pregnancy.
Significance: One of the most debated decisions in US history. It was overruled in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022), which held that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion and returned the issue to the states and their elected representatives.

United States v. Nixon (1974)
Question: During the Watergate investigation, President Richard Nixon refused to turn over subpoenaed White House tape recordings, claiming executive privilege. Is that privilege absolute?
Holding: 8-0 (one justice did not take part): no. Executive privilege is not absolute and must yield to the need for evidence in a criminal trial; Nixon had to release the tapes.
Significance: Nixon resigned about two weeks later, on August 9, 1974. The case confirmed that the President is not above the law.

New Jersey v. T.L.O. (1985)
Question: Did a school official violate the Fourth Amendment by searching a student's purse without a warrant?
Holding: 6-3: no. The Fourth Amendment applies to public school officials, but they need only "reasonable suspicion," not a warrant or probable cause, to search a student.
Significance: Sets the standard for searches of students at school.

Question: Could a principal remove articles from a school-sponsored student newspaper?
Holding: 5-3: yes. Schools may control the content of school-sponsored student speech, such as newspapers produced in class, when the limits are reasonably related to legitimate educational concerns.
Significance: Narrowed student press rights for school-sponsored publications; Tinker still governs students' personal expression.

Texas v. Johnson (1989)
Question: Gregory Lee Johnson burned an American flag in protest outside the 1984 Republican National Convention in Dallas. Is flag burning protected by the First Amendment?
Holding: 5-4: yes. Burning the flag as political protest is symbolic speech protected by the First Amendment.
Significance: Congress then passed the Flag Protection Act of 1989, which the Court struck down in United States v. Eichman (1990).

Bush v. Gore (2000)
Question: In the close 2000 presidential election, could Florida continue the statewide manual recount ordered by the Florida Supreme Court?
Holding: The Court ruled 7-2 that the recount, with no uniform standards for counting ballots, raised equal protection problems, and 5-4 that no valid recount could be completed by the deadline, which ended the recount.
Significance: George W. Bush won Florida's electoral votes and the presidency; Al Gore conceded the next day.

On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus, an Italian (Genoese) navigator sailing for Spain's King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella, landed on an island in the Bahamas, believing he had reached Asia. His three ships were the Nina, the Pinta, and the Santa Maria.
He made four voyages in all (1492-1504). His arrival began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas, including the Columbian Exchange of plants, animals, people, and diseases.
Indigenous peoples had lived in the Americas for thousands of years, and Norse explorers led by Leif Erikson reached North America around 1000 CE. European colonization brought conquest, enslavement, and epidemics that devastated Native populations.

Founded in 1607 in Virginia by the Virginia Company of London, Jamestown was the first permanent English settlement in North America.
Early years brought disease, hunger, and conflict with the Powhatan Confederacy; the winter of 1609-1610 is known as the "Starving Time." Leaders included John Smith.
Tobacco, introduced as a cash crop by John Rolfe around 1612, made the colony profitable. Rolfe married Pocahontas, daughter of the Powhatan leader, in 1614.
In 1619 the House of Burgesses, the first elected representative assembly in the English colonies, met at Jamestown, and the first recorded enslaved Africans arrived in English Virginia that August.

In 1620 the Mayflower carried about 100 passengers, including Separatists seeking religious freedom (later called Pilgrims), to Plymouth in present-day Massachusetts. Before landing they signed the Mayflower Compact.
About half died during the first winter. The Wampanoag people, led by Massasoit, made an alliance with the colonists, and Tisquantum (Squanto) helped them plant corn.
In autumn 1621 the colonists and Wampanoag shared a harvest feast often called the first Thanksgiving.
In 1630 Puritans founded the larger Massachusetts Bay Colony (Boston).

The French and Indian War (1754-1763) was fought between Britain and France, each with Native American allies, over control of North America. It was part of the global Seven Years' War.
A young George Washington fought in its first battles.
Britain won. In the Treaty of Paris (1763), France gave up Canada and its lands east of the Mississippi River to Britain.
The war left Britain in debt, so Parliament began taxing the colonies (such as the Stamp Act of 1765), and the Proclamation of 1763 barred colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains. These policies angered colonists and helped lead to the Revolution.

Stamp Act (1765): taxed printed materials; colonists protested "no taxation without representation" since they had no members in Parliament. Repealed in 1766.
Townshend Acts (1767): taxes on imported goods such as glass, paper, and tea.
Boston Massacre (March 5, 1770): British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston, killing five colonists, including Crispus Attucks.
Tea Act (1773) and Boston Tea Party (December 16, 1773): colonists, some disguised as Mohawk Indians, dumped 342 chests of British East India Company tea into Boston Harbor.
Coercive (Intolerable) Acts (1774): punished Massachusetts and closed Boston Harbor.
First Continental Congress (September 1774): delegates from 12 colonies met in Philadelphia to coordinate resistance.

April 19, 1775: the war began with the Battles of Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts.
June 1775: the Second Continental Congress made George Washington commander of the Continental Army; the Battle of Bunker Hill was fought near Boston.
July 4, 1776: the Declaration of Independence was adopted.
1777: the American victory at Saratoga, New York, is called the turning point because it convinced France to ally with the Americans (1778).
Winter 1777-1778: Washington's army endured hardship at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania.
October 19, 1781: British General Charles Cornwallis surrendered to American and French forces at Yorktown, Virginia, effectively ending major fighting.
1783: the Treaty of Paris recognized American independence, with a western boundary at the Mississippi River.

t: George Washington becomes the first President (1789)

George Washington was unanimously elected by the Electoral College and inaugurated as the first President on April 30, 1789, in New York City, then the temporary capital. John Adams was the first Vice President.
He served two terms (1789-1797), set the two-term tradition, and created the first Cabinet, including Thomas Jefferson (Secretary of State) and Alexander Hamilton (Secretary of the Treasury).
His Farewell Address (1796) warned against political parties and permanent foreign alliances. The capital moved to Washington, D.C., in 1800.

In 1803, President Thomas Jefferson's administration bought the Louisiana Territory from France (ruled by Napoleon) for about $15 million.
The roughly 828,000 square miles between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains about doubled the size of the United States.
Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore the territory (1804-1806). Their Corps of Discovery reached the Pacific Ocean, aided by the Shoshone interpreter Sacagawea.

a: why did the war of 1812 start

The United States declared war on Britain in June 1812, over British impressment (forcing American sailors into the Royal Navy), trade restrictions, and British support for Native American resistance in the West.
In 1814 British troops burned Washington, D.C., including the White House and Capitol. The defense of Fort McHenry in Baltimore inspired Francis Scott Key's poem "The Star-Spangled Banner," later the national anthem (officially adopted in 1931).
The Treaty of Ghent (signed December 1814) ended the war with no major border changes. Andrew Jackson's victory at the Battle of New Orleans (January 1815) came after the treaty was signed but before news arrived.

The Missouri Compromise (1820) kept the balance between free and slave states in the Senate:
Missouri was admitted as a slave state and Maine as a free state.
Slavery was banned in the rest of the Louisiana Territory north of latitude 36 degrees 30 minutes.
The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) effectively repealed it by letting settlers decide on slavery (popular sovereignty), and the Supreme Court declared its slavery ban unconstitutional in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857).

t: Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears (1830-1839)

The Indian Removal Act of 1830, signed by President Andrew Jackson, authorized the government to negotiate the removal of Native nations from the Southeast to lands west of the Mississippi River (Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma).
The Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Seminole, Chickasaw, and Choctaw nations were forced from their homelands during the 1830s.
In 1838-1839 the US Army forced about 16,000 Cherokee to move west; thousands died of disease, cold, and hunger. The journey is called the Trail of Tears.
The Supreme Court had ruled in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) that Georgia's laws did not apply in Cherokee territory, but the decision was not enforced.

Manifest Destiny was the 19th-century belief that the United States was destined to expand across North America.
After the US annexed Texas (1845), disputes over the Texas border led to war with Mexico in 1846 under President James K. Polk.
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) ended the war. Mexico gave up about half its territory (the Mexican Cession), including California and most of present-day Arizona, New Mexico, Nevada, and Utah, and accepted the Rio Grande as the Texas border; the US paid $15 million.
The question of whether slavery would spread to these lands deepened sectional conflict. Gold was discovered in California in 1848, leading to the Gold Rush of 1849.

The Seneca Falls Convention, held July 19-20, 1848, in Seneca Falls, New York, was the first women's rights convention in the United States.
Organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, it adopted the Declaration of Sentiments, modeled on the Declaration of Independence, stating that "all men and women are created equal."
Its call for women's right to vote was the most controversial resolution; Frederick Douglass spoke in support. Women won the national right to vote with the 19th Amendment in 1920.

After Abraham Lincoln's election in 1860, eleven Southern slave states seceded and formed the Confederate States of America, led by Jefferson Davis. The central cause of the conflict was slavery and its expansion.
April 12, 1861: Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in South Carolina, starting the war.
January 1, 1863: the Emancipation Proclamation took effect.
July 1-3, 1863: the Union won the Battle of Gettysburg in Pennsylvania; on July 4, Vicksburg surrendered, giving the Union control of the Mississippi River.
April 9, 1865: Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrendered to Union General Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, Virginia.
April 14, 1865: Lincoln was shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre and died the next morning.
About 620,000 soldiers died by traditional estimates (some recent estimates are higher), the most of any American war.

Reconstruction was the period after the Civil War when the nation rebuilt the South and dealt with the status of about four million formerly enslaved people.
The Reconstruction Amendments: 13th (1865) abolished slavery; 14th (1868) granted citizenship and equal protection; 15th (1870) barred denying the vote based on race.
The Freedmen's Bureau (1865) provided food, schools, and legal help. Black men voted and held office, including in Congress.
President Andrew Johnson clashed with Congress and was impeached in 1868 but acquitted by one vote in the Senate.
Reconstruction ended with the Compromise of 1877, when federal troops left the South. Southern states then passed Jim Crow segregation laws and used poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence to deny Black citizens their rights.

The first transcontinental railroad was completed on May 10, 1869, when the Union Pacific (building west from Nebraska) and the Central Pacific (building east from California) met at Promontory Summit, Utah Territory. A ceremonial golden spike marked the event.
Thousands of Chinese immigrants did much of the Central Pacific's dangerous work, and many Irish immigrants worked on the Union Pacific.
The railroad cut cross-country travel from months to about a week and sped western settlement, which also brought the destruction of the bison herds and the loss of Native American lands.

After the Civil War, the US became a leading industrial nation. Business leaders such as Andrew Carnegie (steel), John D. Rockefeller (oil), and J. P. Morgan (banking) built huge companies; critics called them "robber barons," supporters "captains of industry."
Mark Twain's term "the Gilded Age" suggested a shiny surface over problems such as corruption, poverty, and dangerous working conditions.
Millions of immigrants arrived, many from southern and eastern Europe; Ellis Island in New York Harbor opened as an immigration station in 1892. The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) barred most Chinese immigration.
Workers formed labor unions, and reformers in the Progressive Era (about 1890s-1920) pushed for laws on child labor, food safety, and monopolies.

In 1898 the United States fought Spain, after the US battleship Maine exploded in Havana Harbor, Cuba (the cause is still uncertain), and amid support for Cuban independence.
The war lasted about four months. Theodore Roosevelt became famous leading the "Rough Riders" volunteer cavalry in Cuba.
In the Treaty of Paris (1898), Spain gave the US Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines (for $20 million), and Cuba became independent under strong US influence. The US also annexed Hawaii in 1898.
It marked the US's emergence as a world power with overseas territories.

t: United States in World War I (1917-1918)

The US stayed neutral when World War I began in 1914, but tensions rose after a German submarine sank the British liner Lusitania (1915), killing 128 Americans.
In 1917 Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, and the Zimmermann Telegram revealed a German proposal for Mexico to join the war against the US.
Congress declared war on Germany on April 6, 1917, at President Woodrow Wilson's request. More than 2 million American troops went to France.
The fighting ended with the armistice on November 11, 1918. Wilson's Fourteen Points proposed a League of Nations, but the US Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles, and the US never joined the League.

t: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)
x:
The stock market crash of October 1929 (including "Black Tuesday," October 29) began the Great Depression, the worst economic downturn in US history. By 1933 about one-quarter of the workforce was unemployed, and thousands of banks had failed.
In the 1930s, drought and dust storms on the Great Plains (the Dust Bowl) drove many farm families west.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt, elected in 1932, launched the New Deal: programs to provide relief, recovery, and reform, such as the Civilian Conservation Corps, the Works Progress Administration, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (insuring bank deposits), and Social Security (1935).
The Depression ended as industry expanded for World War II.

t: United States in World War II (1941-1945)

December 7, 1941: Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, killing about 2,400 Americans. The US declared war on Japan the next day; Germany and Italy declared war on the US on December 11.
On the home front, women entered factory jobs ("Rosie the Riveter"), goods were rationed, and about 120,000 Japanese Americans were forcibly removed to incarceration camps under Executive Order 9066 (1942).
June 6, 1944 (D-Day): Allied forces landed in Normandy, France. Germany surrendered on May 8, 1945 (V-E Day).
August 6 and 9, 1945: the US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan. Japan announced its surrender on August 15 and signed the surrender on September 2, 1945, ending the war.
About 405,000 Americans died in the war.

The Cold War was a long rivalry between the United States and its allies and the Soviet Union and its allies, fought mostly through politics, the arms race, the space race, and proxy wars rather than direct war between the two powers.
Key US policies: containment (stopping the spread of communism); the Truman Doctrine (1947); the Marshall Plan (1948), which gave aid to rebuild Western Europe; and NATO (1949), a military alliance.
Major events: the Berlin Airlift (1948-1949), the Korean War (1950-1953), the Soviet launch of Sputnik (1957), the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962), the Vietnam War, and the US Moon landing (1969).
It ended with the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the breakup of the Soviet Union (1991).

On June 25, 1950, communist North Korea invaded South Korea. A United Nations force, led mainly by the United States, defended the South; China later sent troops to support the North.
Fighting ended with an armistice on July 27, 1953, near the 38th parallel, close to where it started. No peace treaty was signed, and Korea remains divided, separated by the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).
About 36,000 Americans died in the war.

1954: Brown v. Board of Education ruled school segregation unconstitutional.
1955-1956: after Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955, for refusing to give up her bus seat, the Montgomery Bus Boycott, led by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., lasted about 381 days until buses were desegregated.
1957: nine Black students (the Little Rock Nine) integrated Central High School in Arkansas, protected by federal troops.
1960: student sit-ins at segregated lunch counters began in Greensboro, North Carolina. 1961: Freedom Riders challenged segregated interstate buses.
August 28, 1963: about 250,000 people joined the March on Washington, where King gave his "I Have a Dream" speech.
1964: the Civil Rights Act banned discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in public places and employment. 1965: the Selma-to-Montgomery marches led to the Voting Rights Act.
April 4, 1968: King was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee.

In October 1962, US spy planes discovered Soviet nuclear missile sites being built in Cuba, about 90 miles from Florida.
President John F. Kennedy announced a naval "quarantine" (blockade) of Cuba. For 13 days the world was close to nuclear war.
Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a US promise not to invade Cuba; the US also secretly agreed to remove its missiles from Turkey.
Afterward, a direct "hotline" was set up between Washington and Moscow (1963).

President John F. Kennedy was shot and killed on November 22, 1963, while riding in a motorcade in Dallas, Texas.
Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested for the shooting and was himself shot and killed two days later by Jack Ruby. The Warren Commission (1964) concluded that Oswald acted alone.
Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson was sworn in as President aboard Air Force One the same day. Johnson then pushed through civil rights and "Great Society" laws, including the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Medicare and Medicaid (1965).

After France left Indochina in 1954, Vietnam was divided into communist North Vietnam and US-backed South Vietnam. The US sent advisers and aid to the South to contain communism.
1964: after reported attacks on US ships, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, letting President Lyndon Johnson expand military action. The first US combat troops arrived in 1965; US forces peaked at about 540,000 in 1969.
1968: the Tet Offensive, a large North Vietnamese and Viet Cong attack, turned more Americans against the war; protests grew at home.
1973: the Paris Peace Accords led to the withdrawal of US combat troops.
April 30, 1975: Saigon fell to North Vietnam, and Vietnam was reunified under communist rule.
About 58,000 Americans died. In 1973 Congress also passed the War Powers Resolution to limit the President's power to commit troops without congressional approval.

On July 20, 1969, NASA's Apollo 11 lunar module, the Eagle, landed on the Moon. Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, followed by Buzz Aldrin; Michael Collins stayed in orbit in the command module, Columbia.
Armstrong's first words on the surface were "That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind."
The crew returned safely to Earth on July 24, 1969. Between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts walked on the Moon on six Apollo missions. The landing was a major US achievement in the Cold War space race.

In June 1972, five men connected to President Richard Nixon's reelection committee were arrested for breaking into the Democratic National Committee headquarters at the Watergate complex in Washington, D.C.
Investigations by reporters (notably Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein of The Washington Post), a Senate committee, and a special prosecutor revealed a cover-up involving the White House. Secret White House tape recordings became key evidence.
In July 1974 the Supreme Court ordered the tapes released (United States v. Nixon), and the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment.
Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974, the only President to do so. Vice President Gerald Ford became President and pardoned Nixon a month later.

In the 1980s, President Ronald Reagan increased military spending and later negotiated with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, who had introduced reforms called glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring). In 1987 they signed the INF Treaty eliminating a class of nuclear missiles.
On November 9, 1989, the Berlin Wall opened, and communist governments in Eastern Europe fell that year. Germany reunified on October 3, 1990.
The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, leaving the United States as the world's only superpower.
In 1991 a US-led coalition also fought the Persian Gulf War to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait.

On September 11, 2001, 19 terrorists from the extremist group al-Qaeda hijacked four passenger airplanes in the United States.
Two planes struck the North and South Towers of the World Trade Center in New York City, and both towers collapsed. A third hit the Pentagon near Washington, D.C. On the fourth, United Airlines Flight 93, passengers fought the hijackers, and it crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
Nearly 3,000 people were killed, the deadliest terrorist attack in history.
In response, the US and allies invaded Afghanistan in October 2001 to remove the Taliban government that sheltered al-Qaeda; Congress passed the USA PATRIOT Act, and the Department of Homeland Security was created in 2002.

t: BCE, CE, BC, and AD dates
x:
BCE means "Before the Common Era" and is the same as BC ("Before Christ"). CE means "Common Era" and is the same as AD (Anno Domini, Latin for "in the year of the Lord").
The numbering is identical: 500 BCE = 500 BC; 1215 CE = AD 1215.
BCE years count down toward year 1: 500 BCE came before 400 BCE. There is no year 0; 1 BCE is followed directly by 1 CE.
A century is 100 years: the 5th century BCE is 500-401 BCE, and the 15th century CE is the 1400s (1401-1500).

The Neolithic Revolution was the shift from hunting and gathering to farming and settled village life, beginning about 10,000 BCE (roughly 12,000 years ago) in the Fertile Crescent of Southwest Asia, and later developing independently in other regions such as China, Mesoamerica, and the Andes.
People domesticated plants (wheat, barley, rice, maize) and animals (goats, sheep, cattle).
Farming produced food surpluses, which allowed populations to grow, people to specialize in jobs, and permanent villages, and eventually cities and civilizations, to develop.

Mesopotamia ("land between the rivers") lay between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, mostly in present-day Iraq, part of the Fertile Crescent.
Sumerians built some of the first cities, such as Uruk and Ur, by about 3500-3000 BCE. They developed cuneiform, one of the earliest writing systems (about 3200 BCE), wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay tablets. They built ziggurats (stepped temples) and used the wheel and irrigation.
Later empires included the Akkadian Empire under Sargon (about 2300s BCE), Babylon, and Assyria.
King Hammurabi of Babylon issued the Code of Hammurabi (about 1754 BCE), one of the earliest known written law codes, with 282 laws and punishments that often varied by social class ("an eye for an eye").
The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest surviving works of literature.

Ancient Egyptian civilization developed along the Nile River, whose yearly floods left fertile soil.
Upper and Lower Egypt were united around 3100 BCE, traditionally by a king named Narmer (or Menes). Kings called pharaohs were seen as divine rulers.
Egyptians wrote in hieroglyphs, used papyrus, and practiced mummification, believing in an afterlife.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE (during the Old Kingdom); it is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.
History is divided into the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms. Famous rulers include Hatshepsut, Ramses II, Tutankhamun, and Cleopatra VII, the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, after whose death in 30 BCE Egypt became a Roman province.
The Rosetta Stone (found 1799) helped Jean-Francois Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.

The Indus Valley (Harappan) civilization flourished along the Indus River in present-day Pakistan and northwest India, at its height from about 2600 to 1900 BCE.
Its major cities, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, had planned grid streets, standardized baked bricks, and advanced drainage and sewer systems.
People used standardized weights and seals with a script that has not yet been deciphered.
The civilization declined after about 1900 BCE; possible causes being studied include climate change and shifts in rivers.

Chinese civilization developed along the Huang He (Yellow River) and the Yangtze River.
Shang dynasty (about 1600-1046 BCE): the earliest dynasty confirmed by written records; known for oracle bones (with early Chinese writing) and bronze work.
Zhou dynasty (1046-256 BCE): introduced the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that heaven grants rulers the right to rule and takes it away from unjust ones. Confucius and Laozi lived during this period.
Qin dynasty (221-206 BCE): Qin Shi Huang unified China as its first emperor, standardized writing, money, and measurements, began linking walls into an early Great Wall, and was buried with the Terracotta Army.
Han dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE): a golden age; Confucianism became official state philosophy, paper was invented, and the Silk Road trade routes connected China with the West.

Ancient Greece was made up of independent city-states (poleis), such as Athens and Sparta.
Athens developed an early form of direct democracy, usually dated to the reforms of Cleisthenes around 508-507 BCE; only adult male citizens could vote. Sparta was a military society ruled by two kings and a council.
Persian Wars (499-449 BCE): Greek city-states defeated the Persian Empire, including at Marathon (490 BCE) and at Salamis (480 BCE); the Spartans' stand at Thermopylae (480 BCE) became legendary.
Athens' Golden Age under Pericles produced the Parthenon (completed 432 BCE), drama, history writing (Herodotus, Thucydides), and philosophy.
Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE): Sparta and its allies defeated Athens.
Philosophers Socrates, his student Plato, and Plato's student Aristotle shaped Western philosophy. The first recorded Olympic Games were held in 776 BCE.

t: Alexander the Great and the Hellenistic era
x:
Alexander the Great (356-323 BCE), king of Macedonia and a former student of Aristotle, conquered the Persian Empire and built an empire stretching from Greece and Egypt to the Indus River in about 13 years.
He founded many cities, including Alexandria in Egypt, which became a great center of learning with its famous library.
After his death at age 32 in Babylon in 323 BCE, his generals divided the empire into kingdoms. The Hellenistic period (323-31 BCE) spread Greek language and culture across the eastern Mediterranean and Southwest Asia.

According to Roman tradition, Rome was founded in 753 BCE, and the Romans overthrew their last king and set up a republic in 509 BCE.
The Republic was governed by two consuls elected each year, a Senate, and assemblies. Society was divided into patricians (aristocrats) and plebeians (commoners), who gained rights over time. The Twelve Tables (about 450 BCE) were Rome's first written laws.
Rome defeated Carthage in the three Punic Wars (264-146 BCE); the Carthaginian general Hannibal famously crossed the Alps with elephants.
Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, became dictator, and was assassinated by senators on the Ides of March (March 15), 44 BCE.
His adopted heir Octavian defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BCE) and became the first emperor, Augustus, in 27 BCE, ending the Republic.

t: Roman Empire and the Pax Romana
x:
The Roman Empire began when Octavian became Augustus, the first emperor, in 27 BCE.
The Pax Romana ("Roman Peace") was about 200 years of relative peace and stability (27 BCE to 180 CE). Romans built roads, aqueducts, and the Colosseum (completed 80 CE), and Latin spread across the West.
Christianity began in the Roman province of Judea in the 1st century CE. Emperor Constantine legalized it with the Edict of Milan (313 CE) and founded Constantinople (330 CE) as a new capital; Theodosius I made it the official state religion in 380 CE.
In 395 CE the empire was permanently divided into western and eastern halves.

t: Fall of the Western Roman Empire (476 CE)
x:
The traditional date for the fall of the Western Roman Empire is 476 CE, when the Germanic leader Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus.
Contributing causes historians discuss include political instability and civil wars, economic troubles and heavy taxes, overreliance on foreign mercenaries, pressure from migrating and invading groups such as the Visigoths (who sacked Rome in 410) and Vandals (455), and the size of the empire.
The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, centered on Constantinople, lasted almost a thousand years longer, until 1453.
The fall is often used to mark the start of the Middle Ages in Europe.

The Byzantine Empire was the continuation of the Eastern Roman Empire, with its capital at Constantinople (now Istanbul, Turkey). It was Greek-speaking and Christian.
Emperor Justinian I (reigned 527-565) reconquered parts of the West, built the Hagia Sophia church (completed 537), and organized Roman law into the Justinian Code.
The Great Schism of 1054 split Christianity into the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches.
The empire ended when the Ottoman Turks, led by Sultan Mehmed II, captured Constantinople on May 29, 1453.

t: Rise of Islam and the early caliphates (7th-13th centuries)
x:
Islam began in Arabia in the early 7th century with the Prophet Muhammad, who began preaching in Mecca around 610 CE. In 622 he and his followers moved to Medina (the Hijra), the starting year of the Islamic calendar. He died in 632.
Under the caliphs who followed, including the Rashidun, Umayyad (661-750, capital Damascus), and Abbasid (from 750, capital Baghdad) caliphates, Muslim rule spread across Southwest Asia, North Africa, and into Spain and Central Asia.
During the Abbasid period, scholars in centers such as Baghdad's House of Wisdom translated and expanded Greek, Persian, and Indian learning, making advances in mathematics (al-Khwarizmi; the word algebra comes from his book), astronomy, medicine (Ibn Sina), and philosophy, a period often called the Islamic Golden Age.
Mongol forces sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate there.

t: Middle Ages and feudalism in Europe
x:
The Middle Ages (medieval period) in Europe is usually dated from about 500 to about 1500 CE.
Feudalism was a political and military system in which kings granted land (fiefs) to lords and nobles in exchange for loyalty and military service; knights served lords. Under manorialism, peasants and serfs worked the land of a manor in exchange for protection and were bound to it.
The Roman Catholic Church was the most powerful institution in western Europe; monasteries preserved learning.
Charlemagne, king of the Franks, was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III on December 25, 800 CE, and encouraged learning across much of western Europe.
In 1066 William of Normandy conquered England at the Battle of Hastings.

The Crusades were a series of religious wars launched by Latin Christians in Europe, mainly to take control of Jerusalem and the Holy Land, a region sacred to Jews, Christians, and Muslims.
Pope Urban II called for the First Crusade in 1095. The crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099 and set up crusader states.
The Muslim leader Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187. Later crusades had less success, and the last crusader stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291.
Effects included increased trade between Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, the spread of ideas and goods, lasting hostility, and violence against Jewish and Muslim communities as well as Eastern Christians (crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204).

The Magna Carta ("Great Charter") was agreed to by King John of England at Runnymede on June 15, 1215, under pressure from rebellious barons.
It stated that the king was subject to the law. Among its clauses: free men could not be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgment of their peers or by the law of the land, and certain taxes required the consent of the realm's leading men.
The original was soon annulled by the pope, but revised versions were reissued, and it became a symbol of limited government and the rule of law. It influenced the English Parliament, the English Bill of Rights (1689), and the US Constitution and Bill of Rights.

Temujin united the Mongol tribes and was proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206. He and his successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea and China across Central Asia to Eastern Europe.
Mongol armies were known for skilled horse archers and brutal conquests, but the empire also protected Silk Road trade and travel (the Pax Mongolica), helping spread goods, ideas, and, later, disease.
His grandson Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in China (1271); the Venetian traveler Marco Polo described visiting his court.
The empire split into separate khanates, and the Yuan dynasty fell in 1368, replaced by the Ming dynasty.

a: how many died in the black death
x:
The Black Death was a pandemic of plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, that swept through Asia, the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe. It reached Europe in 1347, probably via trade ships arriving in Sicily, and spread across the continent by 1351.
It was spread largely by fleas on rats and other animals and, in some forms, from person to person. Symptoms of the bubonic form included swollen lymph nodes (buboes).
It killed an estimated one-third to one-half of Europe's population, perhaps 25 to 50 million people.
Effects: labor shortages raised wages for surviving peasants, weakening feudalism and serfdom; some people lost faith in institutions; and Jewish communities were falsely blamed and attacked in many places.

The Renaissance ("rebirth") was a period of renewed interest in the art, literature, and learning of ancient Greece and Rome. It began in Italy, especially Florence, in the 14th century and spread through Europe through the 1500s and into the 1600s.
Humanism, a key idea, focused on human potential and achievements and on studying classical texts. Wealthy patrons such as the Medici family of Florence funded artists and scholars.
Major figures: Leonardo da Vinci (Mona Lisa, The Last Supper), Michelangelo (David, the Sistine Chapel ceiling), Raphael, Petrarch, Machiavelli (The Prince), and in northern Europe Erasmus and Shakespeare.
Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type printing press (about 1440, in Mainz, Germany) spread books and ideas quickly; the Gutenberg Bible was printed around 1455.

Seeking spices, gold, sea routes to Asia, and converts to Christianity, European nations sent explorers across the oceans using new ships (caravels) and tools (compass, astrolabe).
Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope (1488), and Vasco da Gama reached India by sea (1498).
Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Americas in 1492.
Ferdinand Magellan's expedition (1519-1522) was the first to sail around the world; Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521, and Juan Sebastian Elcano completed the voyage.
Spanish conquistadors Hernan Cortes (Aztec Empire, 1521) and Francisco Pizarro (Inca Empire, 1530s) conquered major American empires.
The Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals, and diseases between hemispheres; smallpox and other diseases killed huge numbers of Indigenous people, and the Atlantic slave trade forcibly carried about 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic, of whom about 10.7 million survived the voyage.

The Protestant Reformation began in 1517, when the German monk and professor Martin Luther wrote his Ninety-five Theses, criticizing the Catholic Church's sale of indulgences; tradition says he posted them on a church door in Wittenberg on October 31.
Luther taught that salvation comes through faith alone and that the Bible, not the pope, is the highest religious authority. He was excommunicated in 1521. The printing press helped his ideas spread quickly.
Other reformers included John Calvin in Geneva. In England, King Henry VIII broke with the pope and created the Church of England (Act of Supremacy, 1534).
The Catholic Church responded with the Catholic (Counter-) Reformation, including the Council of Trent (1545-1563) and the Jesuit order.
The Reformation split Western Christianity and contributed to religious wars, including the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648), which ended with the Peace of Westphalia.

The Scientific Revolution was a period when thinkers increasingly used observation, experiment, and mathematics to understand nature, challenging older authorities.
Nicolaus Copernicus proposed a heliocentric (Sun-centered) model in a book published in 1543.
Johannes Kepler showed that planets move in elliptical orbits. Galileo Galilei used a telescope to observe Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus; in 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried him and placed him under house arrest for supporting heliocentrism.
Francis Bacon and Rene Descartes promoted new methods of reasoning, which helped shape the scientific method.
Isaac Newton's Principia (1687) described the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

The Enlightenment (Age of Reason) was an 18th-century intellectual movement that applied reason to government, society, and religion.
John Locke (English): people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property; government rests on the consent of the governed, and people may overthrow a government that violates their rights.
Baron de Montesquieu (French): separation of powers among branches of government (The Spirit of the Laws, 1748).
Jean-Jacques Rousseau (French): the social contract and the general will of the people.
Voltaire (French): freedom of speech, freedom of religion, and religious tolerance.
Thomas Hobbes (English, earlier, Leviathan 1651) argued people need a strong ruler to avoid chaos. Adam Smith (Scottish) argued for free markets (The Wealth of Nations, 1776).
These ideas influenced the American and French Revolutions.

Causes: a rigid social structure (three estates, in which the Third Estate of commoners paid most taxes), royal debt and financial crisis, food shortages, and Enlightenment ideas.
1789: King Louis XVI called the Estates-General; the Third Estate formed the National Assembly and swore the Tennis Court Oath. On July 14, 1789, crowds stormed the Bastille prison in Paris (now France's national holiday). In August the Assembly issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.
1792: France became a republic. Louis XVI was executed by guillotine in January 1793, and Queen Marie Antoinette in October 1793.
1793-1794: the Reign of Terror, led by Maximilien Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety, executed many thousands of people; it ended with Robespierre's own execution in July 1794.
1799: Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in a coup.
Its motto was "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity."
