The angle between the legs is the vertex angle. The altitude from the vertex angle bisects the base and the vertex angle.
Example: vertex angle 40° → each base angle = (180 − 40)/2 = 70°.
Example: base angle 52° → vertex angle = 180 − 2 × 52 = 76°.
Equilateral triangle: all sides equal and all angles 60°.

t: Triangle congruence criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL)
x:
Two triangles are congruent (same shape and size) if they match by:
SSS: three pairs of equal sides.
SAS: two sides and the INCLUDED angle (the angle between them).
ASA: two angles and the included side.
AAS: two angles and a non-included side.
HL (right triangles only): hypotenuse and one leg.
NOT valid: SSA (ambiguous) and AAA (gives similar triangles, not necessarily congruent).
CPCTC: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent; used after proving congruence.
Congruence statements match vertex order: △ABC ≅ △DEF means A ↔ D, B ↔ E, C ↔ F.

Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. Scale factor k = (side of image)/(matching side of original).
Triangle similarity tests: AA (two equal angles), SSS~ (all three side ratios equal), SAS~ (two side ratios equal and the included angles equal).
Example: △ABC ~ △DEF with AB = 6, DE = 9, BC = 8 → k = 9/6 = 1.5, so EF = 8 × 1.5 = 12.
With scale factor k: perimeters scale by k, areas by k², volumes by k³.
Example: k = 3 → area is 9 times larger; volume is 27 times larger.
Common mistake: scaling area by k instead of k².

t: Triangle proportionality and angle bisector theorems
x:
Side splitter (triangle proportionality): a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally. If DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC, then AD/DB = AE/EC.
Example: AD = 4, DB = 6, AE = 5 → EC = 7.5.
Midsegment theorem: the segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half as long. Third side 18 → midsegment 9.
Angle bisector theorem: the bisector of angle A splits the opposite side BC into pieces proportional to the adjacent sides: BD/DC = AB/AC.

In a right triangle: a² + b² = c², where a and b are the legs and c is the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle).
Find the hypotenuse: legs 5 and 12 → c = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13.
Find a leg: hypotenuse 10, leg 6 → b = √(100 − 36) = √64 = 8.
Converse: if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c, the triangle is right.
Common mistakes: adding when finding a leg (subtract instead); using it on a triangle that is not right; treating a leg as the hypotenuse.

Whole-number sides (a, b, c) with a² + b² = c². Primitive triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 20-21-29, 9-40-41, 12-35-37, 11-60-61.
Any multiple of a triple is also a triple: 6-8-10, 9-12-15, 12-16-20, 15-20-25 (from 3-4-5); 10-24-26 (from 5-12-13).
Example: a right triangle with legs 9 and 12 has hypotenuse 15 (3 × 3-4-5).
Generating formula: for integers m > n > 0, (m² − n², 2mn, m² + n²) is a triple. m = 2, n = 1 gives 3-4-5.

45°-45°-90°: sides in ratio 1 : 1 : √2. Legs = x, hypotenuse = x√2.
Example: leg 5 → hypotenuse 5√2 ≈ 7.07. Hypotenuse 8 → each leg = 8/√2 = 4√2 ≈ 5.66.
30°-60°-90°: sides in ratio 1 : √3 : 2. Short leg (opposite 30°) = x, long leg (opposite 60°) = x√3, hypotenuse = 2x.
Example: short leg 4 → long leg 4√3 ≈ 6.93, hypotenuse 8. Hypotenuse 10 → short leg 5, long leg 5√3.
Common mistake: putting √3 on the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is always the longest side (2x), and the short leg is opposite the 30° angle.

t: Triangle centers: centroid, circumcenter, incenter, orthocenter
x:
Centroid: where the three medians meet (a median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side). It divides each median 2 : 1, the longer part being on the vertex side. Coordinates: ((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3). It is the balance point.
Circumcenter: where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet; equidistant from the three vertices (center of the circumscribed circle). In a right triangle it is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.
Incenter: where the angle bisectors meet; equidistant from the three sides (center of the inscribed circle). Always inside.
Orthocenter: where the altitudes meet (an altitude is perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side's line).
Example: vertices (0, 0), (6, 0), (3, 9) → centroid (3, 3).

A = ½ × b × h, where b = any side used as the base and h = the perpendicular height from that base to the opposite vertex.
Example: base 10 cm, height 7 cm → A = ½ × 10 × 7 = 35 cm².
Right triangle: the two legs are a base and height: legs 6 and 8 → A = 24.
For an obtuse triangle the height may fall outside the triangle, on the extension of the base.
Other formulas: A = ½ab sin C (two sides and included angle); Heron's formula (three sides).
Common mistake: using a slanted side as the height.

a: area of triangle with three sides
x:
A = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), where a, b, c are the side lengths and s = (a + b + c)/2 is the semiperimeter.
Example: sides 13, 14, 15: s = 21; A = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = √7056 = 84.
Example: sides 3, 4, 5: s = 6; A = √(6 × 3 × 2 × 1) = √36 = 6 (matches ½ × 3 × 4).
Common mistake: using the full perimeter instead of half.

For side s: height h = (√3/2) × s and area A = (√3/4) × s².
Example: s = 10 → h = 5√3 ≈ 8.66, A = 25√3 ≈ 43.30.
Perimeter = 3s. Each angle is 60°.
The height splits the triangle into two 30-60-90 triangles with short leg s/2.

t: Interior and exterior angles of polygons
a: how many sides does a polygon have
x:
Sum of interior angles of an n-sided polygon = (n − 2) × 180°.
Each interior angle of a REGULAR polygon = (n − 2) × 180° ÷ n.
Sum of exterior angles (one at each vertex) of any convex polygon = 360°; each exterior angle of a regular polygon = 360° ÷ n. Interior + exterior at a vertex = 180°.
Examples: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°, octagon 1080°, decagon 1440°.
Regular hexagon: each interior angle = 720 ÷ 6 = 120°; each exterior = 60°.
Finding n: if each exterior angle is 24°, n = 360 ÷ 24 = 15 sides.

t: Polygon names and number of diagonals
x:
Names by number of sides: 3 triangle, 4 quadrilateral, 5 pentagon, 6 hexagon, 7 heptagon, 8 octagon, 9 nonagon, 10 decagon, 11 hendecagon, 12 dodecagon; n sides = n-gon.
Regular polygon: all sides equal AND all angles equal.
Number of diagonals = n(n − 3)/2.
Examples: hexagon 6 × 3/2 = 9 diagonals; octagon 8 × 5/2 = 20; decagon 10 × 7/2 = 35.
Convex: every interior angle is less than 180°. Concave: at least one interior angle is more than 180°.

Parallelogram: both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal; opposite angles equal; consecutive angles supplementary; diagonals bisect each other.
Rectangle: a parallelogram with four right angles; diagonals are equal.
Rhombus: a parallelogram with four equal sides; diagonals are perpendicular and bisect the angles.
Square: both a rectangle and a rhombus (all properties above).
Trapezoid: at least one pair of parallel sides (bases) in the inclusive definition; some books say exactly one pair. Isosceles trapezoid: equal legs, equal base angles, equal diagonals. Midsegment = (b₁ + b₂)/2.
Kite: two pairs of adjacent equal sides; diagonals are perpendicular; one pair of opposite angles is equal.
All quadrilaterals have interior angles summing to 360°.

t: Area and perimeter of rectangles and squares
x:
Rectangle: A = l × w; P = 2l + 2w, where l = length, w = width.
Square with side s: A = s²; P = 4s; diagonal = s√2.
Rectangle diagonal: d = √(l² + w²).
Example: 8 m by 5 m rectangle: A = 40 m², P = 26 m, diagonal = √89 ≈ 9.43 m.
Example: square with area 49 cm² has side 7 cm and perimeter 28 cm.
Common mistake: area uses square units (m²); perimeter uses plain length units (m).

A = b × h, where b = length of a base and h = perpendicular height between that base and the opposite side.
Example: base 12 cm, slanted side 7 cm, height 5 cm → A = 12 × 5 = 60 cm².
With an angle: A = a × b × sin θ, where a and b are adjacent sides and θ the angle between them.
Perimeter = 2(a + b).
Common mistake: multiplying the base by the slanted side (12 × 7 = 84 is wrong).

A = ½ × (b₁ + b₂) × h, where b₁ and b₂ are the parallel sides (bases) and h is the perpendicular height between them.
Example: bases 6 cm and 10 cm, height 4 cm → A = ½ × 16 × 4 = 32 cm².
Equivalent: A = (average of the bases) × height = midsegment × height.
Common mistake: using the slanted side instead of the perpendicular height.

t: Area of a rhombus or kite (diagonals)
x:
A = (d₁ × d₂)/2, where d₁ and d₂ are the lengths of the two diagonals. Works for any rhombus, kite, or square (any quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals).
Example: diagonals 10 and 24 → A = 240/2 = 120.
Rhombus side from diagonals: the diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so side = √((d₁/2)² + (d₂/2)²) = √(25 + 144) = 13 here; perimeter 52.
A rhombus is also a parallelogram, so A = base × height works too.

A = ½ × a × P, where a = apothem (distance from the center perpendicular to a side) and P = perimeter.
Regular hexagon with side s: it is six equilateral triangles, so A = (3√3/2) × s² and apothem = (√3/2) × s.
Example: hexagon with side 6: apothem = 3√3 ≈ 5.196, P = 36, A = ½ × 5.196 × 36 ≈ 93.53 (= 54√3).
Central angle of a regular n-gon = 360° ÷ n.
Common mistake: using the radius (center to vertex) as the apothem. In a hexagon, radius = side = 6, but apothem ≈ 5.196.

t: Area of composite and shaded figures
x:
Split the figure into basic shapes (rectangles, triangles, circles, ...), find each area, then ADD the pieces, or SUBTRACT the cut-out parts.
Shaded region = area of outer shape − area of inner shape.
Example: a 10 × 6 rectangle with a semicircle of diameter 6 attached on one short side: 60 + ½π(3²) = 60 + 4.5π ≈ 74.14.
Example: a square of side 8 with a circle of radius 2 cut out: 64 − 4π ≈ 51.43.
Check that every length used is the right one for its piece (for example, a radius is half the diameter).

t: Circumference and area of a circle
x:
Circumference C = 2πr = πd. Area A = πr². Here r = radius, d = diameter = 2r, π ≈ 3.14159.
Example: r = 5 cm → C = 10π ≈ 31.42 cm and A = 25π ≈ 78.54 cm².
From the diameter: d = 12 → r = 6 → A = 36π ≈ 113.10.
From the area: A = 50 → r = √(50/π) ≈ 3.99.
π is the ratio C/d for every circle.
Common mistakes: using the diameter in πr²; confusing 2πr (circumference, a length) with πr² (area, in square units).

Degrees: arc length s = (θ/360°) × 2πr. Radians: s = r × θ. Here θ = central angle, r = radius.
Example: r = 6, θ = 60° → s = (60/360) × 12π = 2π ≈ 6.28.
Same arc in radians: θ = π/3, s = 6 × π/3 = 2π.
Arc MEASURE (in degrees) equals its central angle; arc LENGTH is a distance.
Common mistake: using s = rθ with θ in degrees.

Degrees: A = (θ/360°) × πr². Radians: A = ½ × r² × θ. Here θ = central angle, r = radius.
Example: r = 6, θ = 60° → A = (1/6) × 36π = 6π ≈ 18.85.
Radians check: ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π.
Segment (region between a chord and its arc) = sector area − triangle area. For r = 6 and 60°: 6π − (√3/4)(36) = 6π − 9√3 ≈ 3.26 (the triangle is equilateral here).

Central angle (vertex at the center) = measure of its intercepted arc.
Inscribed angle (vertex on the circle) = ½ × its intercepted arc. Example: arc 100° → inscribed angle 50°.
Inscribed angles that intercept the same arc are equal.
An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle (Thales' theorem): if one side of an inscribed triangle is a diameter, the opposite angle is 90°.
Cyclic quadrilateral (all four vertices on a circle): opposite angles are supplementary (add to 180°).
Tangent-chord angle = ½ × intercepted arc.

A tangent line is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.
Two tangent segments from the same outside point are equal in length.
A radius (or diameter) perpendicular to a chord bisects the chord.
Chord length = 2√(r² − d²), where d = distance from the center to the chord. Example: r = 5, d = 3 → chord = 2√16 = 8.
Equal chords are the same distance from the center.
Example (tangent): radius 5, distance from an outside point to the center 13 → tangent length = √(13² − 5²) = 12.

t: Chord, secant and tangent segment theorems
x:
Two chords crossing inside: (part × part) = (part × part). If one chord is split into 3 and 8 and the other into 4 and x: 3 × 8 = 4x → x = 6.
Two secants from an outside point: outside × whole = outside × whole. Outside 4, inside 5 (whole 9) and outside 3, inside x: 4 × 9 = 3(3 + x) → x = 9.
Tangent and secant from an outside point: tangent² = outside × whole. Secant outside 4, whole 9 → tangent = √36 = 6.
Common mistake: for secants, multiply by the WHOLE secant, not the inside piece.

t: Angles formed by chords, secants and tangents
x:
Vertex inside the circle (two chords crossing): angle = ½ × (sum of the two intercepted arcs). Arcs 70° and 110° → angle 90°.
Vertex on the circle (inscribed angle or tangent-chord): angle = ½ × intercepted arc.
Vertex outside the circle (two secants, a secant and a tangent, or two tangents): angle = ½ × (far arc − near arc). Arcs 130° and 50° → angle 40°.
Two tangents: the angle plus the near (minor) arc = 180°.

(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r², where (h, k) is the center and r is the radius.
Example: center (2, −3), radius 4 → (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 16.
General form → standard form by completing the square: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 → (x² − 6x + 9) + (y² + 4y + 4) = 12 + 9 + 4 → (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25. Center (3, −2), radius 5.
Centered at the origin: x² + y² = r².
Common mistakes: (x + 3)² means h = −3; the right side is r², so r = √(right side) (16 → r = 4, not 16).

π radians = 180°. Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π.
Examples: 150° = 150 × π/180 = 5π/6; 3π/4 = 3 × 180/4 = 135°; 2 rad = 360/π ≈ 114.59°.
Common values: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 270° = 3π/2, 360° = 2π.
One radian is the central angle whose arc length equals the radius; 1 rad ≈ 57.30°.
Set your calculator to the right mode (DEG or RAD) before using trig functions.

Any prism or cylinder: V = B × h, where B = area of the base and h = perpendicular height between the two bases.
Rectangular prism (box): V = l × w × h. Example: 4 × 5 × 6 = 120 cm³.
Cube with edge s: V = s³. Example: s = 4 → 64.
Cylinder: V = πr²h. Example: r = 3, h = 10 → 90π ≈ 282.74.
Triangular prism: V = (½ × base × height of triangle) × length of prism.
Common mistake: using the diameter as r in πr²h.

Pyramid: V = ⅓ × B × h, where B = area of the base and h = perpendicular height (apex to base).
Cone: V = ⅓ × πr² × h.
Example (square pyramid): base 6 × 6, height 10 → V = ⅓ × 36 × 10 = 120.
Example (cone): r = 3, h = 4 → V = ⅓ × 9π × 4 = 12π ≈ 37.70.
A cone or pyramid holds exactly ⅓ of the prism or cylinder with the same base and height.
Common mistake: using the slant height instead of the perpendicular height. If given slant height l, find h = √(l² − r²) first.

t: Volume and surface area of a sphere
x:
Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³ and surface area SA = 4πr², where r = radius.
Example: r = 3 → V = (4/3)π(27) = 36π ≈ 113.10 and SA = 4π(9) = 36π ≈ 113.10 (equal numbers only because r = 3; the units differ).
Hemisphere: V = (2/3)πr³; curved surface = 2πr²; total with the flat circular base = 3πr².
Doubling the radius multiplies volume by 8 and surface area by 4.
Common mistake: cubing the diameter instead of the radius.

t: Surface area of prisms and cylinders
a: surface area of a rectangular prism
x:
Rectangular prism: SA = 2(lw + lh + wh). Example: 4 × 5 × 6 → 2(20 + 24 + 30) = 148.
Cube with edge s: SA = 6s². Example: s = 4 → 96.
Cylinder: SA = 2πr² + 2πrh (two circles + the rolled-out rectangle). Lateral area = 2πrh.
Example: r = 3, h = 10 → 18π + 60π = 78π ≈ 245.04.
Any prism: SA = 2B + P × h, where B = base area and P = base perimeter.
For an open-top container, leave out the top face.

t: Surface area of pyramids and cones
x:
Cone: SA = πr² + πrl, where r = radius and l = slant height (from the apex to the edge of the base). Lateral area = πrl.
Example: r = 3, l = 5 → SA = 9π + 15π = 24π ≈ 75.40.
Slant height from perpendicular height: l = √(r² + h²). With r = 3, h = 4: l = 5.
Regular pyramid: SA = B + ½ × P × l, where B = base area, P = base perimeter, l = slant height of a face.
Example: square base side 6, slant height 5: SA = 36 + ½ × 24 × 5 = 96.
Common mistake: using the perpendicular height h where the slant height l is required.

t: Euler's formula and the Platonic solids
x:
For any convex polyhedron: V − E + F = 2, where V = vertices (corners), E = edges, F = faces.
Example: cube has V = 8, E = 12, F = 6 → 8 − 12 + 6 = 2.
Example: triangular prism V = 6, E = 9, F = 5 → 2. Square pyramid V = 5, E = 8, F = 5 → 2.
The five Platonic solids (regular faces, same number meeting at each vertex): tetrahedron (4 triangular faces), cube (6 squares), octahedron (8 triangles), dodecahedron (12 pentagons), icosahedron (20 triangles).

d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²) for points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂). It is the Pythagorean theorem on the coordinate plane.
Example: (1, 2) to (4, 6): d = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.
Example: (−2, 5) to (3, −7): d = √(5² + (−12)²) = √169 = 13.
In 3D: d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²).
Common mistake: subtracting a negative incorrectly: 3 − (−2) = 5.

M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2): average the x-coordinates and average the y-coordinates.
Example: (−2, 3) and (4, 7) → M = (1, 5).
Finding a missing endpoint: midpoint (1, 5) and one endpoint (−2, 3): other endpoint = (2 × 1 − (−2), 2 × 5 − 3) = (4, 7).
Common mistake: subtracting instead of adding the coordinates.

t: Dividing a segment in a given ratio
x:
The point P that divides the directed segment from A(x₁, y₁) to B(x₂, y₂) in the ratio m : n (AP : PB = m : n) is
P = (x₁ + (m/(m + n))(x₂ − x₁), y₁ + (m/(m + n))(y₂ − y₁)).
Example: A(1, 2), B(7, 14), ratio 1 : 2 → fraction 1/3 → P = (1 + 2, 2 + 4) = (3, 6).
Common mistake: using m/n (here 1/2) instead of m/(m + n) (here 1/3).

t: Distance from a point to a line
a: distance from a point to a line
x:
Distance from (x₀, y₀) to the line Ax + By + C = 0 is |Ax₀ + By₀ + C| / √(A² + B²).
Example: point (1, 2) to 3x + 4y − 1 = 0: |3 + 8 − 1| / √(9 + 16) = 10/5 = 2.
Write the line in the form Ax + By + C = 0 first: y = 2x + 3 becomes 2x − y + 3 = 0.
The shortest distance is always measured along the perpendicular.

t: Area of a polygon from coordinates (shoelace formula)
x:
For vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), ..., (xₙ, yₙ) listed in order around the polygon:
A = ½ |(x₁y₂ − x₂y₁) + (x₂y₃ − x₃y₂) + ... + (xₙy₁ − x₁yₙ)|.
Triangle form: A = ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.
Example: (0, 0), (4, 0), (1, 3): A = ½ |0(0 − 3) + 4(3 − 0) + 1(0 − 0)| = ½ × 12 = 6.
If the result is 0, the points are collinear.
The vertices must go around the shape in order, not criss-cross.

Translation by (a, b): (x, y) → (x + a, y + b). Example: (2, −1) moved 3 left and 4 up → (−1, 3).
Reflection over the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y).
Reflection over the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y).
Reflection over y = x: (x, y) → (y, x). Over y = −x: (x, y) → (−y, −x).
Reflection over x = k: (x, y) → (2k − x, y). Over y = k: (x, y) → (x, 2k − y).
Example: (3, 5) reflected over the x-axis → (3, −5); over y = x → (5, 3).
Translations and reflections are rigid motions: they preserve lengths and angles.

Rotations about the origin (counterclockwise is the positive direction):
90° counterclockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x).
180°: (x, y) → (−x, −y).
270° counterclockwise = 90° clockwise: (x, y) → (y, −x).
Example: (3, 1) rotated 90° counterclockwise → (−1, 3); rotated 180° → (−3, −1); rotated 90° clockwise → (1, −3).
Rotations are rigid motions (lengths and angles stay the same).
Common mistake: mixing up clockwise and counterclockwise; check with (1, 0), which goes to (0, 1) under a 90° counterclockwise turn.

Dilation about the origin with scale factor k: (x, y) → (kx, ky).
About a center (a, b): (x, y) → (a + k(x − a), b + k(y − b)).
|k| > 1 enlarges, 0 < |k| < 1 shrinks; a negative k also flips the image through the center.
Example: (4, −2) dilated by k = 3 about the origin → (12, −6); by k = ½ → (2, −1).
Dilations preserve angles and shape (the image is similar), but lengths multiply by |k| and areas by k².
A dilation is NOT a rigid motion unless |k| = 1.

Line (reflectional) symmetry: a line divides the figure into mirror-image halves.
Rotational symmetry: the figure looks the same after a rotation of less than 360° about its center. The order is how many times it matches itself in a full turn.
A regular n-gon has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n (smallest angle 360°/n).
Examples: square: 4 lines, order 4 (90°). Rectangle (non-square): 2 lines, order 2. Rhombus (non-square): 2 lines, order 2. Isosceles triangle: 1 line. Parallelogram (general): 0 lines, order 2. Circle: infinitely many lines.

For an acute angle θ in a right triangle:
sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse (SOH); cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse (CAH); tan θ = opposite/adjacent (TOA).
Opposite = side across from θ; adjacent = the leg touching θ; hypotenuse = side across from the right angle.
Example: hypotenuse 10, θ = 35°: opposite = 10 sin 35° ≈ 5.74; adjacent = 10 cos 35° ≈ 8.19.
Example: θ = 50°, adjacent 6 → opposite = 6 tan 50° ≈ 7.15.
Common mistakes: labelling sides relative to the wrong angle; calculator in radian mode when the angle is in degrees.

t: Finding an angle with inverse trig functions
x:
If you know two sides of a right triangle, pick the ratio that uses them, then apply the inverse function: θ = sin⁻¹(opp/hyp), θ = cos⁻¹(adj/hyp), θ = tan⁻¹(opp/adj).
Example: opposite 3, adjacent 4 → θ = tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.87°.
Example: opposite 5, hypotenuse 13 → θ = sin⁻¹(5/13) ≈ 22.62°.
The other acute angle is 90° − θ.
Ranges (principal values): sin⁻¹ gives −90° to 90°; cos⁻¹ gives 0° to 180°; tan⁻¹ gives between −90° and 90°.
Common mistake: sin⁻¹(x) is the inverse function (arcsin), not 1/sin x (which is csc x).

csc θ = 1/sin θ = hypotenuse/opposite.
sec θ = 1/cos θ = hypotenuse/adjacent.
cot θ = 1/tan θ = cos θ/sin θ = adjacent/opposite.
Quotient identities: tan θ = sin θ/cos θ; cot θ = cos θ/sin θ.
Example: if sin θ = 3/5 (θ acute), then cos θ = 4/5, tan θ = 3/4, csc θ = 5/3, sec θ = 5/4, cot θ = 4/3.
Memory aid: each 'co-' function pairs with a function without 'co-': csc ↔ sin, sec ↔ cos.

t: Exact trig values for special angles

a: cos and sin on unit circle
x is cos y is sin
x:
The unit circle has radius 1, centered at the origin. For an angle θ measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis, the point on the circle is (cos θ, sin θ), and tan θ = y/x.
First-quadrant points: 30° → (√3/2, 1/2); 45° → (√2/2, √2/2); 60° → (1/2, √3/2); 90° → (0, 1).
Other quadrants use the same numbers with signs: 120° → (−1/2, √3/2); 135° → (−√2/2, √2/2); 150° → (−√3/2, 1/2); 210° → (−√3/2, −1/2); 225° → (−√2/2, −√2/2); 240° → (−1/2, −√3/2); 300° → (1/2, −√3/2); 315° → (√2/2, −√2/2); 330° → (√3/2, −1/2).
Example: sin 240° = −√3/2; cos 135° = −√2/2; tan 150° = (1/2)/(−√3/2) = −√3/3.
For any angle on a circle of radius r: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.

Signs by quadrant (All Students Take Calculus): QI all positive; QII sin (and csc) positive; QIII tan (and cot) positive; QIV cos (and sec) positive.
Reference angle = the acute angle to the x-axis: QII: 180° − θ; QIII: θ − 180°; QIV: 360° − θ.
To evaluate: find the reference angle, take its trig value, attach the quadrant's sign.
Example: cos 210°: reference 30°, QIII where cos is negative → −√3/2.
Example: tan 300°: reference 60°, QIV where tan is negative → −√3.
Coterminal angles differ by multiples of 360° (2π) and have identical trig values: 405° ≡ 45°; −30° ≡ 330°.

sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
1 + tan²θ = sec²θ (divide the first by cos²θ).
1 + cot²θ = csc²θ (divide the first by sin²θ).
Example: sin θ = 5/13 and θ in quadrant II → cos²θ = 1 − 25/169 = 144/169, cos θ = −12/13 (negative in QII), tan θ = −5/12.
Rearranged forms: sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ; cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ.
Notation: sin²θ means (sin θ)², not sin(θ²).

Cofunction: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ; cos(90° − θ) = sin θ; tan(90° − θ) = cot θ (in radians, use π/2 − θ).
Example: sin 20° = cos 70°.
Even/odd: cos(−θ) = cos θ (cosine is even); sin(−θ) = −sin θ and tan(−θ) = −tan θ (odd).
Example: sin(−30°) = −1/2; cos(−60°) = 1/2.
Supplementary angles: sin(180° − θ) = sin θ; cos(180° − θ) = −cos θ.

sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B.
cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B (note the sign flips).
tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B).
Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4 ≈ 0.9659.
Example: cos 15° = cos(45° − 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.
Common mistake: sin(A + B) ≠ sin A + sin B.

sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ.
cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 2cos²θ − 1 = 1 − 2sin²θ.
tan 2θ = 2 tan θ/(1 − tan²θ).
Example: sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5 → sin 2θ = 2(3/5)(4/5) = 24/25; cos 2θ = 16/25 − 9/25 = 7/25.
Power-reducing forms: sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2; cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2.
Common mistake: sin 2θ ≠ 2 sin θ.

sin(θ/2) = ±√((1 − cos θ)/2).
cos(θ/2) = ±√((1 + cos θ)/2).
tan(θ/2) = (1 − cos θ)/sin θ = sin θ/(1 + cos θ).
The ± sign is chosen by the quadrant of θ/2, not of θ.
Example: sin 15° = √((1 − cos 30°)/2) = √((1 − √3/2)/2) = √(2 − √3)/2 ≈ 0.2588 (positive, since 15° is in QI).

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C, where lowercase letters are sides and each capital is the angle OPPOSITE that side. Works for any triangle.
Use it when you know two angles and a side (AAS, ASA) or two sides and a non-included angle (SSA, see the ambiguous case).
Example: A = 40°, B = 60°, a = 10 → b = 10 × sin 60°/sin 40° ≈ 13.47. Then C = 80° and c = 10 × sin 80°/sin 40° ≈ 15.32.
Common mistake: pairing a side with an angle that is not opposite it.

t: Ambiguous case (SSA) of the law of sines
x:
Given sides a and b and angle A (opposite a), with A acute, let h = b sin A:
a < h: no triangle. a = h: one right triangle. h < a < b: TWO triangles. a ≥ b: one triangle.
If A is obtuse: one triangle if a > b, none if a ≤ b.
Example: A = 30°, a = 7, b = 10: h = 10 sin 30° = 5, and 5 < 7 < 10 → two triangles. sin B = 10 sin 30°/7 ≈ 0.714, so B ≈ 45.58° or B ≈ 180° − 45.58° = 134.42°.
Check each candidate: the angles must sum to less than 180° before adding C.

c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C, where C is the angle between sides a and b (opposite side c). Same pattern for a² and b².
Use for SAS (find the third side) or SSS (find an angle).
Example (SAS): a = 5, b = 7, C = 60° → c² = 25 + 49 − 70 × ½ = 39 → c ≈ 6.24.
Angle form: cos C = (a² + b² − c²)/(2ab). Example (SSS): sides 7, 8, 9, angle opposite 9: cos C = (49 + 64 − 81)/112 = 2/7 → C ≈ 73.4°.
When C = 90°, it reduces to the Pythagorean theorem.
Common mistake: computing (a² + b² − 2ab) × cos C; the cos C multiplies only 2ab.

t: Area of a triangle using sine
x:
Area = ½ × a × b × sin C, where a and b are two sides and C is the angle BETWEEN them (included angle).
Example: a = 8, b = 11, C = 30° → Area = ½ × 8 × 11 × ½ = 22.
Example: two sides 6 and 6 with included angle 60° (equilateral) → ½ × 36 × √3/2 = 9√3 ≈ 15.59.
For a parallelogram with sides a, b and angle θ: Area = ab sin θ.

t: Graphs of sine and cosine: amplitude, period, shifts
x:
For y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D or y = A cos(B(x − C)) + D:
Amplitude = |A|. Period = 2π/|B| (or 360°/|B|). Phase (horizontal) shift = C (right if C > 0). Midline y = D; maximum D + |A|, minimum D − |A|.
Example: y = 3 sin(2(x − π/4)) + 1: amplitude 3, period π, shift π/4 right, midline y = 1, range 1 − 3 to 1 + 3 = [−2, 4].
If written y = A sin(Bx − c), factor B out first: the shift is c/B.
Parent graphs: sin x starts at (0, 0) going up; cos x starts at its maximum (0, 1). Both have period 2π and range [−1, 1].

t: Graph of tangent and other trig graphs
x:
y = tan x has period π (180°), zeros at x = kπ, and vertical asymptotes at x = π/2 + kπ (where cos x = 0). Range: all real numbers. No amplitude.
For y = A tan(Bx), period = π/|B|.
y = cot x has period π with asymptotes at x = kπ.
y = sec x and y = csc x have period 2π, with asymptotes where cos x = 0 and sin x = 0 respectively; their ranges are y ≤ −1 or y ≥ 1.
Example: y = tan(2x) has period π/2 and asymptotes at x = π/4 + kπ/2.

Angle of elevation: measured UP from the horizontal to the line of sight. Angle of depression: measured DOWN from the horizontal. For two observers looking at each other, the angle of elevation from one equals the angle of depression from the other (alternate interior angles).
Sketch a right triangle with the horizontal as one leg, then use SOH-CAH-TOA.
Example: standing 50 m from a tree, the angle of elevation to the top is 32° → height = 50 tan 32° ≈ 31.2 m.
Example: from a 40 m cliff, the angle of depression to a boat is 25° → horizontal distance = 40/tan 25° ≈ 85.8 m.
Common mistake: measuring the depression angle from the vertical cliff instead of the horizontal.

A point (r, θ): r = distance from the origin, θ = angle from the positive x-axis.
Polar → rectangular: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. Example: (2, 150°) → (2 × (−√3/2), 2 × ½) = (−√3, 1).
Rectangular → polar: r = √(x² + y²), tan θ = y/x. Example: (3, 4) → r = 5, θ = tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ 53.13°.
Choose θ in the correct quadrant: for (−3, −4), r = 5 and θ ≈ 233.13°, not 53.13°.
Complex numbers: a + bi = r(cos θ + i sin θ).

1) Isolate the trig function. 2) Find the reference angle. 3) Use quadrant signs to find all angles in one period. 4) Add multiples of the period for the general solution.
Example: 2 sin x − 1 = 0 → sin x = ½ → in [0, 2π): x = π/6 or 5π/6. General: x = π/6 + 2πk or 5π/6 + 2πk.
Example: tan x = −1 on [0°, 360°): reference 45°, tan negative in QII and QIV → x = 135° or 315°.
Quadratic in form: 2cos²x − cos x − 1 = 0 → (2cos x + 1)(cos x − 1) = 0 → cos x = −½ or 1 → x = 2π/3, 4π/3, 0 on [0, 2π).
Common mistake: dividing both sides by sin x or cos x and losing solutions where it equals 0.

a: median of even number of values
x:
Mean (average) = sum of the values ÷ number of values.
Median = middle value after sorting; with an even count, the mean of the two middle values.
Mode = the most frequent value (there can be none, one, or several). Range = maximum − minimum.
Example: 4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 8, 9 → sorted 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 8, 9. Mean = 43/7 ≈ 6.14; median = 6; mode = 8; range = 9 − 3 = 6.
Even count: 2, 5, 7, 10 → median = (5 + 7)/2 = 6.
Missing value: if 4 tests average 85, the total is 4 × 85 = 340.
Common mistake: finding the median without sorting first.

Weighted mean = Σ(wᵢ × xᵢ) / Σwᵢ, where xᵢ are the values and wᵢ their weights.
Example: tests 90 worth 40% and final 80 worth 60% → 0.4 × 90 + 0.6 × 80 = 36 + 48 = 84.
Example (GPA): 3 credits of A (4.0) and 4 credits of B (3.0): (3 × 4.0 + 4 × 3.0)/7 = 24/7 ≈ 3.43.
Combining groups: class of 20 averaging 70 and class of 30 averaging 80 → (20 × 70 + 30 × 80)/50 = 76, not 75.
If the weights are percentages that add to 100%, no division is needed.

t: Quartiles, IQR, box plots and outliers
x:
Five-number summary: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum (drawn as a box plot). Q1 = median of the lower half, Q3 = median of the upper half (the common school method leaves the overall median out of both halves when n is odd).
IQR = Q3 − Q1 (spread of the middle 50%).
Outlier rule: a value is an outlier if it is below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
Example: 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12: median 6.5; Q1 = (3 + 4)/2 = 3.5; Q3 = (8 + 10)/2 = 9; IQR = 5.5. Fences: 3.5 − 8.25 = −4.75 and 9 + 8.25 = 17.25, so no outliers.
Calculators and software sometimes use slightly different quartile methods, so answers can differ a little.

MAD = (Σ|xᵢ − x̄|)/n: the average distance of the data values from the mean x̄.
Steps: find the mean; find each value's distance from the mean (absolute value); average those distances.
Example: 2, 4, 6, 8: mean 5; distances 3, 1, 1, 3; MAD = 8/4 = 2.
A larger MAD means the data are more spread out. (Standard deviation is a related measure that squares the distances instead.)

Population: σ² = Σ(xᵢ − μ)²/N and σ = √σ². Sample: s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/(n − 1) and s = √s². μ or x̄ = mean; N or n = number of values.
Example: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: mean 5; squared deviations 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16 (sum 32). Population: σ² = 32/8 = 4, σ = 2. Sample: s² = 32/7 ≈ 4.57, s ≈ 2.14.
Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean, in the data's units; variance is in squared units.
Adding a constant to every value leaves σ unchanged; multiplying every value by k multiplies σ by |k|.
Common mistakes: forgetting the square root; dividing by n when the data are a sample (use n − 1).

z = (x − μ)/σ, where x = the value, μ = mean, σ = standard deviation. z tells how many standard deviations x is above (z > 0) or below (z < 0) the mean.
Example: score 85, mean 70, standard deviation 10 → z = 15/10 = 1.5.
Reverse: x = μ + zσ. With μ = 70, σ = 10, z = −2 → x = 50.
Comparing: 85 on a test with mean 70, σ 10 (z = 1.5) beats 90 on a test with mean 80, σ 8 (z = 1.25).
For a normal distribution, |z| > 2 is unusual (about 5% of values) and |z| > 3 is very rare (about 0.3%).

A normal distribution is a symmetric bell curve; mean = median = mode at the center.
Empirical rule: about 68% of values lie within 1σ of the mean, about 95% within 2σ, about 99.7% within 3σ.
Pieces: mean to +1σ ≈ 34%; +1σ to +2σ ≈ 13.5%; +2σ to +3σ ≈ 2.35%; beyond +3σ ≈ 0.15%.
Example: IQ with mean 100, σ = 15: about 68% between 85 and 115; about 95% between 70 and 130; about 2.5% above 130; about 16% above 115.
More precisely, 95% lies within 1.96σ. For other z-values use a z-table or calculator (normalcdf).

t: Shape of a distribution: skew and resistant measures
x:
Skewed right (positive skew): long tail to the right; usually mean > median. Example: incomes.
Skewed left (negative skew): long tail to the left; usually mean < median. Example: scores on an easy test.
Symmetric: mean ≈ median.
The mean is pulled toward the tail and toward outliers; the median is resistant (barely affected). Use median and IQR for skewed data or data with outliers; mean and standard deviation for roughly symmetric data.
Example: 20, 22, 23, 25, 200 → mean 58, median 23. The median better describes a typical value.
Skew direction is named after the TAIL, not the peak.

Population: the whole group of interest. Sample: the part actually measured. Parameter: a number describing a population (μ, σ, p). Statistic: a number computed from a sample (x̄, s, p̂).
Simple random sample: every group of n individuals is equally likely to be chosen.
Stratified: split into groups (strata), randomly sample within each. Cluster: randomly choose whole groups and use everyone in them. Systematic: every k-th individual after a random start.
Biased methods: convenience samples and voluntary-response samples (people choose to respond).
Observational studies can show association; only randomized experiments can show cause and effect.

t: Standard error and margin of error
x:
Standard error of a sample mean: SE = σ/√n (use s when σ is unknown). Of a sample proportion: SE = √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Margin of error = z* × SE, with z* = 1.645 (90%), 1.96 (95%), 2.576 (99%). Confidence interval = estimate ± margin of error.
Example: p̂ = 0.60 from n = 400: SE = √(0.24/400) ≈ 0.0245; 95% margin ≈ 1.96 × 0.0245 ≈ 0.048, so the interval is about 0.552 to 0.648.
To halve the margin of error you need 4 times the sample size.
For means from small samples with unknown σ, use t* from the t-distribution instead of z*.

r measures the strength and direction of a LINEAR relationship between two quantitative variables. −1 ≤ r ≤ 1.
r > 0: positive (both increase together); r < 0: negative; r near 0: little linear relationship. |r| close to 1 means points lie close to a line.
r has no units and does not change if you swap x and y or change units.
r² (coefficient of determination) = fraction of the variation in y explained by the linear model. r = −0.8 → r² = 0.64, i.e. 64%.
Correlation does not imply causation; r can be near 0 for a strong curved relationship; outliers can change r a lot.

ŷ = a + bx, with slope b = r × (s_y/s_x) and intercept a = ȳ − b × x̄. The line always passes through (x̄, ȳ). Here r = correlation, s_x and s_y = standard deviations, x̄ and ȳ = means.
Slope meaning: predicted change in y for each 1-unit increase in x.
Residual = observed y − predicted ŷ. Positive residual: the point lies above the line.
Example: ŷ = 12 + 3.5x predicts ŷ = 12 + 3.5 × 4 = 26 at x = 4; if the actual y is 29, the residual is 29 − 26 = 3.
Extrapolation (predicting far outside the range of the data) is unreliable.

P(event) = (number of favorable outcomes)/(total number of equally likely outcomes). 0 ≤ P ≤ 1: 0 = impossible, 1 = certain.
Example: rolling an even number on a fair die: 3/6 = 1/2.
Example: drawing a heart from a standard 52-card deck: 13/52 = 1/4. A deck has 4 suits of 13 cards; 12 face cards (J, Q, K); 4 aces.
Experimental probability = (times it happened)/(number of trials). It approaches the theoretical value over many trials (law of large numbers).
Sum of two dice: 36 equally likely outcomes; P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6 (7 is the most likely sum).

P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
'At least one' problems are usually easiest as 1 − P(none).
Example: P(at least one 6 in 4 rolls of a die) = 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 1 − 0.482 = 0.518.
Example: P(at least one head in 3 coin flips) = 1 − (1/2)³ = 7/8.
Common mistake: adding probabilities for 'at least one' (1/6 × 4 = 4/6 is wrong).

t: Addition rule (A or B) and mutually exclusive events
x:
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Subtract the overlap so it is not counted twice.
Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events cannot happen together: P(A and B) = 0, so P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
Example: one card is a king or a heart: 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13.
Example: a die shows 1 or 6: 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3 (mutually exclusive).
Set notation: A ∪ B = A or B (union); A ∩ B = A and B (intersection).
Common mistake: confusing mutually exclusive with independent; disjoint events with nonzero probabilities are never independent.

t: Multiplication rule (A and B), independent and dependent events
x:
Independent events (one does not affect the other): P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
Dependent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A), where P(B | A) is the probability of B once A has happened.
Example (independent): two heads in two coin flips = ½ × ½ = ¼.
Example (without replacement): two aces in a row from a deck = 4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221.
With replacement, the draws are independent: 4/52 × 4/52 = 1/169.
Test for independence: A and B are independent exactly when P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B), read 'probability of A given B' (P(B) > 0). B becomes the new whole.
Example (two-way table): of 100 students, 40 play a sport; 25 students both play a sport and are in band. P(band | sport) = 25/40 = 0.625.
Example: rolling a die, P(6 | even) = (1/6)/(1/2) = 1/3.
In a table, divide by the row or column total of the condition, not by the grand total.
Common mistake: P(A | B) is usually not equal to P(B | A).

a: probability of disease given positive test
x:
P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) / P(B), where P(B) = P(B | A)P(A) + P(B | not A)P(not A).
Example: a disease affects 1% of people; a test is positive for 90% of people who have it and for 5% of people who do not. P(disease | positive) = (0.90 × 0.01)/(0.90 × 0.01 + 0.05 × 0.99) = 0.009/0.0585 ≈ 0.154, only about 15%.
A tree diagram or a table of 10,000 imaginary people gives the same answer: 90 true positives versus 495 false positives.
Lesson: when a condition is rare, most positive results can be false positives.

If one choice can be made in m ways and a second, independent choice in n ways, together there are m × n ways. Extend to any number of choices.
Example: 3 shirts, 4 pants, 2 pairs of shoes → 3 × 4 × 2 = 24 outfits.
Example: license plates with 3 letters then 4 digits (repeats allowed): 26³ × 10⁴ = 175,760,000.
Example: a 4-digit PIN with digits 0-9: 10⁴ = 10,000; with no repeated digits: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5,040.
Use multiplication for 'and then' choices; use addition for separate 'either/or' cases.

P(n, r) = n!/(n − r)!: the number of ways to choose AND ORDER r items from n different items.
Example: gold, silver and bronze among 10 runners: P(10, 3) = 10 × 9 × 8 = 720.
All n items in a row: n! ways. 5 books on a shelf: 5! = 120.
With repeated items: n!/(n₁! n₂! ...). Letters of MISSISSIPPI (11 letters: 4 I, 4 S, 2 P, 1 M): 11!/(4! × 4! × 2!) = 34,650.
Around a circle: (n − 1)! ways. 6 people at a round table: 5! = 120.
Use permutations when positions or roles differ (first/second, president/vice-president).

C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!): the number of ways to choose r items from n when order does NOT matter. Also written nCr or 'n choose r'.
Example: a committee of 3 from 10 people: C(10, 3) = 720/6 = 120.
Example: 5-card poker hands from 52 cards: C(52, 5) = 2,598,960.
Facts: C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1; C(n, 1) = n; C(n, r) = C(n, n − r).
Relationship: C(n, r) = P(n, r)/r!.
Probability with combinations: P(both cards red, drawn from a deck) = C(26, 2)/C(52, 2) = 325/1326 = 25/102.
Common mistake: using permutations for groups/committees where order is irrelevant.

E(X) = Σ xᵢ × P(xᵢ): multiply each outcome by its probability and add. It is the long-run average per trial.
Example: win $10 with probability 0.2, lose $3 with probability 0.8: E = 10(0.2) + (−3)(0.8) = 2 − 2.4 = −$0.40 per play.
Example: one roll of a fair die: E = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 3.5.
A game is fair when its expected value is 0.
Common mistake: forgetting to subtract the cost to play from the prize amounts.

P(X = k) = C(n, k) × pᵏ × (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, where n = number of independent trials, p = probability of success on each trial, k = number of successes.
Conditions: fixed n, two outcomes per trial, constant p, independent trials.
Example: exactly 3 heads in 5 fair coin flips: C(5, 3)(0.5)³(0.5)² = 10/32 = 0.3125.
Mean = np; standard deviation = √(np(1 − p)). Example: n = 20, p = 0.3 → mean 6, SD ≈ 2.05.
'At least' questions: add the needed terms, or use 1 − P(fewer).

Odds in favor = (favorable outcomes) : (unfavorable outcomes). Odds against = unfavorable : favorable.
Probability = favorable/(total). Odds a : b in favor → probability a/(a + b).
Example: rolling a 6: probability 1/6; odds in favor 1 : 5; odds against 5 : 1.
Example: odds in favor 3 : 7 → probability 3/10.
Common mistake: odds of 1 : 5 does not mean probability 1/5.

lim x→a f(x) = L means f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x approaches a (from both sides), whatever f(a) itself is.
One-sided limits: x→a⁻ (from the left), x→a⁺ (from the right). The two-sided limit exists only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal.
Direct substitution: for polynomials, and for rational, root, trig, exponential and log functions at points in their domain, just plug in: lim x→2 (x² + 3x) = 10.
The limit does not exist (DNE) if the one-sided limits differ, the function grows without bound, or it oscillates. Example: lim x→0 of |x|/x: left = −1, right = 1, so DNE.
If substitution gives 0/0, the limit is not yet determined; simplify first.

0/0 is an indeterminate form: try algebra before giving up.
Factor and cancel: lim x→3 (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = lim x→3 (x + 3) = 6.
Rationalize: lim x→0 (√(x + 4) − 2)/x: multiply by (√(x + 4) + 2)/(√(x + 4) + 2) → lim 1/(√(x + 4) + 2) = 1/4.
Combine fractions: lim x→0 (1/(x + 2) − 1/2)/x = lim −1/(2(x + 2)) = −1/4.
Other tools: special trig limits and L'Hôpital's rule.
A nonzero number over 0 (like 5/0) is not indeterminate: the function goes to ±∞ (vertical asymptote) and the limit does not exist as a finite number.

lim x→0 (sin x)/x = 1 (x in radians).
lim x→0 (1 − cos x)/x = 0.
lim n→∞ (1 + 1/n)ⁿ = e ≈ 2.71828; more generally lim n→∞ (1 + k/n)ⁿ = eᵏ.
lim x→0 (eˣ − 1)/x = 1.
Example: lim x→0 sin(5x)/x = 5 × lim sin(5x)/(5x) = 5.
Example: lim x→0 sin(3x)/sin(2x) = 3/2.

t: Limits at infinity and horizontal asymptotes
x:
For a rational function as x → ±∞, compare the degrees of top (m) and bottom (n):
m < n → limit 0. m = n → ratio of the leading coefficients. m > n → the function goes to ±∞ (no finite limit).
Example: lim x→∞ (3x² + 1)/(5x² − x) = 3/5.
Example: lim x→∞ (2x + 7)/(x³ − 4) = 0.
Technique: divide every term by the highest power of x in the denominator.
Growth order for large x: ln x ≪ xᵖ (p > 0) ≪ aˣ (a > 1) ≪ x!. So lim x→∞ x²/eˣ = 0.

If lim f(x)/g(x) gives 0/0 or ±∞/±∞, then lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f′(x)/g′(x), provided the new limit exists (or is ±∞).
Differentiate the top and the bottom SEPARATELY (not the quotient rule).
Example: lim x→0 (eˣ − 1)/x = lim eˣ/1 = 1.
Example: lim x→∞ x/eˣ (∞/∞) = lim 1/eˣ = 0.
It may be applied repeatedly while the form stays indeterminate: lim x→0 (1 − cos x)/x² = lim sin x/(2x) = lim cos x/2 = 1/2.
Other forms (0 × ∞, ∞ − ∞, 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰) must be rewritten as a fraction (or by taking ln) first.
Common mistake: using it when the form is not indeterminate.

t: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem
x:
f is continuous at x = a when: (1) f(a) is defined, (2) lim x→a f(x) exists, and (3) lim x→a f(x) = f(a).
Discontinuities: removable (a hole; the limit exists but differs from f(a) or f(a) is undefined), jump (one-sided limits differ), infinite (vertical asymptote).
Intermediate value theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and N is between f(a) and f(b), then f(c) = N for some c in [a, b].
Example: f(x) = x³ + x − 1 is continuous, f(0) = −1 < 0 and f(1) = 1 > 0, so f has a root between 0 and 1.
Differentiable implies continuous, but not the reverse: |x| is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there (corner).

f′(x) = lim h→0 [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. It is the instantaneous rate of change of f, and the slope of the tangent line to y = f(x).
At a point: f′(a) = lim x→a [f(x) − f(a)]/(x − a).
Example: f(x) = x²: [(x + h)² − x²]/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h → 2x as h → 0. So f′(x) = 2x.
Notation: f′(x), y′, dy/dx, d/dx[f(x)].
Average rate of change on [a, b] = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a) (slope of the secant line).
A derivative fails to exist at corners, cusps, vertical tangents and discontinuities.

t: Power, constant and sum rules for derivatives
x:
Power rule: d/dx[xⁿ] = n × xⁿ⁻¹ (any real n).
Constant: d/dx[c] = 0. Constant multiple: d/dx[c × f(x)] = c × f′(x). Sum/difference: (f ± g)′ = f′ ± g′.
Example: d/dx[4x⁵ − 3x² + 7x − 2] = 20x⁴ − 6x + 7.
Rewrite roots and fractions as powers first: √x = x^(1/2) → 1/(2√x); 1/x² = x⁻² → −2x⁻³ = −2/x³.
Common mistakes: the derivative of a constant like 7 is 0, not 7; d/dx[eˣ] is not x × eˣ⁻¹ (the power rule needs a variable base and a constant exponent).

d/dx[f(x) × g(x)] = f′(x)g(x) + f(x)g′(x). Memory: first-prime times second plus first times second-prime.
Example: d/dx[x² sin x] = 2x sin x + x² cos x.
Example: d/dx[x eˣ] = eˣ + x eˣ = eˣ(x + 1).
Common mistake: (fg)′ is NOT f′ × g′. For x² × x³: the correct derivative is 5x⁴, but f′g′ = 2x × 3x² = 6x³.

a: low d high minus high d low
x:
d/dx[f(x)/g(x)] = [f′(x)g(x) − f(x)g′(x)] / [g(x)]². Memory: 'low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared'.
Example: d/dx[(x² + 1)/(x − 1)] = [2x(x − 1) − (x² + 1)(1)]/(x − 1)² = (x² − 2x − 1)/(x − 1)².
Example: d/dx[sin x / x] = (x cos x − sin x)/x².
The ORDER in the numerator matters (it is a subtraction).
Tip: for a constant numerator, rewrite as a power: 3/x⁴ = 3x⁻⁴ → −12x⁻⁵.

d/dx[f(g(x))] = f′(g(x)) × g′(x). Equivalently dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) with u = g(x). Differentiate the outside function (keep the inside the same), then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
Example: d/dx[(3x² + 1)⁵] = 5(3x² + 1)⁴ × 6x = 30x(3x² + 1)⁴.
Example: d/dx[sin(4x)] = 4 cos(4x). d/dx[e^(x²)] = 2x e^(x²). d/dx[ln(x² + 1)] = 2x/(x² + 1).
Nested: d/dx[sin²(3x)] = 2 sin(3x) × cos(3x) × 3 = 6 sin(3x)cos(3x).
Common mistake: forgetting to multiply by the inside derivative.

d/dx sin x = cos x.
d/dx cos x = −sin x.
d/dx tan x = sec²x.
d/dx cot x = −csc²x.
d/dx sec x = sec x tan x.
d/dx csc x = −csc x cot x.
These hold with x in radians. The 'co-' functions get a minus sign.
With the chain rule: d/dx cos(5x) = −5 sin(5x); d/dx tan(x²) = 2x sec²(x²).

t: Derivatives of exponential and logarithmic functions
x:
d/dx eˣ = eˣ.
d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a (a > 0).
d/dx ln x = 1/x (x > 0); d/dx ln|x| = 1/x (x ≠ 0).
d/dx log_a x = 1/(x ln a).
With the chain rule: d/dx e^(3x) = 3e^(3x); d/dx 2ˣ = 2ˣ ln 2; d/dx ln(5x) = 5/(5x) = 1/x.
Logarithmic differentiation (for y = xˣ): ln y = x ln x → y′/y = ln x + 1 → y′ = xˣ(ln x + 1).
Common mistake: d/dx eˣ is not x eˣ⁻¹.

d/dx arcsin x = 1/√(1 − x²) (|x| < 1).
d/dx arccos x = −1/√(1 − x²) (|x| < 1).
d/dx arctan x = 1/(1 + x²).
d/dx arccot x = −1/(1 + x²).
d/dx arcsec x = 1/(|x|√(x² − 1)) (|x| > 1).
With the chain rule: d/dx arctan(2x) = 2/(1 + 4x²).
arcsin x is the same as sin⁻¹ x.

When y is not isolated: differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x (so every derivative of a y-term gets a factor dy/dx by the chain rule), then solve for dy/dx.
Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y. At (3, 4): slope = −3/4.
Example: xy + y³ = 10 → (y + x dy/dx) + 3y² dy/dx = 0 → dy/dx = −y/(x + 3y²).
Common mistakes: d/dx[y²] = 2y(dy/dx), not 2y; use the product rule on terms like xy.

Tangent line to y = f(x) at x = a: y − f(a) = f′(a)(x − a).
Example: f(x) = x³ at x = 2: f(2) = 8, f′(x) = 3x², f′(2) = 12 → y − 8 = 12(x − 2), i.e. y = 12x − 16.
Normal line: perpendicular to the tangent, slope −1/f′(a).
Linear approximation: f(x) ≈ L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) for x near a.
Example: √4.1 with f(x) = √x, a = 4: f′(4) = 1/(2√4) = 1/4 → √4.1 ≈ 2 + 0.25 × 0.1 = 2.025 (true value ≈ 2.02485).

t: Critical points, increasing/decreasing and the first derivative test
x:
Critical points: x-values in the domain where f′(x) = 0 or f′(x) does not exist.
f′ > 0 on an interval → f increasing; f′ < 0 → f decreasing.
First derivative test: f′ changes + to − at c → local maximum; − to + → local minimum; no sign change → neither.
Example: f(x) = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1); critical points x = −1, 3. f′ is + before −1, − between, + after 3. Local max f(−1) = 10; local min f(3) = −22.
Absolute extrema on a closed interval [a, b]: compare f at the critical points AND at the endpoints a and b (closed interval method).

t: Second derivative, concavity and inflection points
x:
f″ > 0 → concave up (holds water, slopes increasing); f″ < 0 → concave down.
Inflection point: where the concavity changes (f″ changes sign); f″ = 0 alone is not enough. For f(x) = x⁴, f″(0) = 0 but there is no inflection point.
Second derivative test at a critical point c with f′(c) = 0: f″(c) > 0 → local min; f″(c) < 0 → local max; f″(c) = 0 → the test fails (use the first derivative test).
Example: f(x) = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5: f″(x) = 6x − 6. f″(−1) = −12 < 0 → local max at x = −1; f″(3) = 12 > 0 → local min at x = 3; inflection point at x = 1, the point (1, −6).

1) Draw a picture and name the variables. 2) Write the quantity to optimize as a function. 3) Use the constraint to reduce it to one variable. 4) Find the domain. 5) Set the derivative to 0 and solve. 6) Confirm max/min (sign chart, second derivative, or endpoints). 7) Answer the question asked, with units.
Example: 100 m of fence for a rectangle along a river (no fence on the river side). Width x, length 100 − 2x. Area A(x) = x(100 − 2x) = 100x − 2x², 0 < x < 50. A′(x) = 100 − 4x = 0 → x = 25. A″ = −4 < 0, so maximum: 25 m by 50 m, area 1,250 m².
Without the river (four sides), the best rectangle is a 25 m square with area 625 m².

a: implicit differentiation with respect to time
x:
1) Identify the given rate and the wanted rate (both are derivatives with respect to time t). 2) Write an equation linking the quantities. 3) Differentiate both sides with respect to t (chain rule). 4) Substitute the values at the instant asked about, only AFTER differentiating. 5) Solve.
Example: a circle's radius grows at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area growing when r = 5 cm? A = πr² → dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt) = 2π(5)(2) = 20π ≈ 62.8 cm²/s.
Example (ladder): x² + y² = 13²; base slides out at dx/dt = 2 ft/s when x = 5, so y = 12: 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0 → dy/dt = −(5 × 2)/12 = −5/6 ft/s (the top slides down).
Common mistake: plugging in numbers for changing quantities before differentiating.

t: Mean value theorem and Rolle's theorem
x:
Mean value theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then there is at least one c in (a, b) with f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a): at some point the instantaneous rate equals the average rate.
Example: f(x) = x² on [1, 3]: average rate = (9 − 1)/2 = 4; f′(c) = 2c = 4 → c = 2.
Rolle's theorem (special case): if also f(a) = f(b), then f′(c) = 0 for some c in (a, b).
Both hypotheses matter: f(x) = |x| on [−1, 1] is not differentiable at 0 and has no c with f′(c) = 0.

Velocity v(t) = s′(t); acceleration a(t) = v′(t) = s″(t). Speed = |v(t)|.
The object is at rest when v = 0 and changes direction when v changes sign. It speeds up when v and a have the same sign, slows down when the signs differ.
Example: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t: v(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3); a(t) = 6t − 12. At rest at t = 1 and t = 3.
Displacement from t = a to b = ∫ v(t) dt from a to b. Total distance = ∫ |v(t)| dt from a to b.
In the example, displacement on [0, 3] is s(3) − s(0) = 0, but distance is 4 + 4 = 8 (out to s(1) = 4 and back).

t: Antiderivatives and the power rule for integrals
x:
F is an antiderivative of f if F′(x) = f(x). ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant of integration.
Power rule: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C for n ≠ −1. For n = −1: ∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C.
∫ k dx = kx + C; constants factor out; integrate sums term by term.
Example: ∫ (6x² − 4x + 5) dx = 2x³ − 2x² + 5x + C.
Example: ∫ √x dx = ∫ x^(1/2) dx = (2/3)x^(3/2) + C.
Initial value: if f′(x) = 2x and f(1) = 5, then f(x) = x² + C and 1 + C = 5, so f(x) = x² + 4.
Common mistake: forgetting + C, or integrating a product term by term (∫ fg dx ≠ ∫ f dx × ∫ g dx).

∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C. ∫ aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + C. ∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C.
∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C. ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C.
∫ sec²x dx = tan x + C. ∫ csc²x dx = −cot x + C.
∫ sec x tan x dx = sec x + C. ∫ csc x cot x dx = −csc x + C.
∫ tan x dx = −ln|cos x| + C = ln|sec x| + C. ∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C.
∫ 1/(1 + x²) dx = arctan x + C. ∫ 1/√(1 − x²) dx = arcsin x + C.
Linear inside: ∫ e^(kx) dx = e^(kx)/k + C; ∫ cos(kx) dx = sin(kx)/k + C; ∫ 1/(ax + b) dx = (1/a) ln|ax + b| + C.
Check any antiderivative by differentiating it.

∫ from a to b of f(x) dx is the signed area between y = f(x) and the x-axis from x = a to x = b: area above the axis counts positive, below counts negative.
∫ from a to a of f(x) dx = 0. ∫ from a to b of f dx = −∫ from b to a of f dx (swapping the limits flips the sign).
∫ from a to b of f dx + ∫ from b to c of f dx = ∫ from a to c of f dx. ∫ from a to b of [kf + g] dx = k × ∫ from a to b of f dx + ∫ from a to b of g dx.
Symmetry: f odd → ∫ from −a to a of f dx = 0; f even → ∫ from −a to a of f dx = 2∫ from 0 to a of f dx.
Example: ∫ from −2 to 2 of x³ dx = 0 (odd function).
For total geometric area, integrate |f(x)|, splitting at the zeros.

Part 2 (evaluation): if F′ = f and f is continuous on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).
Example: ∫ from 1 to 3 of x² dx = [x³/3] from 1 to 3 = 27/3 − 1/3 = 26/3 ≈ 8.67.
Example: ∫ from 0 to π of sin x dx = [−cos x] from 0 to π = 1 − (−1) = 2.
Part 1 (derivative of an integral): d/dx ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt = f(x).
With a variable upper limit g(x): d/dx ∫ₐ^g(x) f(t) dt = f(g(x)) × g′(x). Example: d/dx ∫₀^(x²) sin t dt = 2x sin(x²).
No + C is needed for definite integrals.

Reverses the chain rule. Choose u = an inside function whose derivative also appears (up to a constant factor).
1) Let u = g(x); compute du = g′(x) dx. 2) Rewrite the integral entirely in u. 3) Integrate. 4) Substitute back x.
Example: ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁵ dx: u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx → ∫ u⁵ du = u⁶/6 + C = (x² + 1)⁶/6 + C.
Example: ∫ cos(3x) dx: u = 3x, du = 3 dx → (1/3) sin(3x) + C.
Definite integrals: change the limits too. ∫ from 0 to 1 of 2x e^(x²) dx: u from 0 to 1 → ∫ from 0 to 1 of eᵘ du = e − 1 ≈ 1.718.
Common mistake: leaving some x's in the integral after substituting.

∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. It reverses the product rule.
Choose u by LIATE (pick the first type that appears): Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic (polynomials), Trig, Exponential. dv is the rest.
Example: ∫ x eˣ dx: u = x, dv = eˣ dx → du = dx, v = eˣ → x eˣ − ∫ eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C.
Example: ∫ ln x dx: u = ln x, dv = dx → du = dx/x, v = x → x ln x − ∫ 1 dx = x ln x − x + C.
Example: ∫ x cos x dx = x sin x − ∫ sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C.
Repeat for higher powers (∫ x² eˣ dx needs two rounds), or use the tabular method.

Area = ∫ₐᵇ [top function − bottom function] dx, where a and b are where the curves meet (or the given bounds).
Example: y = x and y = x² between their intersections x = 0 and x = 1 (x is on top there): ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6.
If the curves switch places, split the integral at each crossing.
For curves given as x = f(y), use ∫ (right − left) dy.
Common mistake: subtracting in the wrong order gives a negative 'area'.

t: Volumes of revolution (disk, washer and shell)
x:
Disk (rotate about the x-axis): V = π ∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx.
Washer: V = π ∫ₐᵇ ([R(x)]² − [r(x)]²) dx, where R = outer radius, r = inner radius.
Shell (rotate about the y-axis): V = 2π ∫ₐᵇ x × f(x) dx.
Example (disk): y = √x from 0 to 4 about the x-axis: V = π ∫ from 0 to 4 of x dx = π × 8 = 8π ≈ 25.13.
Example (washer): region between y = x and y = x² on [0, 1] about the x-axis: V = π ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x² − x⁴) dx = π(1/3 − 1/5) = 2π/15.
Common mistake: in the washer method, (R − r)² is wrong; use R² − r².

Average value of f on [a, b] = (1/(b − a)) × ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx.
Example: f(x) = x² on [0, 3]: (1/3) × [x³/3] from 0 to 3 = (1/3) × 9 = 3.
Mean value theorem for integrals: if f is continuous, f(c) equals this average for some c in [a, b]. Here c² = 3 → c = √3.
Do not confuse it with the average RATE of change, [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a).

t: Riemann sums and the trapezoidal rule
x:
Split [a, b] into n equal pieces of width Δx = (b − a)/n.
Left sum: Δx[f(x₀) + f(x₁) + ... + f(xₙ₋₁)]. Right sum: Δx[f(x₁) + ... + f(xₙ)]. Midpoint sum: use the midpoint of each piece.
Trapezoidal rule: (Δx/2)[f(x₀) + 2f(x₁) + 2f(x₂) + ... + 2f(xₙ₋₁) + f(xₙ)].
Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of x² dx with n = 2 (Δx = 1, points 0, 1, 2): left = 0 + 1 = 1; right = 1 + 4 = 5; trapezoid = ½(0 + 2 + 4) = 3. Exact value 8/3 ≈ 2.67.
For an increasing function the left sum underestimates and the right sum overestimates. As n → ∞ all of them approach the definite integral.

Taylor series of f centered at x = a: f(x) = Σ from n = 0 to ∞ of f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x − a)ⁿ/n! = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + f″(a)(x − a)²/2! + f‴(a)(x − a)³/3! + ...
Maclaurin series = Taylor series centered at a = 0.
The n-th degree Taylor polynomial Pₙ(x) keeps terms up to (x − a)ⁿ and approximates f near a.
Example: f(x) = eˣ at a = 0: all derivatives equal 1, so P₃(x) = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6. e^0.1 ≈ 1 + 0.1 + 0.005 + 0.000167 = 1.105167 (true 1.105171).
Lagrange error bound: |error| ≤ M|x − a|ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)!, where M bounds |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾| between a and x.
Common mistake: forgetting the n! in the denominators.

eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + x⁴/4! + ... (all real x).
sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − x⁷/7! + ... (all real x; odd powers).
cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − x⁶/6! + ... (all real x; even powers).
1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + x³ + ... (|x| < 1).
ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − x⁴/4 + ... (−1 < x ≤ 1).
arctan x = x − x³/3 + x⁵/5 − x⁷/7 + ... (|x| ≤ 1).
New series by substitution: e^(−x²) = 1 − x² + x⁴/2! − x⁶/3! + ...
Example: sin 0.2 ≈ 0.2 − 0.008/6 ≈ 0.198667 (true 0.198669).

The seven SI base units:
length – metre (m)
mass – kilogram (kg)
time – second (s)
electric current – ampere (A)
temperature – kelvin (K)
amount of substance – mole (mol)
luminous intensity – candela (cd)
All other units are derived from these, e.g. newton N = kg·m/s², joule J = N·m, watt W = J/s, pascal Pa = N/m², coulomb C = A·s, volt V = J/C, ohm Ω = V/A.
Classic mistake: the base unit of mass is the kilogram, not the gram.

tera (T) = 10¹²
giga (G) = 10⁹
mega (M) = 10⁶
kilo (k) = 10³
hecto (h) = 10²
deca (da) = 10¹
deci (d) = 10⁻¹
centi (c) = 10⁻²
milli (m) = 10⁻³
micro (μ) = 10⁻⁶
nano (n) = 10⁻⁹
pico (p) = 10⁻¹²

Average speed = total distance ÷ total time (a scalar, no direction).
Average velocity v = Δx ÷ Δt, where Δx is displacement (change in position, m) and Δt is time (s). Velocity is a vector: it has size and direction.
Units: m/s. 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h.
Example: running 400 m around a track in 80 s and ending at the start: average speed = 400 ÷ 80 = 5 m/s, but average velocity = 0 because displacement is 0.

a = Δv ÷ Δt = (v − v₀) ÷ t, where a is acceleration (m/s²), v₀ is initial velocity (m/s), v is final velocity (m/s) and t is time (s).
Acceleration is a vector. Negative acceleration means it points in the negative direction; it slows an object only if it is opposite to the velocity.
Example: a car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s: a = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s².
An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, because its direction changes.

Valid only when acceleration is constant:
1) v = v₀ + at
2) Δx = v₀t + ½at²
3) v² = v₀² + 2aΔx
4) Δx = ½(v₀ + v)t
v₀ = initial velocity (m/s), v = final velocity (m/s), a = acceleration (m/s²), t = time (s), Δx = displacement (m).
Pick the equation that contains your three knowns and the one unknown.
Example: from rest with a = 3 m/s² for 4 s: v = 0 + 3×4 = 12 m/s; Δx = ½×3×4² = 24 m.

In free fall (only gravity acts, no air resistance) every object accelerates downward at g ≈ 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface (standard value 9.80665 m/s²), regardless of mass.
Dropped from rest: v = gt, d = ½gt², v = √(2gd), where d is distance fallen (m) and t is time (s).
Example: a stone dropped from rest for 2 s: v = 9.8×2 = 19.6 m/s, d = ½×9.8×2² = 19.6 m.
At the top of an upward throw the velocity is 0 but the acceleration is still 9.8 m/s² downward.
Classic mistake: heavier objects do not fall faster without air resistance.

Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately (no air resistance):
horizontal: vₓ = v₀cosθ stays constant, x = vₓt
vertical: v_y = v₀sinθ − gt, y = v₀sinθ·t − ½gt²
On level ground: time of flight T = 2v₀sinθ ÷ g, maximum height H = v₀²sin²θ ÷ (2g), range R = v₀²sin(2θ) ÷ g.
v₀ = launch speed (m/s), θ = launch angle above horizontal, g = 9.8 m/s².
Maximum range on level ground is at θ = 45°; complementary angles (30° and 60°) give the same range.
Example: v₀ = 20 m/s at 45°: R = 20²×sin90° ÷ 9.8 ≈ 40.8 m, T ≈ 2.89 s, H ≈ 10.2 m.
A ball dropped and a ball fired horizontally from the same height land at the same time.

An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless acted on by a net (unbalanced) external force.
Inertia is the tendency to resist changes in motion; more mass means more inertia.
If the net force is zero, velocity is constant (which includes being at rest).
Example: passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly because their bodies keep moving.
Classic mistake: a moving object does not need a force to keep moving; it needs a force to change its motion.

F_net = m × a, where F_net is the net (total) force in newtons (N), m is mass in kilograms (kg) and a is acceleration in m/s².
1 N = 1 kg·m/s². Acceleration is in the same direction as the net force.
Rearranged: a = F_net ÷ m, m = F_net ÷ a.
Example: a 30 N push and 10 N of friction act on a 5 kg box: F_net = 30 − 10 = 20 N, so a = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s².
Classic mistake: using one force instead of the net force (add all forces as vectors first).

When object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts a force on A that is equal in size and opposite in direction.
The two forces act on different objects, so they never cancel each other.
They are the same type of force (e.g. both gravitational, both contact forces).
Example: a swimmer pushes water backward; the water pushes the swimmer forward. A rocket pushes exhaust gas down; the gas pushes the rocket up.
Classic mistake: weight and the normal force on a book on a table are NOT a third-law pair (both act on the book).

Mass (m) is the amount of matter, measured in kilograms (kg); it is the same everywhere.
Weight (W) is the gravitational force on an object, measured in newtons (N): W = m × g.
On Earth g ≈ 9.8 N/kg (= 9.8 m/s²); on the Moon g ≈ 1.6 N/kg, about 1/6 of Earth's.
Example: a 60 kg person weighs 60 × 9.8 = 588 N on Earth and about 60 × 1.6 = 96 N on the Moon, but their mass is 60 kg in both places.
Classic mistake: bathroom scales show kilograms, but they actually measure force and convert it.

Kinetic (sliding) friction: f_k = μ_k × N
Static friction (not sliding): f_s ≤ μ_s × N, up to a maximum of μ_s × N
f = friction force (N), μ = coefficient of friction (no units), N = normal force (N).
Friction acts parallel to the surfaces, opposite to the motion or attempted motion. Usually μ_k < μ_s, so it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.
Example: a 10 kg box slides on a level floor with μ_k = 0.3: N = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N, f_k = 0.3 × 98 = 29.4 N.
Classic mistake: static friction is not always μ_sN; it is only as large as needed to prevent sliding.

The normal force N is the push of a surface on an object, perpendicular to the surface.
On a level surface with no other vertical forces: N = mg.
On a ramp at angle θ to the horizontal, split weight mg into:
along the slope (down the ramp): mg sinθ
perpendicular to the slope: mg cosθ, so N = mg cosθ (no other perpendicular forces)
Frictionless ramp: a = g sinθ down the slope.
Example: θ = 30°, frictionless: a = 9.8 × sin30° = 4.9 m/s².
Classic mistake: swapping sin and cos; check that at θ = 0° the along-slope part is 0.

t: Uniform circular motion and centripetal force
x:
For an object moving in a circle at constant speed:
centripetal acceleration a_c = v² ÷ r (points toward the centre)
centripetal force F_c = m v² ÷ r
speed v = 2πr ÷ T
v = speed (m/s), r = radius (m), m = mass (kg), T = period, time for one revolution (s).
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it is the net inward force supplied by tension, gravity, friction, etc.
Example: a 0.5 kg ball on a 1 m string at 4 m/s: F_c = 0.5 × 4² ÷ 1 = 8 N of tension.
If the string breaks, the ball flies off along the tangent, not outward along the radius.

F = G × m₁ × m₂ ÷ r²
F = attractive force between the two masses (N), G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², m₁ and m₂ = masses (kg), r = distance between their centres (m).
The force is an inverse-square law: doubling r makes F one quarter as large.
Surface gravity of a planet: g = GM ÷ R² (M = planet mass, R = planet radius).
Example: Earth M = 5.972 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.371 × 10⁶ m gives g = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ × 5.972×10²⁴ ÷ (6.371×10⁶)² ≈ 9.82 m/s².
Classic mistake: r is measured centre to centre, not surface to surface.

For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm ÷ r² = mv² ÷ r.
Orbital speed v = √(GM ÷ r); period T = 2πr ÷ v = 2π√(r³ ÷ GM).
v = speed (m/s), G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², M = mass of the central body (kg), r = orbit radius from the centre of the central body (m).
The satellite's own mass m cancels out.
Example: low Earth orbit about 400 km up, r ≈ 6.771 × 10⁶ m: v = √(6.674×10⁻¹¹ × 5.972×10²⁴ ÷ 6.771×10⁶) ≈ 7.7 km/s.
Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they are in continuous free fall, not because gravity is absent.

1) Law of ellipses: each planet orbits the Sun in an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus.
2) Law of equal areas: a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves fastest when closest to the Sun (perihelion) and slowest when farthest (aphelion).
3) Law of periods: T² ∝ a³, where T is the orbital period and a is the semi-major axis (average distance).
For planets orbiting the Sun, with T in Earth years and a in AU: T² = a³.
Example: a planet at a = 4 AU has T = √(4³) = √64 = 8 years.

W = F × d × cosθ
W = work (joules, J), F = force (N), d = displacement (m), θ = angle between the force and the displacement.
1 J = 1 N·m.
If force and motion are in the same direction, W = Fd. If the force is perpendicular to the motion (θ = 90°), W = 0. If opposite (θ = 180°), work is negative (e.g. friction).
Example: pushing a cart with 50 N for 4 m in the direction it moves: W = 50 × 4 = 200 J.
Classic mistake: carrying a box horizontally at constant velocity — your upward force does no work on the box, because it is perpendicular to the motion.

KE = ½ × m × v²
KE = kinetic energy (J), m = mass (kg), v = speed (m/s).
Because speed is squared, doubling the speed makes KE four times as large.
KE is never negative and has no direction.
Work–energy theorem: the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy, W_net = ΔKE.
Example: a 1,000 kg car at 20 m/s: KE = ½ × 1000 × 20² = 200,000 J = 200 kJ.

PE = m × g × h
PE = gravitational potential energy (J), m = mass (kg), g = 9.8 m/s², h = height above a chosen reference level (m).
Only changes in PE matter, so you may choose any zero level (often the ground).
This formula is valid near Earth's surface where g is nearly constant.
Example: lifting a 2 kg book 1.5 m onto a shelf increases its PE by 2 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 29.4 J.

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed (law of conservation of energy).
With no friction or air resistance, mechanical energy is conserved: KE₁ + PE₁ = KE₂ + PE₂, i.e. ½mv₁² + mgh₁ = ½mv₂² + mgh₂.
With friction, some mechanical energy becomes thermal energy, but total energy is still conserved.
Dropped from rest through height h: v = √(2gh), independent of mass.
Example: a ball falls 5 m from rest: v = √(2 × 9.8 × 5) = √98 ≈ 9.9 m/s.

P = W ÷ t = E ÷ t, and for a constant force along the motion, P = F × v
P = power (watts, W), W = work done (J), E = energy transferred (J), t = time (s), F = force (N), v = speed (m/s).
1 W = 1 J/s. 1 kW = 1,000 W. 1 horsepower (hp) ≈ 746 W.
Example: lifting a 50 kg crate 2 m in 4 s: W = 50 × 9.8 × 2 = 980 J, P = 980 ÷ 4 = 245 W.
Classic mistake: do not confuse W (watt, the unit) with W (work, the quantity).

Efficiency = (useful energy output ÷ total energy input) × 100%
You may also use power: (useful power out ÷ power in) × 100%.
No real machine is 100% efficient; the wasted energy usually becomes heat (and sound).
Example: a motor uses 500 J of electrical energy and does 400 J of useful work: efficiency = 400 ÷ 500 × 100% = 80%; the other 100 J is wasted.
Classic mistake: an answer above 100% means input and output were swapped.

Momentum p = m × v, in kg·m/s; it is a vector in the direction of the velocity.
Impulse J = F × Δt = Δp = m(v − v₀), in N·s (1 N·s = 1 kg·m/s).
F = average force (N), Δt = contact time (s), m = mass (kg), v₀ and v = initial and final velocity (m/s).
For the same change in momentum, a longer contact time means a smaller force — this is why airbags, crumple zones and bending your knees on landing reduce injury.
Example: a 0.15 kg ball goes from 0 to 40 m/s: Δp = 0.15 × 40 = 6 kg·m/s; if contact lasts 0.01 s, F = 6 ÷ 0.01 = 600 N.

If no net external force acts, total momentum is conserved: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁' + m₂v₂' (primes = after).
Elastic collision: momentum AND kinetic energy are conserved.
Inelastic collision: momentum is conserved, but some kinetic energy becomes heat, sound or deformation.
Perfectly inelastic: the objects stick together: v' = (m₁v₁ + m₂v₂) ÷ (m₁ + m₂).
Example: a 2 kg cart at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg cart at rest and they stick: v' = (2×3 + 1×0) ÷ 3 = 2 m/s. KE drops from 9 J to 6 J.
Classic mistake: momentum is a vector — give velocities in opposite directions opposite signs.

τ = r × F × sinθ
τ = torque (N·m), r = distance from the pivot to where the force acts (m), F = force (N), θ = angle between r and F. If F is perpendicular to the lever arm, τ = rF.
Equilibrium (no linear or angular acceleration): net force = 0 and net torque = 0, so clockwise torques = counterclockwise torques.
Example: 20 N pushed perpendicular at the end of a 0.5 m wrench: τ = 0.5 × 20 = 10 N·m.
Seesaw: a 30 kg child 2 m from the pivot balances a 40 kg child at 30 × 2 ÷ 40 = 1.5 m on the other side.
Torque's unit N·m is not called a joule, even though it has the same base units.

t: Hooke's law and spring potential energy
x:
Hooke's law: F = −k × x (the size of the force is kx)
F = restoring force of the spring (N), k = spring constant (N/m), x = stretch or compression from the natural length (m). The minus sign means the force points back toward equilibrium.
Elastic potential energy stored: PE = ½ × k × x²
Valid only within the elastic limit (the spring returns to its original shape).
Example: a spring with k = 200 N/m stretched 0.1 m: F = 200 × 0.1 = 20 N, PE = ½ × 200 × 0.1² = 1 J.

t: Simple harmonic motion: spring and pendulum periods
x:
Simple harmonic motion: back-and-forth motion where the restoring force is proportional to displacement.
Mass on a spring: T = 2π√(m ÷ k)
Simple pendulum (small angles, about 15° or less): T = 2π√(L ÷ g)
T = period, time for one full cycle (s), m = mass (kg), k = spring constant (N/m), L = pendulum length (m), g = 9.8 m/s². Frequency f = 1 ÷ T (Hz).
A pendulum's period does not depend on its mass or (for small swings) its amplitude.
Example: L = 1.0 m: T = 2π√(1 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 2.0 s. A 0.5 kg mass on a 50 N/m spring: T = 2π√(0.01) ≈ 0.63 s.

ρ = m ÷ V
ρ (rho) = density, m = mass, V = volume. Units: kg/m³ or g/cm³ (1 g/cm³ = 1,000 kg/m³). 1 cm³ = 1 mL.
Water has a density of about 1.00 g/cm³ (1,000 kg/m³); objects denser than a liquid sink in it, less dense ones float.
Rearranged: m = ρV, V = m ÷ ρ.
Example: a 54 g block with volume 20 cm³: ρ = 54 ÷ 20 = 2.7 g/cm³ (the density of aluminium).
Ice (about 0.92 g/cm³) is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats.

P = F ÷ A
P = pressure (pascals, Pa), F = force perpendicular to the surface (N), A = area (m²). 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
Standard atmospheric pressure: 1 atm = 101,325 Pa ≈ 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg ≈ 14.7 psi.
The same force on a smaller area gives more pressure (why knives are sharp and snowshoes are wide).
Example: a 600 N person standing on 0.04 m² of shoe sole: P = 600 ÷ 0.04 = 15,000 Pa.

t: Pressure in a fluid at depth
x:
Pressure at depth h in a fluid: P = P₀ + ρgh
P₀ = pressure at the surface (often atmospheric, 101,325 Pa), ρ = fluid density (kg/m³), g = 9.8 m/s², h = depth below the surface (m).
ρgh alone is the gauge pressure (pressure above atmospheric).
Pressure depends on depth, fluid density, g and the surface pressure, not on the shape or width of the container.
Example: 10 m down in fresh water: ρgh = 1000 × 9.8 × 10 = 98,000 Pa, about one extra atmosphere, so total ≈ 199 kPa.

Pascal's principle: a pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid.
Hydraulic lift: F₁ ÷ A₁ = F₂ ÷ A₂, so F₂ = F₁ × (A₂ ÷ A₁).
F = force (N), A = piston area (m²).
The small piston must move farther: work in = work out (ignoring friction), so force is multiplied but energy is not.
Example: 100 N on a 0.01 m² piston connected to a 0.5 m² piston lifts 100 × 50 = 5,000 N.

Archimedes' principle: an object in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
F_b = ρ_fluid × V_displaced × g
F_b = buoyant force (N), ρ_fluid = density of the fluid (kg/m³), V_displaced = volume of fluid pushed aside (m³), g = 9.8 m/s².
An object floats if its average density is less than the fluid's; a floating object displaces its own weight of fluid.
Example: a fully submerged 0.002 m³ rock in water: F_b = 1000 × 0.002 × 9.8 = 19.6 N upward.
Classic mistake: use the fluid's density, not the object's density.

Electric charge Q is measured in coulombs (C). One electron carries −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; a proton carries +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. Charge is conserved.
Current I = Q ÷ t, in amperes (A); 1 A = 1 C/s. t = time (s).
Conventional current flows from + to − in the external circuit; electrons actually drift the opposite way, from − to +.
Example: 30 C passes a point in 10 s: I = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 A.
Ammeters are connected in series; voltmeters are connected in parallel.

V = I × R, where V is voltage (potential difference) in volts (V), I is current in amperes (A) and R is resistance in ohms (Ω).
Rearranged: I = V ÷ R, R = V ÷ I.
Example: a 12 V battery across a 4 Ω resistor gives I = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 A.
Ohm's law holds for ohmic conductors (constant R at constant temperature); a filament bulb's resistance rises as it heats up.
Resistance of a wire: R = ρL ÷ A — longer wires have more resistance, thicker wires less (ρ = resistivity in Ω·m, L = length in m, A = cross-sectional area in m²).

In a series circuit components are connected end to end in one loop.
Total resistance: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + …
Current is the same through every component.
Voltages add up: V_total = V₁ + V₂ + … (each Vᵢ = I × Rᵢ).
If one component breaks, the whole circuit stops (old-style holiday lights).
Example: 3 Ω and 6 Ω in series on a 9 V battery: R_total = 9 Ω, I = 9 ÷ 9 = 1 A, V₁ = 3 V, V₂ = 6 V.

In a parallel circuit components are on separate branches across the same two points.
Total resistance: 1 ÷ R_total = 1 ÷ R₁ + 1 ÷ R₂ + …
For two resistors: R_total = (R₁ × R₂) ÷ (R₁ + R₂).
Voltage is the same across every branch. Branch currents add: I_total = I₁ + I₂ + …
R_total is always smaller than the smallest single resistor. Household outlets are wired in parallel.
Example: 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel on 6 V: R_total = 18 ÷ 9 = 2 Ω, I_total = 3 A (2 A through the 3 Ω, 1 A through the 6 Ω).
Classic mistake: forgetting to flip 1/R_total at the end.

P = V × I = I² × R = V² ÷ R
P = power (W), V = voltage (V), I = current (A), R = resistance (Ω).
Energy used: E = P × t (joules if P in W and t in s).
Electricity bills use kilowatt-hours: 1 kWh = 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
Example: a 100 W bulb on for 10 hours uses 0.1 kW × 10 h = 1 kWh. On 120 V it draws I = 100 ÷ 120 ≈ 0.83 A.
Classic mistake: a kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not power.

F = k × q₁ × q₂ ÷ r²
F = electric force between two point charges (N), k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² (k = 1 ÷ 4πε₀), q₁ and q₂ = charges (C), r = distance between them (m).
Like charges repel, opposite charges attract. Inverse-square: doubling r gives one quarter of the force.
Example: two +1 μC charges (1 × 10⁻⁶ C each) 0.1 m apart: F = 8.99×10⁹ × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 0.1² ≈ 0.90 N, repulsive.
Classic mistake: forgetting to convert μC to C (× 10⁻⁶) or cm to m.

Electric field E = F ÷ q, the force per unit positive test charge; units N/C (same as V/m).
Point charge Q: E = kQ ÷ r², with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² and r = distance from the charge (m).
Uniform field between parallel plates: E = V ÷ d (V = voltage across the plates, d = separation in m).
Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges; closer lines mean a stronger field.
Example: 100 V across plates 0.02 m apart: E = 100 ÷ 0.02 = 5,000 V/m.

v = f × λ
v = wave speed (m/s), f = frequency (hertz, Hz = waves per second), λ (lambda) = wavelength (m).
Period T = 1 ÷ f (s).
For light and other electromagnetic waves in vacuum, v = c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.
Wave speed is set by the medium; changing the frequency changes the wavelength, not the speed.
Example: a 440 Hz sound in air at 343 m/s: λ = 343 ÷ 440 ≈ 0.78 m.
Amplitude (height of the wave) relates to energy and loudness/brightness, not to speed.

Transverse wave: particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction the wave travels; has crests and troughs. Examples: light and all electromagnetic waves, waves on a string, S-waves.
Longitudinal wave: particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel; has compressions and rarefactions. Examples: sound, P-waves.
