Mechanical waves (sound, water, seismic) need a medium; electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum.
Waves transfer energy, not matter.
Wavelength = distance between two neighbouring crests (or compressions); amplitude = maximum displacement from rest.

Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave; it cannot travel through a vacuum.
Speed of sound in dry air ≈ 331 + 0.6T m/s (T in °C), so about 343 m/s at 20 °C. Sound is faster in liquids (about 1,500 m/s in water) and usually faster still in solids.
Pitch depends on frequency; loudness depends on amplitude (intensity).
Human hearing range: roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Below is infrasound, above is ultrasound.
Echo: distance to a wall = v × t ÷ 2 (the sound goes there and back).
Example: an echo returns after 2 s in 343 m/s air: distance = 343 × 2 ÷ 2 = 343 m.

β = 10 × log₁₀(I ÷ I₀)
β = sound intensity level (decibels, dB), I = intensity (W/m²), I₀ = 1 × 10⁻¹² W/m² (threshold of hearing, 0 dB).
Every +10 dB is 10 times the intensity; +20 dB is 100 times; +3 dB is about double.
Example: I = 10⁻⁶ W/m²: β = 10 × log₁₀(10⁶) = 60 dB.
Classic mistake: 80 dB is not twice as intense as 40 dB; it is 10⁴ = 10,000 times as intense.

When a source and observer move toward each other the observed frequency is higher; when they move apart it is lower.
Sound: f' = f × (v + v_o) ÷ (v − v_s) for approaching motion; for receding use f' = f × (v − v_o) ÷ (v + v_s).
f' = observed frequency, f = emitted frequency (Hz), v = speed of sound (m/s), v_o = observer speed, v_s = source speed (m/s).
Example: a 500 Hz siren approaches a still listener at 20 m/s (v = 343 m/s): f' = 500 × 343 ÷ 323 ≈ 531 Hz; moving away: 500 × 343 ÷ 363 ≈ 472 Hz.
Light: galaxies moving away show redshift (longer wavelength); approaching objects show blueshift.
The source's actual frequency does not change; only the observed one does.

From longest wavelength / lowest frequency / lowest photon energy to shortest / highest:
radio waves → microwaves → infrared → visible light → ultraviolet → X-rays → gamma rays.
All travel at c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum.
Visible light is roughly 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Order of colours by decreasing wavelength: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (ROYGBIV).
Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are ionizing radiation and can damage cells and DNA.
Mnemonic: Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns.

t: Law of reflection and plane mirrors
a: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
x:
Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (a line perpendicular to the surface).
The incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane.
Plane mirror image: virtual, upright, same size as the object, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front; left and right appear reversed.
Specular reflection is from smooth surfaces (clear image); diffuse reflection is from rough surfaces (no image).
Classic mistake: measuring angles from the mirror surface instead of from the normal.

Refraction is the bending of a wave when it changes speed entering a new medium.
Index of refraction n = c ÷ v, where c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s (speed in vacuum) and v = speed in the medium. n has no units and is ≥ 1.
Typical values: vacuum 1 (air ≈ 1.0003), water 1.33, typical glass about 1.5, diamond 2.42.
Light entering a higher-n material slows and bends toward the normal; entering a lower-n material it bends away from the normal.
The frequency stays the same; the wavelength changes.
Example: in water v = 3.00×10⁸ ÷ 1.33 ≈ 2.26 × 10⁸ m/s.

a: n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2
x:
n₁ × sinθ₁ = n₂ × sinθ₂
n₁, n₂ = indices of refraction of the first and second media; θ₁ = angle of incidence, θ₂ = angle of refraction, both measured from the normal.
Example: light goes from air (n = 1.00) into water (n = 1.33) at 30°: sinθ₂ = 1.00 × sin30° ÷ 1.33 = 0.376, so θ₂ ≈ 22.1° (bent toward the normal).
Classic mistake: measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal, or leaving the calculator in radians.

t: Critical angle and total internal reflection
x:
Total internal reflection happens when light goes from a higher-n medium to a lower-n medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle; all the light reflects back.
Critical angle: sinθ_c = n₂ ÷ n₁ (requires n₁ > n₂), where n₁ is the medium the light starts in.
Example: water to air: sinθ_c = 1.00 ÷ 1.33, θ_c ≈ 48.8°.
Uses: optical fibres, binocular and periscope prisms; it also makes diamonds sparkle (high n, small critical angle).
It cannot happen when light goes from air into glass or water.

1 ÷ f = 1 ÷ d_o + 1 ÷ d_i, and magnification m = h_i ÷ h_o = −d_i ÷ d_o
f = focal length, d_o = object distance, d_i = image distance, h_o and h_i = object and image heights (all in the same unit).
Common sign convention: f > 0 for converging (convex) lenses and concave mirrors; f < 0 for diverging (concave) lenses and convex mirrors. d_i > 0 means a real image, d_i < 0 a virtual image. m < 0 means inverted, |m| > 1 means enlarged.
For a spherical mirror f = R ÷ 2 (R = radius of curvature).
Example: converging lens f = 10 cm, object at 30 cm: 1/d_i = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, d_i = 15 cm; m = −15 ÷ 30 = −0.5 (real, inverted, half size).
Lens power in diopters = 1 ÷ f with f in metres.

t: Images formed by lenses and mirrors
x:
Converging (convex) lens or concave mirror, object distance compared with focal length f:
beyond 2f: real, inverted, smaller (camera, eye)
at 2f: real, inverted, same size
between f and 2f: real, inverted, larger (projector)
at f: no image forms (rays come out parallel)
inside f: virtual, upright, larger (magnifying glass, makeup mirror)
Diverging (concave) lens or convex mirror: always virtual, upright and smaller (security and car side mirrors).
Real images can be projected onto a screen; virtual images cannot.
Nearsightedness is corrected with diverging lenses; farsightedness with converging lenses.

K = °C + 273.15 (often rounded to + 273)
°F = (9/5) × °C + 32
°C = (°F − 32) × 5/9
Reference points (at 1 atm): water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F = 273.15 K and boils at 100 °C = 212 °F = 373.15 K.
Absolute zero = 0 K = −273.15 °C = −459.67 °F. Kelvin has no negative values and is written K, not °K.
−40 °C = −40 °F (the two scales cross there).
Example: 25 °C = 9/5 × 25 + 32 = 77 °F = 298.15 K.

Q = m × c × ΔT
Q = heat added (J; negative if heat is removed), m = mass (kg or g), c = specific heat capacity (J/(kg·°C) or J/(g·°C)), ΔT = T_final − T_initial (°C or K; a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K).
Approximate specific heats: liquid water 4,186 J/(kg·°C) = 4.18 J/(g·°C) = 1 cal/(g·°C); ice about 2,100 J/(kg·°C); aluminium about 900; iron about 450; copper about 385.
Water's high specific heat is why it heats and cools slowly.
Example: heating 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C: Q = 2 × 4186 × 60 = 502,320 J ≈ 502 kJ.
This formula does not apply during a phase change (use Q = mL).

Q = m × L
Q = heat (J), m = mass (kg), L = specific latent heat (J/kg).
Water: latent heat of fusion (melting/freezing) L_f ≈ 334,000 J/kg = 334 J/g; latent heat of vaporization (boiling/condensing) L_v ≈ 2,260,000 J/kg = 2,260 J/g.
During a phase change the temperature stays constant; the energy breaks or forms bonds between particles (flat parts of a heating curve).
Example: melting 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C: Q = 0.5 × 334,000 = 167,000 J = 167 kJ.
To go from ice below 0 °C to steam, add each step separately: warm ice (mcΔT), melt (mL_f), warm water (mcΔT), boil (mL_v), warm steam.

Heat always flows on its own from hotter to colder objects.
Conduction: transfer through direct contact, particle to particle; best in solids, especially metals. Example: a metal spoon getting hot in soup.
Convection: transfer by movement of a fluid (liquid or gas); warm fluid rises, cool fluid sinks, forming convection currents. Example: boiling water, sea breezes, mantle convection.
Radiation: transfer by electromagnetic waves (mostly infrared); needs no medium, so it works through space. Example: heat from the Sun or a campfire.
Insulators (air, plastic, wool) are poor conductors.

At constant temperature and amount of gas: P₁ × V₁ = P₂ × V₂
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional: halve the volume and the pressure doubles.
P = pressure (any unit, the same on both sides), V = volume (any unit, the same on both sides).
Example: 2.0 L of gas at 100 kPa is allowed to expand until the pressure is 50 kPa: V₂ = 100 × 2.0 ÷ 50 = 4.0 L.

At constant pressure and amount of gas: V₁ ÷ T₁ = V₂ ÷ T₂
Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
V = volume, T = temperature in KELVIN.
Example: 3.0 L of gas at 300 K is heated to 600 K at constant pressure: V₂ = 3.0 × 600 ÷ 300 = 6.0 L.
Classic mistake: using °C. Doubling from 20 °C to 40 °C does not double the volume (293 K → 313 K is only about a 7% increase).

At constant volume and amount of gas: P₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂ ÷ T₂
Pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
P = pressure, T = temperature in kelvin.
Example: a sealed tank at 200 kPa and 300 K is heated to 450 K: P₂ = 200 × 450 ÷ 300 = 300 kPa.
This is why heated aerosol cans can burst and why tyre pressure rises on hot days.

For a fixed amount of gas: (P₁ × V₁) ÷ T₁ = (P₂ × V₂) ÷ T₂
P = pressure, V = volume, T = temperature in kelvin. Use the same units for P and for V on both sides.
It contains Boyle's (T constant), Charles's (P constant) and Gay-Lussac's (V constant) laws.
Example: 10.0 L at 1.00 atm and 300 K changes to 2.00 atm and 450 K: V₂ = 1.00 × 10.0 × 450 ÷ (300 × 2.00) = 7.5 L.
Adding the amount of gas n gives the ideal gas law PV = nRT.

If object A is in thermal equilibrium with object C, and object B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
Thermal equilibrium means no net heat flows between objects in contact; they are at the same temperature.
This is what makes thermometers work: the thermometer plays the role of C.

Energy is conserved: ΔU = Q − W
ΔU = change in internal energy of the system (J), Q = heat added TO the system (J), W = work done BY the system (J).
Many chemistry books write ΔU = Q + W, where W is work done ON the system; it is the same law with a different sign convention.
Example: a gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work pushing a piston: ΔU = 500 − 200 = 300 J.
Consequence: no machine can produce more energy than it takes in (no perpetual motion machine of the first kind).

t: Second law of thermodynamics and entropy
x:
Heat flows spontaneously only from hotter to colder objects.
The total entropy (a measure of disorder, or the spread of energy) of an isolated system never decreases.
No heat engine can turn heat completely into work; some heat must be released to a colder reservoir.
Maximum (Carnot) efficiency = 1 − T_cold ÷ T_hot, with temperatures in kelvin.
Example: an engine working between 500 K and 300 K: max efficiency = 1 − 300 ÷ 500 = 0.40 = 40%.
Refrigerators move heat from cold to hot only because they use work (electricity).

The entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as its temperature approaches absolute zero (0 K).
A consequence: absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps; it can only be approached.
Absolute zero is 0 K = −273.15 °C.

E = h × f = h × c ÷ λ
E = energy of one photon (J), h = Planck's constant = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, f = frequency (Hz), c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, λ = wavelength (m).
Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) means more energetic photons: a UV photon carries more energy than a red one.
1 electronvolt (eV) = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Example: green light λ = 500 nm = 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m: E = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ × 3.00×10⁸ ÷ 5.00×10⁻⁷ ≈ 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 2.48 eV.
Classic mistake: forgetting to convert nm to m (× 10⁻⁹).

Light shining on a metal can eject electrons, but only if each photon has enough energy.
KE_max = h × f − φ
KE_max = maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron (J or eV), h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, f = light frequency (Hz), φ (phi) = work function of the metal (minimum energy needed to free an electron).
Threshold frequency f₀ = φ ÷ h; below it no electrons are emitted no matter how bright the light.
Brighter light (at the same frequency) ejects more electrons, but not faster ones.
Einstein's explanation (1905) showed light comes in photons; he received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

E = m × c²
E = energy (J), m = mass (kg), c = speed of light = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s (c² ≈ 8.99 × 10¹⁶ m²/s²).
A small mass corresponds to a huge energy.
Example: 1 g = 0.001 kg: E = 0.001 × (2.998×10⁸)² ≈ 8.99 × 10¹³ J.
Mass defect: a nucleus has less mass than its separate protons and neutrons; the missing mass Δm times c² is the nuclear binding energy.
In nuclear energy units, 1 atomic mass unit (u) is equivalent to about 931.5 MeV.
Nuclear fission and fusion release energy because the products have slightly less total mass than the reactants.

Alpha (α): a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons), charge +2. Most ionizing, least penetrating; stopped by a sheet of paper or the outer layer of skin. Dangerous if swallowed or inhaled.
Beta-minus (β⁻): a fast electron emitted when a neutron changes into a proton; charge −1. Stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
Beta-plus (β⁺): a positron emitted when a proton changes into a neutron; charge +1.
Gamma (γ): a high-energy photon (electromagnetic wave), no charge, no mass. Least ionizing, most penetrating; reduced by thick lead or concrete.
Alpha and beta decay change the element; gamma emission does not.
In a magnetic or electric field α and β bend in opposite directions; γ is not deflected.

Half-life (T½) is the time for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.
N = N₀ × (½)^(t ÷ T½)
N = amount remaining, N₀ = starting amount (same units: grams, atoms or activity), t = time elapsed, T½ = half-life (same time unit as t).
Number of half-lives n = t ÷ T½; fraction left = (½)ⁿ.
Example: 80 g of an isotope with T½ = 5 days, after 15 days (3 half-lives): 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g.
Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years and is used to date once-living material up to roughly 50,000 years old.
Decay of a single nucleus is random; half-life describes large numbers of nuclei and is not changed by temperature or pressure.

Fission: a heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239) splits into two smaller nuclei plus a few neutrons, releasing energy. Those neutrons can split more nuclei, causing a chain reaction. Used in nuclear power plants and atomic bombs.
Example: ¹n + ²³⁵U → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3 ¹n + energy.
Fusion: light nuclei (such as hydrogen isotopes) join to form a heavier nucleus (such as helium), releasing energy. It needs extremely high temperature and pressure. Fusion powers the Sun and other stars.
Both release energy because the products have less mass than the reactants (E = mc²).

c = 299,792,458 m/s exactly (by definition of the metre since 1983).
Commonly rounded to 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, or about 300,000 km/s.
All electromagnetic waves travel at c in vacuum; nothing with mass can reach it.
Light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds (≈ 499 s) to travel from the Sun to Earth.

Standard gravity g₀ = 9.80665 m/s² exactly (defined value).
Commonly rounded to 9.8 m/s² or 9.81 m/s²; some problems use 10 m/s² for easy arithmetic.
The actual value varies slightly across Earth's surface (about 9.78 m/s² at the equator to 9.83 m/s² at the poles).
g is also the gravitational field strength: 9.8 N/kg.
Do not confuse little g (an acceleration) with big G (the universal gravitational constant).

G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² (CODATA 2018 value 6.67430 × 10⁻¹¹).
It appears in Newton's law of gravitation F = Gm₁m₂ ÷ r².
G is the same everywhere in the universe; it is very small, which is why gravity between everyday objects is too weak to notice.
First measured by Henry Cavendish with a torsion balance (1798).

h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s exactly (fixed in the 2019 SI redefinition).
Commonly rounded to 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
In electronvolts: h ≈ 4.136 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV·s.
Reduced Planck constant ħ = h ÷ 2π ≈ 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
Used in E = hf and the de Broglie wavelength λ = h ÷ p.

e = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C exactly (fixed in the 2019 SI redefinition).
Commonly rounded to 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
A proton has charge +e; an electron has charge −e.
1 coulomb is the charge of about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons.
1 electronvolt (eV) = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

mₑ = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg (CODATA 2018: 9.1093837015 × 10⁻³¹ kg).
In atomic mass units: about 0.000549 u (about 1/1836 of the proton's mass).
Energy equivalent: about 0.511 MeV.

mₚ = 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (CODATA 2018: 1.67262192369 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
In atomic mass units: about 1.00728 u.
Energy equivalent: about 938.3 MeV.
The proton is about 1,836 times as massive as the electron.

mₙ = 1.6749 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (CODATA 2018: 1.67492749804 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
In atomic mass units: about 1.00866 u.
Energy equivalent: about 939.6 MeV.
The neutron is slightly heavier than the proton. A free neutron is unstable and beta-decays with a half-life of roughly 10 minutes.

k = 1 ÷ (4πε₀) ≈ 8.988 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², usually rounded to 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² (sometimes 9.0 × 10⁹).
Used in Coulomb's law F = kq₁q₂ ÷ r² and in E = kq ÷ r².
Do not confuse it with Boltzmann's constant or a spring constant, which also use the letter k.

ε₀ ≈ 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m (C²/(N·m²)); CODATA 2018 value 8.8541878128 × 10⁻¹² F/m.
Related to Coulomb's constant by k = 1 ÷ (4πε₀).
Appears in capacitor formulas, e.g. a parallel-plate capacitor in vacuum has C = ε₀A ÷ d.

Boltzmann constant = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K exactly (fixed in the 2019 SI redefinition).
It links temperature to energy per particle: average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule = (3/2) × k_B × T, with T in kelvin.
It equals the gas constant divided by Avogadro's number: k_B = R ÷ N_A.

1 u (unified atomic mass unit, also called a dalton, Da) = 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
1 u ≈ 1.66054 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (CODATA 2018: 1.66053906660 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
Energy equivalent: about 931.5 MeV.
A mass of x u per particle means x grams per mole, which is why atomic masses on the periodic table double as molar masses.

1 atm = 101,325 Pa exactly = 101.325 kPa
1 atm = 760 mmHg = 760 torr
1 atm ≈ 14.7 psi (pounds per square inch)
1 bar = 100,000 Pa = 100 kPa (slightly less than 1 atm)
Example: 380 mmHg = 380 ÷ 760 = 0.500 atm ≈ 50.7 kPa.

N_A = 6.02214076 × 10²³ per mole exactly (fixed in the 2019 SI redefinition).
Commonly rounded to 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
One mole of anything contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules, ions or formula units).
Example: 2.00 mol of water contains 2.00 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules.

R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) (more precisely 8.314462618)
R = 8.314 L·kPa/(mol·K)
R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) (often rounded to 0.0821)
R = 62.36 L·mmHg/(mol·K) = 62.36 L·torr/(mol·K)
Choose the R whose units match your pressure and volume units; temperature must be in kelvin.
R = N_A × k_B (Avogadro's number times Boltzmann's constant).

Proton: charge +1, mass about 1 u (1.007 u), found in the nucleus.
Neutron: charge 0, mass about 1 u (1.009 u), found in the nucleus.
Electron: charge −1, mass about 1/1836 u (0.000549 u), found in orbitals (electron cloud) around the nucleus.
The nucleus is tiny but holds almost all of the atom's mass; most of an atom's volume is empty space.
A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
The number of protons identifies the element.

Atomic number Z = number of protons (also the number of electrons in a neutral atom).
Mass number A = protons + neutrons.
Neutrons = A − Z.
Notation: ᴬ_Z X, e.g. ³⁵₁₇Cl, or written chlorine-35.
Example: chlorine-35 has Z = 17, so 17 protons, 17 electrons (neutral) and 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons.
Classic mistake: the mass number is a whole-number count; the decimal atomic mass on the periodic table (35.45 for Cl) is a weighted average of isotopes.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers.
Isotopes of an element have nearly identical chemical properties because they have the same electron arrangement.
Examples: carbon-12 (6 neutrons), carbon-13 (7 neutrons), carbon-14 (8 neutrons, radioactive).
Hydrogen: protium ¹H (0 neutrons), deuterium ²H (1 neutron), tritium ³H (2 neutrons, radioactive).
Some isotopes are stable; others are radioactive (radioisotopes).

Average atomic mass = Σ (isotope mass × fractional abundance)
Convert percent abundance to a decimal (75.76% → 0.7576) before multiplying.
Example: chlorine is 75.76% chlorine-35 (34.969 u) and 24.24% chlorine-37 (36.966 u):
34.969 × 0.7576 + 36.966 × 0.2424 ≈ 26.49 + 8.96 = 35.45 u.
With two isotopes, the average is always closer to the mass of the more abundant one.

An ion is an atom or group of atoms with a net electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons (the number of protons never changes in a chemical reaction).
Cation: positive ion; it has lost electrons. Metals usually form cations (Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Al³⁺).
Anion: negative ion; it has gained electrons. Nonmetals usually form anions (Cl⁻, O²⁻, N³⁻).
Electrons in an ion = protons − charge.
Example: Na⁺ has 11 protons and 10 electrons; Cl⁻ has 17 protons and 18 electrons; O²⁻ has 8 protons and 10 electrons.

Aufbau principle: electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first.
Pauli exclusion principle: an orbital holds at most 2 electrons, and they must have opposite spins (no two electrons in an atom have the same four quantum numbers).
Hund's rule: in orbitals of equal energy (e.g. the three 2p orbitals), electrons occupy separate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before any orbital gets a second electron.
Example: nitrogen 1s² 2s² 2p³ has its three 2p electrons in three different 2p orbitals, all with the same spin.
Capacities: s = 1 orbital (2 e⁻), p = 3 orbitals (6 e⁻), d = 5 orbitals (10 e⁻), f = 7 orbitals (14 e⁻). Shell n holds up to 2n² electrons.

t: Orbital filling order and electron configurations
x:
Filling order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s 4f 5d 6p 7s 5f 6d 7p.
Write each sublevel with its electron count as a superscript; the superscripts add up to the number of electrons.
Examples: O (8 e⁻) = 1s² 2s² 2p⁴; Na (11) = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹; Fe (26) = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶.
Noble-gas shorthand: put the previous noble gas in brackets, e.g. Fe = [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶; Na = [Ne] 3s¹.
Known exceptions: Cr = [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ and Cu = [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰ (half-filled and filled d sublevels are extra stable).
Note: 4s fills before 3d, but when transition metals form ions they lose 4s electrons first (Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶).

t: Valence electrons and the octet rule
x:
Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell; they take part in bonding.
Main-group elements: group 1 → 1, group 2 → 2, group 13 → 3, group 14 → 4, group 15 → 5, group 16 → 6, group 17 → 7, group 18 → 8 (helium has 2).
Octet rule: atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to reach 8 valence electrons, like a noble gas. Hydrogen and helium are stable with 2 (duet).
Examples: Na loses 1 electron → Na⁺; Cl gains 1 → Cl⁻; O shares 2 in water.
Exceptions exist: B in BF₃ has 6; S in SF₆ has 12; molecules with odd electron counts such as NO.

Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number (Mendeleev arranged an early version by atomic mass in 1869).
Rows are periods (7); columns are groups or families (18). Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and similar properties.
Group 1: alkali metals (Li, Na, K…; very reactive; hydrogen is in group 1 but is not an alkali metal).
Group 2: alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca…).
Groups 3–12: transition metals.
Group 17: halogens (F, Cl, Br, I…; very reactive nonmetals).
Group 18: noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn; very unreactive).
Lanthanides and actinides are the two rows usually shown below the main table. 118 elements are currently named.

Down a group: atomic radius INCREASES (more electron shells).
Across a period from left to right: atomic radius DECREASES (more protons pull the same shell in more tightly; higher effective nuclear charge).
So the largest atoms are at the lower left (e.g. francium, cesium) and the smallest at the upper right (helium).
Ions: a cation is smaller than its neutral atom (lost electrons, often a whole shell); an anion is larger than its neutral atom (extra electron repulsion).
Example: Na is larger than Cl; Na⁺ is smaller than Na; Cl⁻ is larger than Cl.

Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom.
Across a period left to right: generally INCREASES.
Down a group: DECREASES (the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded).
Noble gases have the highest values in their periods; helium has the highest of all elements. Alkali metals have the lowest in their periods.
Each successive ionization energy is larger; a very big jump shows a core shell has been reached (e.g. Mg's 3rd ionization energy is much larger than its 2nd).
Small exceptions occur (e.g. O is slightly lower than N, B lower than Be).

Electronegativity is an atom's ability to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond.
Across a period left to right: INCREASES. Down a group: DECREASES.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element (3.98 on the Pauling scale, often rounded to 4.0); then oxygen (3.44), then chlorine (3.16) and nitrogen (3.04).
The least electronegative elements are at the lower left (cesium, francium, about 0.7–0.8).
Noble gases are usually not given values because they rarely bond.
Metallic character follows the opposite trend: it increases down and to the left.

Metals (left and centre of the table): shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable and ductile, tend to lose electrons to form cations. All are solid at room temperature except mercury.
Nonmetals (upper right, plus hydrogen): dull, poor conductors, brittle when solid, tend to gain or share electrons. Bromine is the only liquid nonmetal at room temperature; many are gases.
Metalloids (along the staircase line): properties in between; many are semiconductors. Commonly listed: boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium.
About three-quarters of the elements are metals.

An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when electrons are transferred, usually from a metal to a nonmetal.
Example: Na gives one electron to Cl → Na⁺ and Cl⁻ → NaCl.
Ionic compounds form crystal lattices, not separate molecules, so their formulas show the simplest ratio (formula unit).
Typical properties: high melting and boiling points, hard but brittle, conduct electricity when melted or dissolved in water (ions free to move) but not as solids, many dissolve in water.
Rough guide: an electronegativity difference greater than about 1.7–2.0 suggests ionic bonding (textbook cutoffs vary).

A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms, usually two nonmetals.
Single bond = 1 shared pair, double = 2 pairs, triple = 3 pairs. More shared pairs → shorter and stronger bond.
Nonpolar covalent: electrons shared equally (same or similar electronegativity), e.g. H₂, Cl₂, and C–H bonds are close to nonpolar.
Polar covalent: electrons shared unequally; the more electronegative atom gets a partial negative charge (δ−), e.g. the O–H bonds in water.
Rough guide by electronegativity difference: below about 0.4 nonpolar, about 0.4 to 1.7 polar, above that ionic (cutoffs vary by textbook).
A molecule with polar bonds can still be nonpolar overall if it is symmetric (CO₂, CH₄, CCl₄).

In metallic bonding, metal atoms give up their valence electrons to a shared sea of delocalized electrons that moves freely around a lattice of positive metal ions.
This explains metal properties:
electrical and thermal conductivity (mobile electrons),
malleability and ductility (layers of ions can slide without breaking the bonding),
shiny lustre (free electrons interact with light).
Alloys (e.g. steel, brass, bronze) are mixtures of a metal with other elements.

Intermolecular forces are attractions BETWEEN molecules; they are much weaker than the covalent bonds inside molecules.
London dispersion forces: temporary dipoles; present in all molecules; stronger for larger molecules with more electrons. The only IMF in nonpolar substances (e.g. CH₄, I₂).
Dipole–dipole forces: between polar molecules (e.g. HCl).
Hydrogen bonding: an especially strong dipole–dipole attraction when H is bonded to N, O or F and is attracted to a lone pair on another N, O or F (e.g. H₂O, NH₃, HF).
Ion–dipole forces: between an ion and a polar molecule (e.g. Na⁺ in water).
Stronger IMFs → higher boiling and melting points, lower vapour pressure. Hydrogen bonding is why water boils at 100 °C while H₂S, a heavier molecule, is a gas at room temperature.

1) Add up all valence electrons (add one per negative charge, subtract one per positive charge for ions).
2) Choose the central atom: usually the least electronegative one (never H; H forms only one bond).
3) Connect the atoms with single bonds (2 electrons each).
4) Complete octets on the outer atoms with lone pairs.
5) Put any leftover electrons on the central atom.
6) If the central atom has fewer than 8, turn outer lone pairs into double or triple bonds.
Example CO₂: 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 electrons → O=C=O, with two lone pairs on each O.
Check: total electrons drawn must equal the count from step 1.

VSEPR: electron domains (bonds and lone pairs) around a central atom spread out as far apart as possible. A double or triple bond counts as one domain.
2 domains, 0 lone pairs: linear, 180° (CO₂, BeCl₂)
3 domains, 0 lone pairs: trigonal planar, 120° (BF₃)
3 domains, 1 lone pair: bent, slightly less than 120° (SO₂)
4 domains, 0 lone pairs: tetrahedral, 109.5° (CH₄)
4 domains, 1 lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, about 107° (NH₃)
4 domains, 2 lone pairs: bent, about 104.5° (H₂O)
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, squeezing the bond angles smaller.
The shape name describes the atoms only, not the lone pairs.

5 domains, 0 lone pairs: trigonal bipyramidal, 90°, 120° and 180° (PCl₅)
5 domains, 1 lone pair: seesaw (SF₄)
5 domains, 2 lone pairs: T-shaped (ClF₃)
5 domains, 3 lone pairs: linear, 180° (XeF₂)
6 domains, 0 lone pairs: octahedral, 90° (SF₆)
6 domains, 1 lone pair: square pyramidal (BrF₅)
6 domains, 2 lone pairs: square planar, 90° (XeF₄)
In trigonal bipyramidal arrangements, lone pairs go in the equatorial positions.

1) Name the cation first, then the anion.
2) A monatomic anion takes the ending -ide: chloride, oxide, sulfide, nitride.
3) Polyatomic ions keep their names: sulfate, nitrate, ammonium.
4) Metals that can have more than one charge (most transition metals, plus Sn and Pb) get a Roman numeral showing the charge: FeCl₂ = iron(II) chloride, FeCl₃ = iron(III) chloride, CuO = copper(II) oxide.
5) Do not use Greek prefixes (mono-, di-) for ionic compounds.
Examples: NaCl sodium chloride, CaBr₂ calcium bromide, Al₂O₃ aluminium oxide, NH₄NO₃ ammonium nitrate.
Ag⁺, Zn²⁺ and Cd²⁺ have one common charge and usually get no Roman numeral.

Common main-group charges: group 1 → +1, group 2 → +2, Al → +3, group 15 (N, P) → −3, group 16 (O, S) → −2, group 17 → −1.
The total positive charge must equal the total negative charge.
Criss-cross: use the size of each ion's charge as the subscript of the other ion, then reduce to the lowest ratio.
Use parentheses around a polyatomic ion when you need more than one.
Examples: Al³⁺ + O²⁻ → Al₂O₃; Ca²⁺ + PO₄³⁻ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂; Mg²⁺ + O²⁻ → Mg₂O₂ → reduce to MgO; NH₄⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → (NH₄)₂SO₄.
Classic mistake: writing CaOH₂ instead of Ca(OH)₂.

For two nonmetals, use prefixes to give the number of each atom; the second element ends in -ide.
Prefixes: 1 mono, 2 di, 3 tri, 4 tetra, 5 penta, 6 hexa, 7 hepta, 8 octa, 9 nona, 10 deca.
mono- is not used on the first element.
The final a or o of a prefix is usually dropped before oxide (monoxide, pentoxide, but dioxide).
Examples: CO carbon monoxide, CO₂ carbon dioxide, N₂O₄ dinitrogen tetroxide, PCl₅ phosphorus pentachloride, P₄O₁₀ tetraphosphorus decoxide, SF₆ sulfur hexafluoride.
Common names are kept for H₂O (water), NH₃ (ammonia), CH₄ (methane).

Binary acids (H + one nonmetal, no oxygen): hydro- + root + -ic acid. HCl = hydrochloric acid, HBr = hydrobromic acid, HF = hydrofluoric acid, H₂S = hydrosulfuric acid.
Oxyacids (contain a polyatomic ion with oxygen): no hydro- prefix.
anion ending -ate → acid ending -ic: SO₄²⁻ sulfate → H₂SO₄ sulfuric acid; NO₃⁻ nitrate → HNO₃ nitric acid; PO₄³⁻ → H₃PO₄ phosphoric acid; CO₃²⁻ → H₂CO₃ carbonic acid.
anion ending -ite → acid ending -ous: SO₃²⁻ sulfite → H₂SO₃ sulfurous acid; NO₂⁻ nitrite → HNO₂ nitrous acid.
Memory aid: I ate something ic(ky); I bite and it is delicious (-ite → -ous).

ammonium NH₄⁺
hydronium H₃O⁺
hydroxide OH⁻
nitrate NO₃⁻ ; nitrite NO₂⁻
sulfate SO₄²⁻ ; sulfite SO₃²⁻
hydrogen sulfate (bisulfate) HSO₄⁻
phosphate PO₄³⁻ ; hydrogen phosphate HPO₄²⁻ ; dihydrogen phosphate H₂PO₄⁻
carbonate CO₃²⁻ ; hydrogen carbonate (bicarbonate) HCO₃⁻
acetate CH₃COO⁻ (also written C₂H₃O₂⁻)
cyanide CN⁻
NH₄⁺ and H₃O⁺ are the common positive polyatomic ions.

perchlorate ClO₄⁻ ; chlorate ClO₃⁻ ; chlorite ClO₂⁻ ; hypochlorite ClO⁻
(bromine and iodine form the same pattern: bromate BrO₃⁻, iodate IO₃⁻)
permanganate MnO₄⁻
chromate CrO₄²⁻ ; dichromate Cr₂O₇²⁻
peroxide O₂²⁻
thiosulfate S₂O₃²⁻
oxalate C₂O₄²⁻
Pattern: -ate has one more oxygen than -ite with the same charge; per-…-ate has one more oxygen than -ate; hypo-…-ite has one fewer oxygen than -ite.

In a chemical reaction, mass is neither created nor destroyed: the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants (stated by Antoine Lavoisier in the 1780s).
Atoms are only rearranged, so the same number of each kind of atom appears on both sides. This is why chemical equations must be balanced.
Example: 4 g of hydrogen burning completely with 32 g of oxygen produces 36 g of water.
In an open container a mass change can appear because a gas escapes or is absorbed from the air.

1) Write correct formulas for all reactants and products.
2) Count the atoms of each element on each side.
3) Change COEFFICIENTS (numbers in front) only — never change subscripts, which would change the substance.
4) Balance elements that appear in only one compound on each side first; leave H and O (and free elements such as O₂) for last. Treat an unchanged polyatomic ion as one unit.
5) Reduce coefficients to the lowest whole-number ratio and recount.
Example: CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. C is balanced; H: put 2 in front of H₂O; O: now 4 on the right, so 2O₂.
Result: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
Example: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.

Synthesis (combination): A + B → AB. Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
Decomposition: AB → A + B. Example: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.
Single replacement (displacement): A + BC → AC + B. Example: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. A more reactive element replaces a less reactive one.
Double replacement: AB + CD → AD + CB. Example: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃; usually forms a precipitate, a gas or water.
Combustion: fuel + O₂ → products; complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives CO₂ + H₂O. Example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
Neutralization (a type of double replacement): acid + base → salt + water. Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

General guide for ionic compounds in water at room temperature:
Always soluble: compounds of group 1 ions (Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺…) and ammonium NH₄⁺; all nitrates (NO₃⁻); nearly all acetates.
Usually soluble: chlorides, bromides and iodides — except those of Ag⁺, Pb²⁺ and Hg₂²⁺.
Usually soluble: sulfates — except BaSO₄, PbSO₄, SrSO₄ and CaSO₄ (CaSO₄ and Ag₂SO₄ are slightly soluble).
Usually insoluble: carbonates, phosphates, sulfides and hydroxides — except with group 1 ions and NH₄⁺ (hydroxides of Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺ and Ba²⁺ are slightly to moderately soluble).
Example: mixing AgNO₃ and NaCl solutions forms a white precipitate of AgCl.

t: States of matter and phase changes
x:
Solid: fixed shape and volume; particles vibrate in place.
Liquid: fixed volume, takes the shape of its container; particles slide past one another.
Gas: no fixed shape or volume; particles move fast and far apart.
Plasma: ionized gas (in stars, lightning, neon signs).
Phase changes: melting (solid → liquid), freezing (liquid → solid), vaporization — boiling or evaporation (liquid → gas), condensation (gas → liquid), sublimation (solid → gas, e.g. dry ice), deposition (gas → solid, e.g. frost).
Melting, vaporization and sublimation absorb energy; freezing, condensation and deposition release energy.
Temperature stays constant during a phase change.

Physical change: the substance stays the same substance; only its form or state changes. Examples: melting ice, dissolving sugar, cutting paper, boiling water.
Chemical change (chemical reaction): new substances with new properties form. Examples: burning wood, rusting iron, baking a cake, digesting food.
Signs of a chemical change: gas bubbles produced (not from boiling), a precipitate forms, unexpected colour change, light or heat given off or absorbed, a new odour.
Physical properties (colour, density, melting point) can be observed without changing the substance; chemical properties (flammability, reactivity) describe how it reacts.

Pure substances have a fixed composition:
Element: one kind of atom; cannot be broken down chemically (O₂, Fe, He).
Compound: two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio (H₂O, NaCl, CO₂); separated only by chemical reactions.
Mixtures: two or more substances physically combined in any proportion; separated by physical methods (filtering, distillation, evaporation, magnets, chromatography).
Homogeneous mixture (solution): uniform throughout (salt water, air, brass).
Heterogeneous mixture: parts are visibly different (sand in water, salad, granite).
In a solution, the solute is dissolved in the solvent; water is called the universal solvent.

Counting: all nonzero digits are significant. Zeros between nonzero digits are significant (1005 → 4). Leading zeros are never significant (0.0042 → 2). Trailing zeros are significant if there is a decimal point (2.50 → 3; 100. → 3); in 100 with no decimal point they are ambiguous.
Exact numbers (counted items, defined conversions like 100 cm = 1 m) have unlimited significant figures.
Multiplying/dividing: round the answer to the fewest significant figures in the data. Example: 2.5 × 3.42 = 8.55 → 8.6.
Adding/subtracting: round to the fewest decimal places. Example: 12.11 + 0.3 = 12.41 → 12.4.
Scientific notation shows them clearly: 3.00 × 10⁸ has 3 significant figures.

1 mole (mol) = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number).
Molar mass M (g/mol) = the sum of the atomic masses in the formula, read from the periodic table.
n = m ÷ M and N = n × N_A
n = moles (mol), m = mass (g), M = molar mass (g/mol), N = number of particles, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Example: H₂O: M = 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol. 36.04 g of water = 36.04 ÷ 18.02 = 2.000 mol = 1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules.
Example: CO₂: M = 12.01 + 2(16.00) = 44.01 g/mol.
Road map: grams ⇄ moles (use M), moles ⇄ particles (use N_A).

Percent of element = (mass of that element in one mole of compound ÷ molar mass of compound) × 100%
Example: water H₂O, M = 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.016 g/mol:
%H = 2.016 ÷ 18.016 × 100% ≈ 11.19%
%O = 16.00 ÷ 18.016 × 100% ≈ 88.81%
The percentages of all elements in a compound add up to 100%.

Empirical formula = simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; molecular formula = actual numbers of atoms (a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula).
Steps: 1) Assume 100 g, so percent = grams. 2) Convert grams of each element to moles. 3) Divide every mole value by the smallest one. 4) If needed, multiply all by a small whole number to clear fractions (e.g. 1.5 → ×2).
Molecular formula: multiple = molar mass of compound ÷ empirical formula mass.
Example: 40.0% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O → 40.0 ÷ 12.01 = 3.33 mol C, 6.7 ÷ 1.008 = 6.65 mol H, 53.3 ÷ 16.00 = 3.33 mol O → ratio 1 : 2 : 1 → CH₂O (30.03 g/mol).
If the molar mass is 180 g/mol: 180 ÷ 30.03 ≈ 6 → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose).
Memory aid: percent to mass, mass to mole, divide by small, multiply till whole.

Use a BALANCED equation. Path: grams of A → moles of A → moles of B → grams of B.
1) moles A = grams A ÷ molar mass A
2) moles B = moles A × (coefficient of B ÷ coefficient of A) — the mole ratio
3) grams B = moles B × molar mass B
Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. How much water from 4.00 g H₂?
4.00 ÷ 2.016 = 1.984 mol H₂ → × (2/2) = 1.984 mol H₂O → × 18.02 = 35.8 g H₂O.
Classic mistake: using a mass ratio instead of the mole ratio from the coefficients.

The limiting reactant is used up first and sets the maximum amount of product; the other is in excess.
Method: convert each reactant to moles, then calculate how much product each could make (or compare the mole ratio you have with the ratio needed). The smaller amount of product identifies the limiting reactant.
Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O with 3.0 mol H₂ and 2.0 mol O₂.
H₂ could make 3.0 mol H₂O; O₂ could make 4.0 mol H₂O → H₂ is limiting.
Product = 3.0 mol H₂O; O₂ used = 1.5 mol, so 0.5 mol O₂ is left over.
Classic mistake: the reactant with the smaller mass is not automatically the limiting one — compare moles using the equation.

Percent yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100%
Theoretical yield = the maximum product calculated by stoichiometry from the limiting reactant.
Actual yield = the amount really obtained in the experiment (same units).
Example: theoretical yield of water is 35.8 g, but 30.0 g is collected: percent yield = 30.0 ÷ 35.8 × 100% ≈ 83.8%.
Yields below 100% come from incomplete reactions, side reactions and losses during transfer; above 100% usually means the product is still wet or impure.

M = n ÷ V
M = molarity (mol/L, written M), n = moles of solute (mol), V = volume of SOLUTION in litres (L).
Rearranged: n = M × V.
Example: 0.50 mol NaCl dissolved to make 250 mL of solution: M = 0.50 ÷ 0.250 = 2.0 M.
Example: grams needed for 1.00 L of 0.100 M NaCl (58.44 g/mol): 0.100 mol × 58.44 = 5.84 g.
Classic mistakes: forgetting to convert mL to L; using the volume of solvent instead of the final volume of solution.

M₁ × V₁ = M₂ × V₂
M₁, V₁ = concentration and volume of the concentrated (stock) solution; M₂, V₂ = concentration and final total volume of the diluted solution. V₁ and V₂ may be in any unit, as long as both are the same.
The moles of solute stay the same; only water is added.
Example: dilute 50.0 mL of 6.0 M HCl to 2.0 M: V₂ = 6.0 × 50.0 ÷ 2.0 = 150 mL, so add 100 mL of water.
Safety: when diluting acids, add acid to water, not water to acid.
Classic mistake: V₂ is the final total volume, not the volume of water added.

P × V = n × R × T
P = pressure, V = volume (L), n = moles of gas (mol), T = temperature in kelvin (K = °C + 273.15), R = gas constant.
R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) when P is in atm; R = 8.314 L·kPa/(mol·K) when P is in kPa; R = 62.36 L·mmHg/(mol·K) when P is in mmHg. (In SI, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) with P in Pa and V in m³.)
Example: 2.0 mol of gas in a 10.0 L container at 300 K: P = 2.0 × 0.08206 × 300 ÷ 10.0 ≈ 4.9 atm.
Example: 1.00 mol at 273.15 K and 1.00 atm occupies 22.4 L.
Real gases behave most ideally at high temperature and low pressure.
Classic mistake: using °C or mismatching R with the pressure units.

t: STP and molar volume of a gas
x:
Many school textbooks define STP as 0 °C (273.15 K) and 1 atm; there 1 mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 L (22.414 L).
IUPAC (since 1982) defines STP as 0 °C and 100 kPa (1 bar); there the molar volume is 22.7 L (22.711 L).
SATP (standard ambient) is 25 °C (298.15 K) and 100 kPa, molar volume about 24.8 L.
Use whichever definition your course or textbook uses.
Example (0 °C, 1 atm): 44.8 L of O₂ = 44.8 ÷ 22.4 = 2.00 mol = 64.0 g.
The molar volume is the same for any ideal gas, regardless of its identity.

P_total = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + …
Each gas in a mixture exerts its own partial pressure as if it were alone.
Partial pressure Pᵢ = xᵢ × P_total, where xᵢ = mole fraction = moles of gas i ÷ total moles.
Gas collected over water: P_gas = P_total − P_water vapour (look up the water vapour pressure at that temperature).
Example: a mixture of 1.0 mol N₂ and 3.0 mol O₂ at 2.0 atm total: x(N₂) = 0.25, so P(N₂) = 0.50 atm and P(O₂) = 1.5 atm.

rate₁ ÷ rate₂ = √(M₂ ÷ M₁)
rate = rate of effusion (or diffusion), M = molar mass (g/mol).
Lighter gases effuse faster.
Example: H₂ (2.016 g/mol) vs O₂ (32.00 g/mol): rate ratio = √(32.00 ÷ 2.016) ≈ 3.98, so hydrogen effuses about 4 times as fast.
At the same temperature, all gases have the same average kinetic energy; lighter molecules must therefore move faster.

Enthalpy change ΔH = heat absorbed or released at constant pressure, usually in kJ or kJ/mol.
Exothermic: releases heat to the surroundings, ΔH < 0 (negative); the surroundings get warmer. Products are lower in energy than reactants. Examples: combustion, neutralization, freezing, condensation.
Endothermic: absorbs heat from the surroundings, ΔH > 0 (positive); the surroundings get colder. Examples: melting ice, evaporation, photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate (cold packs).
Breaking bonds absorbs energy; forming bonds releases energy.
Example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l), ΔH ≈ −890 kJ per mole of CH₄.

Heat gained by the water/solution: q = m × c × ΔT
q = heat (J), m = mass of solution (g), c = specific heat (water: 4.184 J/(g·°C)), ΔT = T_final − T_initial (°C).
Heat lost by one part = heat gained by the other: q_reaction = −q_solution.
ΔH per mole = q_reaction ÷ moles of the limiting reactant.
Example: a reaction in 100. g of water raises the temperature by 5.0 °C: q_water = 100. × 4.184 × 5.0 = 2,092 J, so the reaction released about 2.09 kJ (q_reaction = −2.09 kJ, exothermic).
Note: 1 calorie = 4.184 J; a food Calorie (capital C) = 1 kcal = 4,184 J.

The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same no matter how many steps it takes: add the ΔH values of steps that add up to the overall equation.
Rules: if you reverse an equation, change the sign of its ΔH. If you multiply an equation by a number, multiply its ΔH by the same number.
Example: find ΔH for C + ½O₂ → CO.
(1) C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ
(2) CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283.0 kJ; reverse it: CO₂ → CO + ½O₂, ΔH = +283.0 kJ
Add (1) and reversed (2): C + ½O₂ → CO, ΔH = −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ.

ΔH°_rxn = Σ n × ΔH°_f(products) − Σ n × ΔH°_f(reactants)
n = coefficient in the balanced equation; ΔH°_f = standard enthalpy of formation (kJ/mol), the enthalpy change to form 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states.
ΔH°_f of an element in its standard state (O₂(g), C(graphite), Fe(s), H₂(g)) is 0.
Example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l), using ΔH°_f: CH₄ −74.8, CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8 kJ/mol:
ΔH° = [−393.5 + 2(−285.8)] − [−74.8 + 0] = −890.3 kJ.
Classic mistake: doing reactants minus products.

ΔG = ΔH − T × ΔS
ΔG = Gibbs free energy change (kJ/mol), ΔH = enthalpy change (kJ/mol), T = temperature (K), ΔS = entropy change (convert J/(mol·K) to kJ/(mol·K) by dividing by 1000).
ΔG < 0: spontaneous; ΔG > 0: non-spontaneous; ΔG = 0: at equilibrium.
ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0: spontaneous at all temperatures.
ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0: never spontaneous.
ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0: spontaneous at low T. ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0: spontaneous at high T.
Spontaneous means thermodynamically favourable, not necessarily fast.

For aA + bB → products: rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ
k = rate constant (depends on temperature), [A] and [B] = molar concentrations, m and n = reaction orders; overall order = m + n.
The orders m and n must be found by experiment; they are NOT simply the coefficients a and b (except for an elementary step).
If doubling [A] doubles the rate, the reaction is first order in A; if it quadruples the rate, second order; if the rate does not change, zero order.
First-order half-life: t½ = 0.693 ÷ k (ln 2 ÷ k), independent of the starting concentration.

At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, so concentrations stop changing (the reactions have not stopped — dynamic equilibrium).
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ ÷ ([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ) — products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient.
Leave pure solids and pure liquids (including water as the solvent) out of the expression.
K > 1: products favoured; K < 1: reactants favoured. K changes only with temperature.
Reaction quotient Q uses the same expression with current concentrations: Q < K → shifts toward products; Q > K → shifts toward reactants; Q = K → at equilibrium.
Example: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ has K = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³).

If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change.
Add a reactant (or remove a product) → shifts toward products (right). Add a product (or remove a reactant) → shifts toward reactants (left).
Increase pressure by decreasing volume → shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas. No change if both sides have equal gas moles.
Temperature: treat heat as a reactant (endothermic) or a product (exothermic). Heating an exothermic reaction shifts it left. Only temperature changes the value of K.
A catalyst causes no shift. Adding an inert gas at constant volume causes no shift.
Example: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ: high pressure and lower temperature favour more NH₃ (Haber process).

Arrhenius: an acid produces H⁺ (H₃O⁺) in water; a base produces OH⁻ in water.
Brønsted–Lowry: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a base is a proton acceptor.
Lewis: an acid is an electron-pair acceptor; a base is an electron-pair donor.
Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺: in NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, NH₃ (base) and NH₄⁺ (its conjugate acid); H₂O (acid) and OH⁻ (its conjugate base).
Water is amphoteric: it can act as an acid or a base.
Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red; bases taste bitter, feel slippery, turn red litmus blue (never taste lab chemicals).

pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] (or [H₃O⁺]); [H⁺] = 10^(−pH)
pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; [OH⁻] = 10^(−pOH)
At 25 °C: pH + pOH = 14 and K_w = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.
[H⁺] and [OH⁻] are in mol/L.
Example: 0.010 M HCl (strong acid): [H⁺] = 0.010 = 10⁻², pH = 2.
Example: 0.0010 M NaOH (strong base): [OH⁻] = 10⁻³, pOH = 3, pH = 14 − 3 = 11.
Example: pH = 4.5 → [H⁺] = 10⁻⁴·⁵ ≈ 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H⁺]: pH 3 is 10 times more acidic than pH 4, not 1 more.

At 25 °C: pH < 7 is acidic, pH = 7 is neutral, pH > 7 is basic (alkaline). Most everyday solutions are between 0 and 14, but values outside that range are possible.
Approximate values:
stomach acid about 1.5–3.5
lemon juice about 2
pure water 7 (at 25 °C)
human blood 7.35–7.45
seawater about 8
household ammonia about 11
Indicators change colour with pH: litmus is red in acid and blue in base; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base (above about pH 8.2).

Strong acids ionize (dissociate) essentially completely in water:
HCl – hydrochloric acid
HBr – hydrobromic acid
HI – hydroiodic acid
HNO₃ – nitric acid
H₂SO₄ – sulfuric acid (first proton only)
HClO₄ – perchloric acid
(HClO₃, chloric acid, is included in some lists.)
All other common acids are weak, e.g. HF, CH₃COOH (acetic acid), H₂CO₃, H₃PO₄.
Classic mistake: HF is a WEAK acid even though it is very dangerous. Strong/weak describes how much it ionizes, not how concentrated it is.

Strong bases dissociate completely in water:
Group 1 hydroxides: LiOH, NaOH (sodium hydroxide, lye), KOH, RbOH, CsOH.
Heavier group 2 hydroxides: Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂ (Ca(OH)₂ is only slightly soluble, but what dissolves is fully dissociated).
Each Ba(OH)₂ releases 2 OH⁻, so 0.10 M Ba(OH)₂ gives [OH⁻] = 0.20 M.
Ammonia (NH₃) is a common WEAK base.

Acid + base → salt + water.
Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
Example: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.
Net ionic equation for a strong acid with a strong base: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
Neutralization is exothermic.
A strong acid + strong base at equivalence gives a neutral solution (pH 7 at 25 °C); a weak acid + strong base gives a basic solution at equivalence; a strong acid + weak base gives an acidic one.
Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂ (e.g. vinegar and baking soda fizz).

A titration finds an unknown concentration by adding a solution of known concentration (the titrant, from a burette) until the reaction is exactly complete.
Equivalence point: moles of H⁺ added = moles of OH⁻ present (or vice versa). Endpoint: where the indicator changes colour; a good indicator makes these nearly the same.
At equivalence: (M_a × V_a × number of H⁺ per acid) = (M_b × V_b × number of OH⁻ per base). For 1:1 acids and bases: M_a × V_a = M_b × V_b.
Example: 25.0 mL of HCl is neutralized by 20.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH: M_a = 0.100 × 20.0 ÷ 25.0 = 0.0800 M.
Example (2:1): 0.100 M NaOH titrating H₂SO₄ needs twice the moles of NaOH as acid.
Phenolphthalein (colourless → pink around pH 8.2–10) is common for strong acid / strong base titrations.

A buffer resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.
It is made of a weak acid and its conjugate base (e.g. CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻) or a weak base and its conjugate acid (e.g. NH₃ and NH₄⁺).
Added H⁺ is absorbed by the base part; added OH⁻ is neutralized by the acid part.
Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKₐ + log₁₀([A⁻] ÷ [HA]); when [A⁻] = [HA], pH = pKₐ.
Blood is buffered mainly by the carbonic acid / bicarbonate (H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻) system, keeping it near pH 7.4.

1) An atom in a pure element is 0 (Na, O₂, Cl₂, S₈).
2) A monatomic ion equals its charge (Na⁺ = +1, Cl⁻ = −1, Fe³⁺ = +3).
3) The sum is 0 for a neutral compound and equals the charge for a polyatomic ion.
4) Fluorine is always −1 in compounds. Group 1 metals are +1 and group 2 metals are +2 in compounds.
5) Hydrogen is +1 with nonmetals, −1 in metal hydrides (NaH).
6) Oxygen is usually −2 (−1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂; +2 in OF₂).
7) Other halogens are usually −1, except when bonded to oxygen or a more electronegative halogen.
Example: S in H₂SO₄: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0 → S = +6.
Example: Mn in MnO₄⁻: Mn + 4(−2) = −1 → Mn = +7.

OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). Also: LEO the lion says GER.
Oxidation → oxidation number increases. Reduction → oxidation number decreases.
Oxidation and reduction always happen together (redox).
The oxidizing agent is the substance that gets reduced; the reducing agent is the substance that gets oxidized.
Example: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.
Zn: 0 → +2, loses 2 e⁻, oxidized (it is the reducing agent).
Cu²⁺: +2 → 0, gains 2 e⁻, reduced (it is the oxidizing agent).
In a balanced redox reaction, electrons lost = electrons gained.

Galvanic (voltaic) cell: a spontaneous redox reaction produces electric current (batteries).
Anode = where oxidation happens; cathode = where reduction happens (memory aid: An Ox, Red Cat).
Electrons flow through the wire from anode to cathode. A salt bridge lets ions move to keep each half-cell electrically neutral.
In a galvanic cell the anode is negative and the cathode positive; in an electrolytic cell (electricity drives a non-spontaneous reaction, e.g. electroplating) the anode is positive and the cathode negative — but oxidation is still at the anode.
Cell voltage: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode (standard reduction potentials); E°cell > 0 means spontaneous.
Example: the Daniell cell, Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu, gives about 1.10 V.

Rule: the mass numbers (top) and the atomic numbers (bottom) must each add up to the same total on both sides.
Alpha decay: emits ⁴₂He; A drops by 4, Z drops by 2. Example: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He.
Beta-minus decay: emits ⁰₋₁e (a neutron becomes a proton); A unchanged, Z rises by 1. Example: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e.
Positron emission (β⁺): emits ⁰₊₁e (a proton becomes a neutron); Z drops by 1. Example: ¹¹₆C → ¹¹₅B + ⁰₊₁e.
Electron capture: the nucleus absorbs ⁰₋₁e; Z drops by 1. Example: ⁷₄Be + ⁰₋₁e → ⁷₃Li.
Gamma emission (⁰₀γ): A and Z unchanged; the nucleus only loses energy.
The new atomic number tells you the new element (90 = thorium, 7 = nitrogen).

The three parts of the cell theory:
1) All living things are made of one or more cells.
2) The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
3) All cells come from pre-existing cells.
Contributors: Robert Hooke named cells (1665) looking at cork; Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first saw living microorganisms; Matthias Schleiden (plants, 1838) and Theodor Schwann (animals, 1839) proposed that all organisms are made of cells; Rudolf Virchow (1855) popularized that cells come from cells.

Prokaryotic cells (bacteria and archaea): no nucleus — DNA is usually a single circular chromosome in a region called the nucleoid; no membrane-bound organelles; smaller ribosomes; usually much smaller cells; many have a cell wall, and some have flagella and plasmids.
Eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi, protists): a true nucleus surrounded by a nuclear envelope; membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, ER and Golgi; linear chromosomes; usually larger.
Both have: a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.
Memory aid: Pro = no nucleus (pro sounds like no); Eu = do have a nucleus.

Only (or mainly) in plant cells: cell wall made of cellulose; chloroplasts for photosynthesis; one large central vacuole. Plant cells often have a fixed, rectangular shape.
Only (or mainly) in animal cells: centrioles (most plant cells lack them); lysosomes are more common; small vacuoles if any. Animal cells have a flexible, often rounded shape.
In both: nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus.
Classic mistake: plant cells DO have mitochondria — they carry out cellular respiration too.

The nucleus contains the cell's DNA (as chromatin, which condenses into chromosomes during division) and controls the cell's activities by controlling which genes are expressed.
It is surrounded by a double membrane called the nuclear envelope, which has nuclear pores that let molecules such as mRNA move in and out.
DNA replication and transcription (making RNA) happen in the nucleus in eukaryotes.
Found in eukaryotic cells only; mature human red blood cells lose their nucleus.

The nucleolus is a dense region inside the nucleus (not surrounded by a membrane).
It makes ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and assembles the ribosome subunits, which then leave through the nuclear pores to the cytoplasm.
Cells that make a lot of protein often have large nucleoli.

Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis (translation): they read mRNA and link amino acids into polypeptide chains.
They are made of rRNA and proteins and are NOT surrounded by a membrane.
Found in all cells, prokaryotic and eukaryotic.
Free ribosomes (in the cytoplasm) make proteins used inside the cell; bound ribosomes (on the rough ER) make proteins for membranes, lysosomes or export out of the cell.

The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rough ER) is a network of membrane sacs studded with ribosomes, which give it its rough appearance.
It makes, folds and modifies proteins that will go into membranes, into lysosomes, or be secreted from the cell.
The proteins are sent in transport vesicles to the Golgi apparatus.
It is continuous with the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope.

The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (smooth ER) is a network of membrane tubes without ribosomes.
Functions: makes lipids (phospholipids, steroid hormones); detoxifies drugs and poisons (especially in liver cells); stores calcium ions (in muscle cells it is called the sarcoplasmic reticulum); helps process carbohydrates.

The Golgi apparatus (Golgi body) is a stack of flattened membrane sacs.
It receives proteins and lipids from the ER, modifies them (for example by adding carbohydrates), sorts them and packages them into vesicles to send to their destinations — the cell membrane, lysosomes, or out of the cell by exocytosis.
Often compared to a post office or shipping centre.
Pathway of a secreted protein: ribosome on rough ER → ER → vesicle → Golgi → vesicle → cell membrane → outside.

Mitochondria (singular: mitochondrion) carry out most of cellular respiration, releasing energy from food (glucose) and storing it as ATP — often called the powerhouse of the cell.
They have a double membrane: the inner membrane is folded into cristae (more surface area for the electron transport chain), around a fluid called the matrix (where the Krebs cycle occurs).
They contain their own circular DNA and ribosomes and divide independently, evidence for the endosymbiotic theory.
Found in nearly all eukaryotic cells, including plant cells. Very active cells such as muscle cells have many.

Chloroplasts are the site of photosynthesis in plants and algae; they convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.
Structure: a double outer membrane; inside are thylakoids (flattened sacs, stacked into grana) where the light-dependent reactions happen, surrounded by the stroma (fluid) where the Calvin cycle happens.
They contain chlorophyll, the green pigment that absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green.
Like mitochondria, they have their own DNA and ribosomes (endosymbiotic theory).
Animal cells do not have chloroplasts.

Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs filled with digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes that work best in their acidic interior (about pH 5).
They break down food particles, worn-out organelles (autophagy), and engulfed bacteria and viruses, recycling the building blocks.
They are made by the Golgi apparatus and are common in animal cells; plant cells use their central vacuole for many similar jobs.
White blood cells that engulf bacteria have many lysosomes.

Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs that store water, nutrients, ions and wastes.
Plant cells have one large central vacuole that can fill much of the cell; when full of water it pushes against the cell wall (turgor pressure), keeping the plant firm. A plant wilts when its vacuoles lose water.
Animal cells have small vacuoles, if any.
Some freshwater protists (e.g. paramecium) have contractile vacuoles that pump out excess water.

The cell membrane surrounds every cell and controls what enters and leaves; it is selectively (semi-) permeable.
Structure (fluid mosaic model): a phospholipid bilayer — hydrophilic (water-loving) phosphate heads face the watery inside and outside, and hydrophobic (water-fearing) fatty-acid tails face each other in the middle.
Embedded proteins act as channels, carriers, pumps and receptors; cholesterol (in animal cells) adjusts fluidity; carbohydrate chains (glycoproteins, glycolipids) help cells recognize each other.
Small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) pass through easily; ions and large polar molecules (glucose) need transport proteins.

a: what is the cell wall made of
x:
The cell wall is a rigid layer OUTSIDE the cell membrane that supports and protects the cell and keeps it from bursting when water enters.
Composition differs by group: plants — cellulose; fungi — chitin; bacteria — peptidoglycan; archaea — other materials (not peptidoglycan).
Animal cells have no cell wall.
The cell wall is fully permeable; the cell membrane, not the wall, controls what enters the cell.

Cytoplasm is everything inside the cell membrane except the nucleus: the jelly-like cytosol plus the organelles suspended in it.
The cytosol is mostly water with dissolved salts, sugars, amino acids and enzymes.
Many chemical reactions happen in the cytosol, including glycolysis (the first stage of cellular respiration) and translation on free ribosomes.

Centrioles are paired cylinders of microtubules found in the centrosome of animal cells (most plant cells lack them).
The centrosome organizes microtubules; during cell division, the centrosomes move to opposite ends of the cell and the spindle fibres that pull chromosomes apart grow from them.
Structures similar to centrioles (basal bodies) anchor cilia and flagella.

Peroxisomes are small membrane-bound organelles containing enzymes that break down fatty acids and detoxify harmful substances (for example alcohol in liver cells).
These reactions produce hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), which the enzyme catalase quickly breaks down: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.
They are found in both plant and animal cells.

Cilia and flagella are hair-like projections used for movement.
Cilia: short and numerous; they beat in waves to move the cell (paramecium) or to move fluid across a surface (cells lining the human airways sweep mucus up and out).
Flagella: long, usually one or a few; they whip or rotate to propel the cell (human sperm cells, many bacteria).
Eukaryotic cilia and flagella are built from microtubules; bacterial flagella have a different structure and rotate like a propeller.

t: Passive transport: diffusion and facilitated diffusion
x:
Passive transport moves substances across a membrane DOWN their concentration gradient (from high to low concentration) and uses no ATP.
Simple diffusion: small or nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) pass directly through the phospholipid bilayer.
Facilitated diffusion: ions and larger polar molecules (glucose, Na⁺, K⁺) pass through channel proteins or carrier proteins — still high to low, still no ATP.
Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane (often through aquaporin channels).
Diffusion continues until equilibrium (equal concentration); molecules keep moving, but with no net change.
Diffusion is faster at higher temperature and with a steeper gradient.

Osmosis: water moves across a membrane from lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration (water follows solute).
Compare the solution OUTSIDE the cell with the inside:
Hypotonic solution (less solute outside): water moves IN. Animal cells swell and may burst (lysis); plant cells become turgid (firm) — the normal healthy state for plants.
Hypertonic solution (more solute outside): water moves OUT. Animal cells shrivel (crenation); plant cells undergo plasmolysis (membrane pulls away from the wall) and wilt.
Isotonic solution (equal solute): no net water movement; animal cells stay normal; plant cells become flaccid (limp).
Example: a red blood cell in pure water bursts; in very salty water it shrivels.
Classic mistake: the terms describe the solution outside relative to the cell, and it is water that moves, not the solute.

t: Active transport and the sodium–potassium pump
x:
Active transport moves substances AGAINST their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration). It requires energy, usually from ATP, and uses carrier proteins called pumps.
Sodium–potassium pump: for each ATP used it pumps 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell, keeping Na⁺ high outside and K⁺ high inside — essential for nerve impulses.
Other examples: root hair cells absorbing mineral ions from soil; cells lining the intestine absorbing glucose.
Compare: passive transport goes downhill (high → low) with no ATP; active transport goes uphill (low → high) with ATP.

ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the main short-term energy carrier in cells.
Structure: adenine (a nitrogen base) + ribose (a 5-carbon sugar) + three phosphate groups.
Energy is released when the bond to the last phosphate is broken by hydrolysis: ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ + energy (ADP = adenosine diphosphate, Pᵢ = inorganic phosphate).
Cells regenerate ATP from ADP mainly during cellular respiration (and photosynthesis in chloroplasts).
ATP powers active transport, muscle contraction, and building large molecules.

6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
carbon dioxide + water + light → glucose + oxygen
It takes place in the chloroplasts of plants and algae; cyanobacteria also photosynthesize, without chloroplasts.
Light energy is captured by chlorophyll and stored as chemical energy in glucose.
Two stages: the light-dependent reactions (thylakoid membranes) and the Calvin cycle, or light-independent reactions (stroma).
The oxygen released comes from splitting water, not from CO₂.
Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are roughly reverse processes.

Location: thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast.
1) Chlorophyll in photosystem II absorbs light and passes high-energy electrons to an electron transport chain.
2) Water is split (photolysis) to replace those electrons: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. The O₂ is released as a by-product.
3) The electron transport chain pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid space; H⁺ flows back out through ATP synthase, making ATP (chemiosmosis).
4) Photosystem I re-energizes the electrons with more light, and they reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH.
Inputs: light, H₂O, ADP, NADP⁺. Outputs: O₂, ATP, NADPH (the ATP and NADPH go to the Calvin cycle).

Location: stroma of the chloroplast. It does not need light directly, but uses the ATP and NADPH made by the light reactions (so it normally runs in daylight; the old name dark reactions is misleading).
1) Carbon fixation: the enzyme rubisco attaches CO₂ to a 5-carbon sugar, RuBP.
2) Reduction: ATP and NADPH convert the products into the 3-carbon sugar G3P.
3) Regeneration: most G3P is used, with more ATP, to regenerate RuBP; the rest leaves the cycle to make glucose and other sugars.
Three CO₂ fixed → one G3P exported; it takes 6 CO₂ (six turns) to make one glucose.
Inputs: CO₂, ATP, NADPH. Outputs: G3P (→ glucose), ADP, NADP⁺.

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP)
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
Aerobic (uses oxygen) cellular respiration happens in most eukaryotes — plants as well as animals — in the cytoplasm and mitochondria.
Stages: glycolysis (cytoplasm) → pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix) → electron transport chain (inner mitochondrial membrane).
Yield: about 30–32 ATP per glucose by current estimates (older textbooks say 36–38).
Classic mistake: cellular respiration is not breathing; breathing supplies the O₂ and removes the CO₂.

Location: cytoplasm (cytosol). Does not require oxygen (anaerobic step), and occurs in nearly all living things.
One glucose (6 carbons) is split into two pyruvate molecules (3 carbons each).
Uses 2 ATP and makes 4 ATP: net gain of 2 ATP per glucose.
Also makes 2 NADH (electron carriers).
With oxygen, pyruvate enters the mitochondria; without oxygen, it goes through fermentation.

t: Pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs (citric acid) cycle
x:
Location: mitochondrial matrix. Requires oxygen indirectly (it stops if the electron transport chain stops).
Pyruvate oxidation: each pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + CO₂, making 1 NADH (per glucose: 2 CO₂, 2 NADH).
Krebs cycle: acetyl-CoA joins a 4-carbon molecule to form citric acid (6 carbons), which is broken down again, releasing CO₂.
Per glucose (two turns of the cycle): 4 CO₂, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂ and 2 ATP (or GTP).
Total CO₂ released per glucose from pyruvate oxidation + Krebs = 6 CO₂.
The NADH and FADH₂ carry high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain.

t: Electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation
x:
Location: inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae).
NADH and FADH₂ give their electrons to a chain of proteins; as electrons pass along, energy is used to pump H⁺ ions into the intermembrane space.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor: it combines with electrons and H⁺ to form water. Without O₂, the chain stops.
H⁺ flows back into the matrix through ATP synthase, which makes ATP (chemiosmosis).
This stage makes most of the ATP: roughly 26–28 of the about 30–32 ATP per glucose (older textbooks: 32–34 of 36–38).
Cyanide is deadly because it blocks the electron transport chain.

Fermentation lets glycolysis continue when oxygen is absent by recycling NADH back to NAD⁺. It makes only the 2 ATP from glycolysis per glucose.
Lactic acid fermentation: pyruvate → lactate (lactic acid). Happens in human muscle cells during intense exercise when O₂ is short, and in bacteria used to make yogurt.
glucose → 2 lactic acid + 2 ATP
Alcoholic fermentation: pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂. Done by yeast and some bacteria; used in bread making (CO₂ makes dough rise) and brewing.
glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 CO₂ + 2 ATP
Aerobic respiration releases far more ATP per glucose (about 30–32).

The cell cycle is the life of a eukaryotic cell from one division to the next.
Interphase (most of the cycle; the cell is not dividing):
G1 (gap 1): cell grows and does its normal work;
S (synthesis): DNA is replicated, so each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids;
G2 (gap 2): more growth, preparation for division.
M phase: mitosis (division of the nucleus) followed by cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm).
G0: a non-dividing resting state (e.g. most mature nerve cells).
Checkpoints (G1, G2, M) check for DNA damage and correct preparation; loss of this control can lead to cancer (uncontrolled division).

Prophase: chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes (each = 2 sister chromatids joined at a centromere); spindle fibres form; the nuclear envelope breaks down (some textbooks call this last step prometaphase).
Metaphase: chromosomes line up single-file along the middle of the cell (metaphase plate).
Anaphase: sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles.
Telophase: nuclear envelopes re-form around the two sets of chromosomes, which uncoil.
Cytokinesis (overlaps telophase): animal cells pinch in with a cleavage furrow; plant cells build a cell plate that becomes a new cell wall.
Result: 2 genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent (in humans 46 → 46).
Used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Memory aid: PMAT (Please Make Another Twin).

Purpose: mitosis — growth, repair, asexual reproduction; meiosis — making gametes for sexual reproduction.
Number of divisions: mitosis 1; meiosis 2.
Daughter cells: mitosis 2; meiosis 4.
Chromosome number: mitosis keeps it the same (diploid → diploid, 46 → 46 in humans); meiosis halves it (diploid → haploid, 46 → 23).
Genetics: mitosis cells are identical to the parent; meiosis cells are genetically different.
Pairing of homologs and crossing over: only in meiosis (prophase I).
Where in humans: mitosis in body (somatic) cells; meiosis only in the ovaries and testes.
Both are preceded by one round of DNA replication in interphase.

A chromosome is a long DNA molecule wound around proteins (histones); genes are segments of it.
Humans have 46 chromosomes in each body cell: 23 pairs = 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX usually female, XY usually male).
Homologous chromosomes: a matching pair, one from each parent, with the same genes (possibly different alleles).
Diploid (2n): two sets of chromosomes, as in body cells (human 2n = 46).
Haploid (n): one set, as in gametes (human n = 23).
A karyotype is a picture of an organism's chromosomes arranged in pairs; it can reveal extra or missing chromosomes (e.g. Down syndrome = three copies of chromosome 21).

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a double helix — two strands twisted like a ladder (Watson and Crick, 1953, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins).
Each nucleotide = a deoxyribose sugar + a phosphate group + a nitrogen base. Sugar and phosphate form the backbone; the bases form the rungs.
Base pairing: adenine (A) with thymine (T) by 2 hydrogen bonds; guanine (G) with cytosine (C) by 3 hydrogen bonds.
Purines (two rings): A and G. Pyrimidines (one ring): C, T (and U in RNA).
The two strands are antiparallel (one runs 5'→3', the other 3'→5').
Chargaff's rule: in DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C. Example: if a DNA sample is 30% A, it is 30% T, 20% G and 20% C.
Complementary strand example: 5'-ATGC-3' pairs with 3'-TACG-5'.

Sugar: DNA has deoxyribose; RNA has ribose.
Bases: DNA uses A, T, G, C; RNA uses A, U (uracil), G, C — U replaces T.
Strands: DNA is usually double-stranded; RNA is usually single-stranded.
Location in eukaryotes: DNA stays mostly in the nucleus (also in mitochondria and chloroplasts); RNA is made in the nucleus and works mainly in the cytoplasm.
Role: DNA stores genetic information long term; RNA helps express it.
Three main types of RNA: mRNA (messenger) carries the code from DNA to the ribosome; tRNA (transfer) brings amino acids to the ribosome; rRNA (ribosomal) forms part of the ribosome.

DNA replication copies DNA before cell division (during the S phase of interphase).
It is semiconservative: each new DNA molecule has one original (parent) strand and one new strand.
1) Helicase unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between bases, opening a replication fork.
2) Primase lays down a short RNA primer.
3) DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides (A with T, G with C), building new DNA only in the 5'→3' direction, and proofreads.
4) The leading strand is made continuously; the lagging strand is made in short pieces (Okazaki fragments).
5) Primers are replaced with DNA, and DNA ligase joins the fragments.
Result: two identical DNA molecules.

Transcription copies a gene's DNA into mRNA. In eukaryotes it happens in the nucleus.
1) RNA polymerase binds to a promoter region at the start of a gene and unwinds the DNA.
2) It reads the template strand and builds mRNA (5'→3') with complementary bases: DNA A → RNA U, T → A, G → C, C → G.
3) It stops at a terminator sequence and the mRNA is released.
In eukaryotes the pre-mRNA is processed: a 5' cap and a poly-A tail are added, and introns (non-coding parts) are spliced out while exons (coding parts) are joined.
Example: DNA template 3'-TACGGA-5' → mRNA 5'-AUGCCU-3'.
The mRNA then leaves the nucleus for a ribosome.

Translation builds a protein from the mRNA code at a ribosome (in the cytoplasm or on the rough ER).
mRNA is read three bases at a time; each triplet is a codon that codes for one amino acid (or stop).
Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to an mRNA codon.
1) Initiation: the ribosome assembles at the start codon AUG (which codes for methionine).
2) Elongation: tRNAs bring amino acids in codon order; the ribosome joins them with peptide bonds.
3) Termination: a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA) releases the finished polypeptide.
Example: mRNA AUG GCA UAA → methionine–alanine, then stop. The tRNA anticodon for AUG is UAC.
Central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein.

There are 4³ = 64 possible codons (3-base mRNA triplets).
61 codons code for amino acids; 3 are stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA.
AUG is the start codon and also codes for methionine (Met).
There are 20 standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon (the code is redundant, or degenerate). Example: GCU, GCC, GCA and GCG all code for alanine.
Each codon codes for only one amino acid (the code is unambiguous).
The code is nearly universal: almost all organisms use the same codons, which is why bacteria can make human insulin from the human gene.

A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence.
Point mutation (substitution): one base replaced by another.
silent — the codon still codes for the same amino acid;
missense — a different amino acid (e.g. sickle-cell anemia: one base change in the β-globin gene swaps glutamic acid for valine);
nonsense — creates a stop codon, cutting the protein short.
Frameshift mutation: an insertion or deletion of bases (not a multiple of 3) shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it; usually very harmful.
Chromosomal mutations: deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation of large segments.
Causes: copying errors and mutagens (UV light, X-rays, certain chemicals). In sexually reproducing organisms, only mutations in gametes (or the cells that make them) are passed to offspring.

Gene: a segment of DNA that codes for a trait (usually for a protein).
Allele: one version of a gene (e.g. B for brown and b for blue).
Genotype: the alleles an organism has (BB, Bb or bb). Phenotype: the trait you can observe (brown eyes).
Homozygous: two identical alleles (BB or bb), also called purebred. Heterozygous: two different alleles (Bb), also called hybrid or carrier.
