Dominant allele (capital letter): shows its trait whenever present. Recessive allele (lowercase): shows only when there is no dominant allele (bb).
P generation = parents; F1 = first offspring generation; F2 = offspring of F1 × F1.

Gregor Mendel worked out the basic rules of heredity from experiments with pea plants (published 1866).
Law of segregation: each organism has two alleles for each gene, and they separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele.
Law of independent assortment: alleles of different genes are sorted into gametes independently of each other (true for genes on different chromosomes or far apart on the same one).
Principle of dominance: when two different alleles are present, the dominant one can mask the recessive one.
The physical basis: homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I of meiosis.

Punnett square: put one parent's possible gametes across the top and the other's down the side, then fill each box with the combined alleles. Each box = 1/4 probability.
Aa × Aa (two heterozygotes): genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; phenotypes 3 dominant : 1 recessive (75% : 25%).
AA × aa: all Aa (100% show the dominant trait).
Aa × aa: 1 Aa : 1 aa (50% dominant, 50% recessive).
AA × Aa: 1 AA : 1 Aa (100% dominant).
Test cross: cross an organism showing the dominant trait with a homozygous recessive (aa). If any offspring show the recessive trait, the unknown parent was Aa.
Ratios are probabilities for each child, not guarantees for a family.

A dihybrid cross follows two genes at once, using a 4 × 4 Punnett square (16 boxes).
Each AaBb parent makes four kinds of gametes in equal amounts: AB, Ab, aB, ab.
AaBb × AaBb (genes assorting independently) gives phenotypes in the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1:
9/16 dominant for both traits, 3/16 dominant A only, 3/16 dominant B only, 1/16 recessive for both.
Shortcut with the product rule: multiply the probabilities for each gene. Example: P(aabb) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16; P(A_B_) = 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16.
AaBb × aabb (dihybrid test cross) gives 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.

t: Incomplete dominance, codominance and other patterns
x:
Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote has a blended, intermediate phenotype. Example: red (RR) × white (WW) snapdragons give pink (RW); pink × pink gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
Codominance: both alleles are fully shown at once. Examples: AB blood type (both A and B antigens); roan cattle with both red and white hairs.
Multiple alleles: a gene has more than two alleles in the population (ABO blood type has Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i), though each person carries only two.
Polygenic traits: controlled by many genes, giving a continuous range (human height, skin colour).
Environment can also affect phenotype (e.g. hydrangea flower colour depends on soil pH).

Sex-linked genes are on the sex chromosomes, usually the X. Females are XX; males are XY.
X-linked recessive traits (red–green colour blindness, hemophilia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy) are much more common in males, because a male has only one X: one recessive allele is enough.
A female needs two copies to show the trait; with one copy she is a carrier.
Sons get their X from their mother; fathers pass their X to all daughters and their Y to all sons.
Example: carrier mother XᴴXʰ × unaffected father XᴴY → daughters: 50% XᴴXᴴ, 50% XᴴXʰ carriers, none affected; sons: 50% XᴴY unaffected, 50% XʰY affected.
An affected father cannot pass an X-linked trait to his sons.

ABO alleles: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant; i is recessive.
Type A: genotype IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi; A antigens on red cells; anti-B antibodies in plasma.
Type B: IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi; B antigens; anti-A antibodies.
Type AB: IᴬIᴮ; both A and B antigens; no anti-A or anti-B antibodies.
Type O: ii; no A or B antigens; both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
Rh: Rh-positive (+) cells have the D antigen; Rh-negative (−) cells do not.
For red-cell transfusions: O− is the universal donor; AB+ is the universal recipient.
Example: Iᴬi × Iᴮi parents can have children of all four types, each with probability 1/4 (AB, A, B, O).

For a gene with two alleles: p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1
p = frequency of the dominant allele, q = frequency of the recessive allele; p² = frequency of homozygous dominant, 2pq = heterozygous, q² = homozygous recessive individuals.
The population stays in equilibrium (no evolution) only if: no mutation, random mating, no natural selection, a very large population (no genetic drift), and no gene flow (migration).
Example: 16% of a population shows the recessive trait: q² = 0.16 → q = 0.4, p = 0.6; carriers 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48 (48%); homozygous dominant p² = 0.36.
Classic mistake: the percentage of recessive individuals is q², not q — take the square root first.

Natural selection (Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace; Darwin's On the Origin of Species, 1859) is the main mechanism of evolution. Its conditions:
1) Variation: individuals in a population differ in their traits.
2) Inheritance: many traits are passed from parents to offspring.
3) Overproduction: more offspring are born than can survive, so there is competition.
4) Differential survival and reproduction: individuals with traits better suited to the environment survive and reproduce more.
Over generations, helpful (adaptive) traits become more common in the population.
Fitness means reproductive success, not strength.
Individuals do not evolve; populations do. Example: bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics.

Fossil record: shows life changing over time, including transitional forms (e.g. Tiktaalik between fish and land animals).
Homologous structures: same basic structure, different functions, from a common ancestor (human arm, bat wing, whale flipper).
Analogous structures: similar function, different structure, from convergent evolution, not common ancestry (bird wing vs insect wing).
Vestigial structures: reduced or no longer used (whale pelvic bones, human tailbone).
Embryology: early embryos of related vertebrates look similar (e.g. all have pharyngeal pouches).
Molecular biology: DNA and protein sequences are more similar in more closely related species.
Biogeography: the distribution of species matches their evolutionary history (e.g. Darwin's finches in the Galápagos).

Carbohydrates: made of C, H, O; monomer = monosaccharide (glucose). Quick energy and structure. Examples: sugars, starch (plant energy store), glycogen (animal energy store), cellulose (plant cell walls).
Lipids: mostly C and H (some O); built from glycerol and fatty acids (not true polymers). Long-term energy storage, insulation, cell membranes (phospholipids), hormones (steroids). Hydrophobic. Examples: fats, oils, waxes, cholesterol.
Proteins: C, H, O, N (often S); monomer = amino acid (20 kinds) joined by peptide bonds. Enzymes, structure, transport, antibodies, movement.
Nucleic acids: C, H, O, N, P; monomer = nucleotide. Store and transmit genetic information (DNA, RNA).
Polymers are built by dehydration synthesis (removing water) and broken down by hydrolysis (adding water).

Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. They are not used up.
The substrate binds to the enzyme's active site; each enzyme is specific to certain substrates (lock-and-key model; the induced-fit model adds that the active site changes shape slightly to fit).
Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH. Human enzymes typically work best near 37 °C; pepsin in the stomach works best near pH 2.
High temperature or extreme pH denatures an enzyme: its shape (and active site) changes, so it stops working.
Rate also depends on enzyme and substrate concentration; inhibitors can block or alter the active site.
Names often end in -ase: amylase (starch), lipase (fats), protease (proteins).

From smallest to largest:
organism (one individual)
population (all individuals of one species in an area)
community (all populations of different species in an area)
ecosystem (the community plus its abiotic, non-living, environment: water, soil, light, temperature)
biome (a large region with a characteristic climate and community, e.g. tundra, desert, tropical rainforest)
biosphere (all parts of Earth where life exists)
Biotic factors are living parts of an environment; abiotic factors are non-living parts.
Within the body: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.

t: Food chains, food webs and trophic levels
x:
Producers (autotrophs) make their own food, mostly by photosynthesis: plants, algae, cyanobacteria. They form the first trophic level.
Primary consumers eat producers (herbivores). Secondary consumers eat primary consumers. Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers. Carnivores eat animals; omnivores eat plants and animals.
Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead matter and wastes, returning nutrients to the soil.
In a food chain, arrows point in the direction energy flows: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk.
A food web is a set of interconnected food chains; it is more realistic and more stable.

On average only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next level (actual values range roughly 5–20%).
The other ~90% is used for life processes (respiration, movement) and lost mostly as heat, or is not eaten or digested.
Example: producers 10,000 kcal → primary consumers 1,000 kcal → secondary consumers 100 kcal → tertiary consumers 10 kcal.
This is why food chains rarely have more than 4–5 levels, and why there are fewer top predators than herbivores.
Energy flows one way through an ecosystem (and must be constantly supplied, mostly by the Sun), while matter (carbon, nitrogen, water) is recycled.
An energy pyramid always has its widest level at the bottom.

Carbon moves between the atmosphere, living things, oceans, rocks and fossil fuels.
Removes CO₂ from the air: photosynthesis (plants, algae) turns CO₂ into sugars; oceans dissolve CO₂.
Returns CO₂ to the air: cellular respiration by all organisms; decomposition of dead organisms; burning (combustion) of fossil fuels and wood; volcanic eruptions.
Carbon passes through food chains when organisms eat each other.
Long-term storage: fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas formed from ancient organisms), carbonate rocks such as limestone, ocean sediments.
Burning fossil fuels and deforestation add CO₂ to the atmosphere faster than it is removed, strengthening the greenhouse effect.

About 78% of the air is nitrogen gas (N₂), but most organisms cannot use N₂ directly. Organisms need nitrogen to make proteins and nucleic acids.
1) Nitrogen fixation: bacteria (some free in soil, others such as Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes like peas and beans) convert N₂ into ammonia (NH₃) / ammonium (NH₄⁺). Lightning and industrial fertilizer production also fix nitrogen.
2) Nitrification: nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrite (NO₂⁻) and then nitrate (NO₃⁻).
3) Assimilation: plants absorb nitrate and ammonium through their roots; animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
4) Ammonification: decomposers return nitrogen from dead matter and wastes to the soil as ammonium.
5) Denitrification: denitrifying bacteria (in low-oxygen soil) convert nitrate back to N₂ gas, which returns to the atmosphere.

Symbiosis: a close, long-term relationship between two different species.
Mutualism (+/+): both benefit. Examples: bees and flowers; clownfish and sea anemones; Rhizobium bacteria and legumes.
Commensalism (+/0): one benefits, the other is unaffected. Examples: barnacles on a whale; birds nesting in a tree.
Parasitism (+/−): the parasite benefits and the host is harmed (usually not killed quickly). Examples: tapeworms, ticks, fleas.
Other interactions: predation (+/−: predator eats prey), competition (−/−: both compete for the same limited resource such as food, water or space).

Exponential growth (J-shaped curve): the population grows faster and faster when resources are unlimited.
Logistic growth (S-shaped curve): growth slows and levels off at the carrying capacity (K), the largest population the environment can support long term.
Limiting factors keep populations near K.
Density-dependent factors grow stronger as the population gets denser: competition, predation, disease, parasites.
Density-independent factors affect a population regardless of its size: natural disasters, weather, fires, human activities such as damming rivers.
Population change = (births + immigration) − (deaths + emigration).

a: domain kingdom phylum class order family genus species
x:
From broadest to most specific: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
Memory aid: Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.
Example (human): Eukarya, Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, Homo, sapiens.
Binomial nomenclature (Carl Linnaeus): every species has a two-part scientific name, Genus species. The genus is capitalized, the species name is lowercase, and the whole name is italicized (or underlined when handwritten): Homo sapiens, Felis catus.
Organisms in the same genus are more closely related than organisms only in the same family, order, and so on.

Domain Bacteria — kingdom Eubacteria: prokaryotic, unicellular, cell walls with peptidoglycan (e.g. E. coli, Streptococcus).
Domain Archaea — kingdom Archaebacteria: prokaryotic, unicellular, often in extreme environments (hot springs, very salty water).
Domain Eukarya — four kingdoms, all with nucleus:
Protista: mostly unicellular, very diverse (amoeba, paramecium, algae).
Fungi: absorb nutrients from their surroundings, cell walls of chitin (mushrooms, yeast, molds).
Plantae: multicellular, photosynthetic, cell walls of cellulose.
Animalia: multicellular, eat other organisms, no cell walls.
Viruses are not placed in any domain or kingdom; most biologists do not consider them living cells.

A virus is a tiny non-cellular particle made of genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat called a capsid; some also have a lipid envelope.
Viruses can only reproduce inside a living host cell, using the host's ribosomes and enzymes. They do not grow, respire or carry out metabolism on their own.
Lytic cycle: the virus takes over the cell, makes many copies, and bursts (lyses) the cell.
Lysogenic cycle: the viral DNA joins the host's DNA and is copied along with it, staying inactive until it later enters the lytic cycle.
A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria.
Antibiotics do not work against viruses; vaccines and antiviral drugs are used instead.

Main parts: heart, blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) and blood.
Function: transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones and heat to cells, and carries away CO₂ and other wastes.
The human heart has four chambers: two atria (upper, receive blood) and two ventricles (lower, pump blood out).
Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart (thick, muscular, high pressure). Veins carry blood TO the heart (thinner walls, have valves to stop backflow). Capillaries are tiny vessels with walls one cell thick where exchange with tissues happens.
Two circuits: pulmonary circulation (heart ↔ lungs) and systemic circulation (heart ↔ body).
Classic mistake: arteries do not always carry oxygenated blood — the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

t: Path of blood through the heart
x:
Deoxygenated blood from the body → superior and inferior vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs (picks up O₂, releases CO₂).
Oxygenated blood → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral (bicuspid) valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → body.
The right side pumps blood to the lungs; the left side pumps blood to the whole body, so the left ventricle has the thickest muscular wall.
The pulmonary arteries are the only arteries carrying deoxygenated blood; the pulmonary veins are the only veins carrying oxygenated blood (in adults).
The heartbeat is started by the sinoatrial (SA) node, the natural pacemaker in the right atrium.

Plasma (about 55% of blood volume): mostly water, carrying dissolved nutrients, hormones, proteins, salts and wastes such as CO₂ and urea.
Red blood cells (erythrocytes): carry oxygen using the iron-containing protein hemoglobin; in mammals they have no nucleus and are disc-shaped (biconcave); they live about 120 days.
White blood cells (leukocytes): fight infection — some engulf pathogens (phagocytes), others (lymphocytes) make antibodies or kill infected cells.
Platelets (thrombocytes): cell fragments that help blood clot.
Blood cells are made in the red bone marrow.

Function: brings O₂ into the body and removes CO₂ (gas exchange).
Path of air: nose/mouth → pharynx (throat) → larynx (voice box) → trachea (windpipe) → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Alveoli are tiny air sacs surrounded by capillaries; O₂ diffuses from the alveoli into the blood and CO₂ diffuses from the blood into the alveoli. Their huge total surface area and thin walls make diffusion fast.
Breathing in (inhalation): the diaphragm contracts and moves down, the rib cage expands, the chest volume increases and the pressure drops, so air flows in. Exhaling reverses this.
The epiglottis covers the trachea when you swallow so food goes down the esophagus.
The brainstem controls breathing rate mainly in response to CO₂ levels in the blood.

Function: breaks food down into small molecules the body can absorb, and removes undigested waste.
Path of food (the alimentary canal): mouth → pharynx → esophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus.
Mouth: teeth chew (mechanical digestion); saliva contains amylase, which starts digesting starch.
Esophagus: moves food by waves of muscle contraction (peristalsis).
Stomach: churns food; hydrochloric acid and pepsin begin protein digestion.
Small intestine: most chemical digestion and nutrient absorption, through villi and microvilli that greatly increase surface area.
Large intestine: absorbs water; bacteria there make some vitamins (such as vitamin K).
Accessory organs (food does not pass through them): liver (makes bile, which breaks fat into small droplets), gallbladder (stores bile), pancreas (makes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate).

Function: detects stimuli and sends fast electrical and chemical signals to coordinate the body.
Central nervous system (CNS): brain and spinal cord. Peripheral nervous system (PNS): all the nerves outside the CNS.
Neurons (nerve cells): dendrites receive signals → cell body → axon carries the impulse away → axon terminals. A myelin sheath around many axons speeds up impulses.
Types: sensory neurons (from receptors to the CNS), interneurons (within the CNS), motor neurons (from the CNS to muscles and glands).
A synapse is the gap between neurons; the signal crosses it by chemical neurotransmitters.
Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (interneuron) → motor neuron → effector (muscle); a fast, automatic response that does not wait for the brain.
Brain parts: cerebrum (thinking, senses, voluntary movement), cerebellum (balance and coordination), brainstem/medulla (breathing, heart rate).

Function: glands release hormones (chemical messengers) into the blood; they act on target cells. Slower but longer-lasting than nerve signals.
Hypothalamus: links the nervous and endocrine systems and controls the pituitary.
Pituitary gland: often called the master gland; releases growth hormone and hormones that control other glands.
Thyroid gland: thyroxine, which regulates metabolism.
Adrenal glands: adrenaline (epinephrine) for fight-or-flight; cortisol for stress responses.
Pancreas: insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.
Ovaries: estrogen and progesterone. Testes: testosterone.
Most hormone levels are controlled by negative feedback: a rise in a level triggers responses that bring it back down (homeostasis).

Function: defends the body against pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites) and cancer cells.
First line (barriers): skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid, tears and saliva with enzymes.
Second line (innate, non-specific): inflammation, fever, and phagocytes (such as macrophages and neutrophils) that engulf invaders.
Third line (adaptive, specific): B cells make antibodies that bind specific antigens; helper T cells coordinate the response; cytotoxic (killer) T cells destroy infected cells. Memory cells allow a faster, stronger response next time (immunity).
Vaccines expose the body to a harmless form or piece of a pathogen so that memory cells form without causing the disease.
Lymphatic system: lymph vessels, lymph nodes, spleen, thymus and tonsils; returns fluid to the blood and is where many white blood cells mature and gather.
Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses.

Functions: supports the body, protects organs (skull → brain, ribs → heart and lungs), allows movement with muscles, makes blood cells in red bone marrow, and stores minerals such as calcium and phosphorus.
An adult human skeleton has 206 bones (babies are born with more, which fuse as they grow).
The largest bone is the femur (thigh bone); the smallest is the stapes in the middle ear.
Ligaments connect bone to bone. Cartilage cushions the ends of bones at joints.
Joint types include: ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (elbow, knee), pivot (top of the neck), gliding (wrist bones), and immovable joints (skull sutures).

Function: movement, posture, and heat production; also moves blood and food through the body.
Three types of muscle:
skeletal muscle — voluntary, striated (striped), attached to bones;
cardiac muscle — involuntary, striated, only in the heart;
smooth muscle — involuntary, not striated, in walls of organs and blood vessels (stomach, intestines, arteries).
Tendons connect muscle to bone.
Muscles can only pull (contract), not push, so they work in antagonistic pairs: the biceps contracts to bend the elbow, the triceps contracts to straighten it.
Muscle contraction uses ATP; muscle fibres contain actin and myosin filaments that slide past each other.

Parts: skin, hair, nails, sweat glands and oil (sebaceous) glands.
The skin is the largest organ of the human body.
Layers: epidermis (outer, protective, constantly replaced; contains melanin, a pigment that absorbs UV), dermis (blood vessels, nerves, sweat glands, hair follicles), and beneath it the hypodermis or subcutaneous layer (fat for insulation and energy storage).
Functions: barrier against pathogens and water loss; temperature regulation (sweating, blood vessels widening or narrowing); sensing touch, pain, heat and cold; making vitamin D when exposed to sunlight.

Function: removes metabolic wastes from the blood and regulates water, salt and pH balance (homeostasis).
Path: kidneys → ureters → urinary bladder → urethra.
The kidneys filter blood through about a million tiny units in each kidney called nephrons; useful substances (water, glucose, salts) are reabsorbed, and the rest leaves as urine.
Urea, the main nitrogen waste, is made in the liver from the breakdown of amino acids and carried by the blood to the kidneys.
Other excretory organs: lungs (CO₂), skin (sweat), liver (breaks down toxins, makes urea).

Function: produces gametes and sex hormones, and in females supports the developing baby.
Male: testes make sperm and testosterone; sperm pass through the epididymis (where they mature), vas deferens and urethra; glands (seminal vesicles, prostate) add fluid to form semen.
Female: ovaries make eggs (ova) and estrogen and progesterone; an egg released at ovulation travels down a fallopian tube (oviduct), where fertilization usually happens; the embryo implants in the lining of the uterus; the cervix connects the uterus to the vagina (birth canal).
The menstrual cycle averages about 28 days, but it varies between people.
Fertilization joins a haploid sperm (23 chromosomes) and a haploid egg (23) into a diploid zygote (46).

Homeostasis is keeping a stable internal environment (temperature, blood glucose, water balance, pH) despite outside changes.
Negative feedback reverses a change back toward the set point — the most common type.
Example: body temperature (about 37 °C) rises → you sweat and skin blood vessels widen → temperature falls. If it drops → you shiver and skin blood vessels narrow.
Example: blood glucose rises after a meal → pancreas releases insulin → cells take up glucose and the liver stores it as glycogen → level falls. Low glucose → glucagon → liver releases glucose.
Positive feedback amplifies a change until an event ends it. Examples: contractions during childbirth (driven by oxytocin), blood clotting.
Diabetes is a failure of blood-glucose homeostasis (too little insulin, or cells not responding to it).

By composition, from the surface inward (Earth's mean radius is about 6,371 km):
Crust: thin, rocky outer layer. Oceanic crust is about 5–10 km thick, dense, mostly basalt; continental crust is about 30–50 km thick (thicker under mountains), less dense, mostly granite-type rock.
Mantle: from the base of the crust to about 2,900 km deep; hot, mostly solid silicate rock that flows very slowly; the largest layer by volume.
Outer core: about 2,900 to 5,150 km deep; LIQUID iron and nickel; its flow generates Earth's magnetic field.
Inner core: about 5,150 km to the centre (6,371 km); SOLID iron and nickel, despite being the hottest part, because of the enormous pressure.
By physical properties: lithosphere (rigid crust + uppermost mantle, broken into tectonic plates) floats on the asthenosphere (a weaker, slowly flowing part of the upper mantle).

Plate tectonics: Earth's lithosphere is broken into large plates that move slowly over the asthenosphere, typically a few centimetres per year (about as fast as fingernails grow).
Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912: the continents were once joined in a supercontinent, Pangaea, that broke apart about 200 million years ago.
Evidence: matching coastlines (South America and Africa); matching fossils across oceans (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris); matching rock layers and mountain belts; glacial deposits in now-tropical places.
Seafloor spreading (proposed by Harry Hess, early 1960s) supplied the mechanism: new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges; rocks get older farther from the ridge, and they record symmetrical stripes of reversed magnetic polarity.
Plate motion is driven mainly by mantle convection and by gravity pulling dense plates down at subduction zones (slab pull).

Divergent boundary: plates move apart; magma rises and forms new crust. Features: mid-ocean ridges, rift valleys. Examples: Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift, Iceland.
Convergent boundary: plates move toward each other.
oceanic–continental: the denser oceanic plate subducts → deep-ocean trench + volcanic mountains on land (Andes).
oceanic–oceanic: one plate subducts → trench + volcanic island arc (Japan, Mariana Trench).
continental–continental: neither subducts → crust crumples into high folded mountains (Himalayas, from India hitting Asia).
Transform boundary: plates slide past each other horizontally; crust is neither made nor destroyed; frequent earthquakes. Example: San Andreas Fault, California.
Memory aid: divergent = divide, convergent = collide, transform = slide.

An earthquake is sudden shaking when rocks along a fault slip, releasing stored energy. The focus (hypocentre) is the point underground where it starts; the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.
P waves (primary): compressional (longitudinal), the fastest, travel through solids, liquids and gases.
S waves (secondary): shear (transverse), slower, travel only through solids.
Surface waves: slowest, travel along the surface, usually cause the most damage.
S waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core, creating an S-wave shadow zone — evidence that the outer core is liquid.
The epicentre is located by triangulation, using the P–S arrival time difference at three or more seismograph stations.
Magnitude scales (Richter, moment magnitude) are logarithmic: each whole number is 10 times the ground motion amplitude and about 32 times the energy released.

The rock cycle shows how the three rock types change into one another over long periods of time.
Magma or lava cools and crystallizes → igneous rock.
Any rock at the surface is weathered and eroded into sediment → sediment is deposited, compacted and cemented → sedimentary rock.
Any rock exposed to high heat and pressure (without melting) → metamorphic rock.
Any rock that melts → magma, which can cool into new igneous rock.
There is no fixed order: igneous rock can become metamorphic directly, metamorphic rock can be weathered into sediment, and so on.
Energy sources: Earth's internal heat drives melting and metamorphism; the Sun (through weather and the water cycle) and gravity drive weathering and erosion.

Igneous rocks form when molten rock (magma underground, lava at the surface) cools and solidifies.
Intrusive (plutonic): cools slowly underground → large crystals, coarse texture. Examples: granite, diorite, gabbro.
Extrusive (volcanic): cools quickly at the surface → small crystals, fine texture. Examples: basalt, rhyolite, andesite.
Very fast cooling gives a glassy texture with no crystals (obsidian). Trapped gas bubbles make vesicular rocks (pumice, which can float on water; scoria).
Rule: slower cooling → bigger crystals.
Basalt makes up most of the oceanic crust; granite is common in continental crust.

Sedimentary rocks form from sediment (fragments of rock, minerals, or remains of living things) that is deposited in layers, then compacted (squeezed) and cemented together.
Clastic: made of rock fragments, named by grain size — conglomerate (rounded pebbles), sandstone (sand), siltstone, shale (clay, very fine).
Chemical: minerals precipitated from water — rock salt, some limestone.
Organic (biochemical): from the remains of organisms — coal (plants), much limestone and chalk (shells and skeletons).
They often show layers (strata) and are the rocks where almost all fossils are found.
Law of superposition: in undisturbed layers, the oldest are at the bottom and the youngest at the top.

Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are changed by heat, pressure and/or chemically active fluids without melting.
Foliated: minerals are lined up in bands or layers by pressure. Examples: slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss (increasing degree of metamorphism, starting from shale).
Non-foliated: no banding. Examples: marble (from limestone), quartzite (from sandstone).
Parent rock → metamorphic rock: shale → slate; limestone → marble; sandstone → quartzite; granite → gneiss.
Regional metamorphism happens over large areas during mountain building; contact metamorphism happens where magma heats nearby rock.

Hardness is resistance to being scratched; a mineral scratches anything softer than itself.
1 talc (softest), 2 gypsum, 3 calcite, 4 fluorite, 5 apatite
6 orthoclase feldspar, 7 quartz, 8 topaz, 9 corundum (ruby, sapphire), 10 diamond (hardest)
Everyday tests: fingernail ≈ 2.5, copper coin ≈ 3.5, glass or steel knife ≈ 5.5. The scale is ordinal: diamond is far more than 10/9 as hard as corundum.
Memory aid: Tall Giraffes Can Find Alligators Or Quietly Travel Close Distances.

Weathering: breaking down rock in place.
Mechanical (physical) weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its composition: frost wedging (ice-wedging — water freezes and expands in cracks), abrasion, plant roots, animals burrowing.
Chemical weathering changes the minerals: oxidation (rusting of iron-rich rock), dissolving of limestone by slightly acidic rain (forms caves), hydrolysis of feldspar into clay.
Chemical weathering is fastest in warm, wet climates.
Erosion: moving weathered material away. Agents: water (the most important), wind, glaciers (ice), waves, and gravity (landslides, mass movement).
Deposition: dropping sediment when the agent slows down (e.g. deltas at river mouths, sand dunes, glacial moraines).

From the ground up (heights are approximate and vary with latitude and season):
Troposphere: 0 to about 12 km (about 8 km at the poles, about 16–18 km at the equator). All weather happens here; it holds most of the air's mass; temperature drops with height (about 6.5 °C per km on average).
Stratosphere: to about 50 km. Contains the ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet light; temperature rises with height. Jet aircraft often cruise near its base.
Mesosphere: to about 85 km. The coldest layer (around −90 °C at its top); most meteors burn up here; temperature drops with height.
Thermosphere: to roughly 500–1,000 km. Very thin air; temperature rises greatly with height; auroras occur here; the International Space Station orbits within it (about 400 km).
Exosphere: the outermost, extremely thin layer that fades into space.
Memory aid: The Strong Man's Triceps Explode.

Dry air near sea level, by volume:
nitrogen (N₂) about 78%
oxygen (O₂) about 21%
argon (Ar) about 0.93%
carbon dioxide (CO₂) about 0.04% and rising (over 400 parts per million)
plus small traces of neon, helium, methane, krypton, hydrogen and others.
Water vapour varies from almost 0% to about 4% depending on place and weather, so it is usually listed separately.
Air pressure and density decrease with altitude.

Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms Earth's surface. The warm surface gives off infrared radiation (heat). Greenhouse gases absorb much of this infrared and re-emit it, some back toward the surface, keeping the lower atmosphere warmer.
Main greenhouse gases: water vapour (H₂O), carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), ozone (O₃) and fluorinated gases.
The natural greenhouse effect makes life possible: Earth's average surface temperature is about 15 °C instead of about −18 °C without it.
Human activities, mainly burning fossil fuels and deforestation, have increased the amount of CO₂ and other greenhouse gases, enhancing the effect and causing global warming and climate change.
N₂ and O₂, the main gases in air, are not greenhouse gases.
The greenhouse effect is not the same as the ozone hole (ozone depletion), which lets in more UV.

The water cycle (hydrologic cycle) is the continuous movement of water around Earth, powered by the Sun's energy and gravity.
Evaporation: liquid water (mostly from oceans) turns into water vapour.
Transpiration: plants release water vapour through their leaves.
Condensation: water vapour cools and forms tiny droplets, making clouds and fog.
Precipitation: water falls as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
Collection: water gathers in oceans, lakes and rivers, flows over land (runoff), or soaks into the ground (infiltration) to become groundwater.
About 97% of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans; most fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers.

An air mass is a huge body of air with similar temperature and humidity throughout. A front is the boundary between two air masses.
Cold front: cold air pushes under warm air, forcing it up quickly → tall cumulonimbus clouds, short heavy rain or thunderstorms, then cooler, clearer weather.
Warm front: warm air slides up over cold air gradually → layered clouds and long periods of light rain or drizzle, then warmer weather.
Stationary front: neither air mass moves much → several days of similar weather. Occluded front: a cold front overtakes a warm front.
Low-pressure systems usually bring clouds and precipitation (rising air); high-pressure systems usually bring clear, calm weather (sinking air).
Wind blows from high pressure toward low pressure.

Earth formed about 4.54 billion (4,540 million) years ago.
Geologic time divisions, largest to smallest: eon → era → period → epoch.
Eons: Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic (together often called Precambrian), and Phanerozoic (the last ~539 million years, with abundant complex life).
Phanerozoic eras: Paleozoic (ancient life; ended with the largest mass extinction about 252 million years ago), Mesozoic (age of reptiles and dinosaurs), Cenozoic (age of mammals, up to today).
The non-avian dinosaurs went extinct about 66 million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous period, most likely after a large asteroid impact.
Relative dating puts rocks in order (law of superposition: lower layers are older); absolute (radiometric) dating finds actual ages using radioactive half-lives.

a: why is it hot in summer
x:
Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, about 23.4° from perpendicular to its orbit — NOT by changes in Earth's distance from the Sun.
The axis keeps pointing the same direction in space (toward Polaris) as Earth orbits. When a hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, sunlight hits it more directly (more energy per square metre) and days are longer → summer. Tilted away → winter.
Northern Hemisphere (Southern is the reverse): June solstice around June 20–21 = longest day, start of summer; December solstice around December 21–22 = shortest day; equinoxes around March 20 and September 22–23 = day and night roughly equal everywhere.
Earth is actually closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January, during Northern Hemisphere winter.
Classic mistake: summer is not when Earth is closest to the Sun.

a: why does the moon have phases
x:
The Moon does not make its own light; it reflects sunlight. Half of it is always lit by the Sun; the phases are how much of that lit half we see from Earth as the Moon orbits us.
Order: new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → third (last) quarter → waning crescent → new moon.
Waxing = the lit part is growing; waning = shrinking. Crescent = less than half lit; gibbous = more than half lit; a quarter moon looks like a half circle.
One full cycle (new moon to new moon) takes about 29.5 days. (The Moon orbits Earth once relative to the stars in about 27.3 days.)
In the Northern Hemisphere a waxing moon is lit on the right side; a waning moon on the left.
Classic mistake: phases are not caused by Earth's shadow — that is a lunar eclipse.

Solar eclipse: the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth (order Sun–Moon–Earth), and the Moon's shadow falls on Earth. Can only happen at new moon. A total solar eclipse is seen only along a narrow path inside the Moon's dark shadow (umbra); a wider area sees a partial eclipse. Never look at the Sun without proper eclipse protection.
Lunar eclipse: Earth passes between the Sun and Moon (order Sun–Earth–Moon), and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Can only happen at full moon, and is visible from the whole night side of Earth. During totality the Moon often looks reddish (blood moon), because Earth's atmosphere bends red sunlight onto it.
Eclipses do not happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° relative to Earth's orbit, so usually the Moon passes above or below the shadow.
An annular solar eclipse (ring of fire) happens when the Moon is far enough away to look slightly smaller than the Sun.

Tides are mainly caused by the Moon's gravity pulling unevenly on Earth: it creates two bulges of ocean water, one on the side facing the Moon and one on the opposite side.
Most coasts get two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours 50 minutes (the extra 50 minutes is because the Moon moves along its orbit each day).
The Sun also produces tides, a little under half as strong as the Moon's.
Spring tides (largest range: highest highs, lowest lows) happen at new and full moon, when the Sun, Moon and Earth line up.
Neap tides (smallest range) happen at first and third quarter, when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles.
Spring tides have nothing to do with the season spring.

Average distance from Earth: about 384,400 km.
Diameter: about 3,474 km, a little over one quarter of Earth's.
Surface gravity: about 1/6 of Earth's (1.62 m/s²).
The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates once for each orbit, so the same side always faces Earth. The far side is not permanently dark; it gets sunlight too.
It has almost no atmosphere, so there is no weather or wind, and temperatures swing widely between day and night. Its surface is covered with impact craters and dark plains of old lava called maria.
It probably formed about 4.5 billion years ago from debris after a Mars-sized body hit the early Earth (giant-impact hypothesis).
First crewed landing: Apollo 11, July 20, 1969 (Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin).

a: what kind of star is the sun
x:
The Sun is a star: a G-type main-sequence star (G2V), sometimes called a yellow dwarf, about 4.6 billion years old.
It holds about 99.8% of the mass of the solar system; its diameter is about 109 times Earth's.
It shines by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core (about 15 million °C).
Visible surface (photosphere): about 5,500 °C (about 5,800 K). Outer layers: chromosphere and corona (the corona is over a million degrees).
Internal layers: core → radiative zone → convective zone.
Sunspots are cooler, darker regions caused by magnetic activity; their numbers rise and fall in a cycle of about 11 years.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.

There are 8 planets. From the Sun outward: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Memory aid: My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos.
Inner (terrestrial) planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — small, rocky, dense, few or no moons, no rings.
Outer planets: the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn (mostly hydrogen and helium) and the ice giants Uranus and Neptune (more water, ammonia and methane ices) — large, low density, many moons, all have ring systems.
The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter. Beyond Neptune is the Kuiper Belt, home of Pluto and other dwarf planets.
Largest planet: Jupiter. Smallest: Mercury. Hottest: Venus. Densest: Earth.

Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun (about 0.39 AU) and the smallest planet in the solar system.
Year (one orbit): about 88 Earth days — the shortest of any planet.
It rotates slowly (once every about 59 Earth days); one full day–night cycle lasts about 176 Earth days.
It has no moons and almost no atmosphere, so temperatures swing from about 430 °C in the day to about −180 °C at night.
Its surface is heavily cratered, similar to the Moon.
Despite being closest to the Sun, it is not the hottest planet (Venus is).

Venus is the second planet from the Sun (about 0.72 AU) and is nearly the same size as Earth.
It is the hottest planet, about 465 °C at the surface, because its very thick carbon dioxide atmosphere causes a runaway greenhouse effect. Surface pressure is about 90 times Earth's.
Its clouds contain sulfuric acid and hide the surface.
It rotates backward (retrograde) and very slowly: one rotation takes about 243 Earth days, longer than its year of about 225 Earth days.
It has no moons.
After the Moon, it is the brightest natural object in the night sky, often called the morning star or evening star.

Earth is the third planet from the Sun, at 1 AU (about 150 million km).
Year: about 365.25 days (the extra quarter day is why we add a leap day about every 4 years).
One rotation relative to the Sun: 24 hours; axial tilt about 23.4°, which causes the seasons.
It has one natural satellite, the Moon.
About 71% of its surface is covered by water. It is the only planet known to have liquid water on its surface and the only place known to have life.
It is the densest planet (about 5.5 g/cm³) and the largest of the four rocky planets. Mean diameter about 12,742 km.
Its atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen; its magnetic field protects it from much of the solar wind.

Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun (about 1.52 AU), called the Red Planet because iron oxide (rust) in its soil and dust makes it look red.
Its diameter is about half of Earth's; its surface gravity is about 38% of Earth's.
Year: about 687 Earth days. Day: about 24 hours 37 minutes — very close to Earth's.
It has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.
Its atmosphere is very thin and mostly carbon dioxide.
It has polar ice caps (water ice plus frozen CO₂), and evidence that liquid water once flowed on its surface.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system; Valles Marineris is a canyon system far larger than the Grand Canyon.

Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun (about 5.2 AU) and the largest planet: about 11 times Earth's diameter and more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined.
It is a gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface to stand on.
Year: about 12 Earth years (11.86). It spins fastest of all the planets: a day is just under 10 hours.
The Great Red Spot is a giant storm, wider than Earth, that has been observed for well over 150 years.
It has many moons. The four largest — Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto — are the Galilean moons, discovered by Galileo in 1610. Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system (bigger than Mercury); Io is the most volcanically active body known; Europa has an ice shell over a liquid-water ocean.
It has faint rings.

Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun (about 9.5 AU) and the second-largest planet.
It is a gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
It has the largest and brightest ring system of any planet, made of countless pieces of ice and rock, from dust-sized to house-sized.
Its average density (about 0.69 g/cm³) is less than that of water — the lowest of any planet.
Year: about 29.5 Earth years. Day: about 10½ hours.
It has many moons. The largest, Titan, is the second-largest moon in the solar system and the only moon with a thick atmosphere (mostly nitrogen); it has lakes of liquid methane and ethane.
Enceladus sprays jets of water ice from an ocean beneath its surface.

Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun (about 19.2 AU). It is an ice giant, made mainly of water, ammonia and methane ices around a small rocky core, with a hydrogen–helium atmosphere.
Its axis is tilted about 98°, so it rotates on its side; this gives it extreme seasons, each lasting about 21 years.
Year: about 84 Earth years. Like Venus, it rotates in the retrograde (backward) direction.
Methane in its atmosphere absorbs red light, giving it a blue-green colour.
It has faint rings and many moons.
It was the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781. Only one spacecraft, Voyager 2 (1986), has visited it.

Neptune is the eighth and farthest planet from the Sun (about 30 AU). It is an ice giant, similar in size and makeup to Uranus.
Year: about 165 Earth years.
Its deep blue colour comes partly from methane in its atmosphere. It has the fastest winds measured on any planet, reaching about 2,000 km/h.
It was the first planet found by mathematical prediction: Urbain Le Verrier calculated its position from irregularities in Uranus's orbit, and Johann Galle observed it in 1846.
Its largest moon, Triton, orbits in the opposite direction to Neptune's rotation (retrograde), suggesting it was captured. Neptune also has faint rings.
Only Voyager 2 has visited it (1989).

In 2006 the International Astronomical Union (IAU) defined a planet as a body that (1) orbits the Sun, (2) is massive enough for its gravity to make it nearly round, and (3) has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit.
Pluto meets the first two but not the third, so it was reclassified as a dwarf planet.
Recognized dwarf planets include Ceres (in the asteroid belt), Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake (the last four beyond Neptune).
Pluto lies in the Kuiper Belt, a region of icy bodies beyond Neptune. Its largest moon is Charon. Its orbit takes about 248 Earth years and is so elongated that it is sometimes closer to the Sun than Neptune.
NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto in 2015.

Asteroid: a rocky or metallic body orbiting the Sun, smaller than a planet; most are in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
Comet: a ball of ice, dust and rock (a dirty snowball) on a usually very elongated orbit. Near the Sun its ice turns to gas, forming a glowing coma and tails that always point away from the Sun (pushed by sunlight and the solar wind). Many come from the Kuiper Belt or the distant Oort Cloud.
Meteoroid: a small rock or particle in space.
Meteor: the streak of light when a meteoroid burns up in Earth's atmosphere (a shooting star; not a star at all).
Meteorite: a piece that survives the fall and lands on Earth's surface.
Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through the trail of debris left by a comet.

1 astronomical unit (AU) = the average distance from Earth to the Sun.
Defined exactly as 149,597,870,700 m (IAU, 2012) ≈ 1.496 × 10⁸ km ≈ 150 million km ≈ 93 million miles.
Used for distances within the solar system: Mercury about 0.39 AU, Mars about 1.52 AU, Jupiter about 5.2 AU, Neptune about 30 AU from the Sun.
Light takes about 499 seconds (8 minutes 19 seconds) to travel 1 AU.

a: distance light travels in a year
x:
A light-year (ly) is a unit of DISTANCE, not time: the distance light travels in vacuum in one Julian year (365.25 days).
1 ly = 9,460,730,472,580.8 km exactly ≈ 9.461 × 10¹⁵ m ≈ 9.46 trillion km ≈ 63,241 AU.
The nearest star to the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.24 light-years away.
Looking at an object 100 light-years away, you see light that left it 100 years ago.
Classic mistake: light-year measures how far, not how long.

A parsec (pc) is the distance at which 1 AU appears to span an angle of 1 arcsecond (1/3600 of a degree). The name comes from parallax arcsecond.
1 pc ≈ 3.086 × 10¹³ km = 3.086 × 10¹⁶ m ≈ 3.26 light-years ≈ 206,265 AU.
Parallax distance formula: d = 1 ÷ p, where d is in parsecs and p is the parallax angle in arcseconds.
Example: a star with a parallax of 0.5 arcseconds is 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 pc ≈ 6.5 light-years away.
Larger units: kiloparsec (kpc) = 1,000 pc; megaparsec (Mpc) = 1,000,000 pc.

All stars begin in a nebula, a cloud of gas (mostly hydrogen) and dust. Gravity pulls material together into a protostar; when the core is hot enough for hydrogen fusion, it becomes a main-sequence star — where stars spend most of their lives.
Low- and medium-mass stars (like the Sun): main sequence → red giant (when core hydrogen runs out) → outer layers drift off as a planetary nebula → the core remains as a white dwarf, which slowly cools.
High-mass stars (roughly 8 or more times the Sun's mass): main sequence → red supergiant → supernova explosion → neutron star, or, for the most massive, a black hole.
The more massive a star, the hotter and brighter it is, and the SHORTER its life.
Elements heavier than helium (carbon, oxygen, iron and beyond) were made inside stars and spread by supernovae and stellar winds.

t: Star colour, temperature and the H–R diagram
x:
A star's colour shows its surface temperature: blue stars are hottest, then white, yellow, orange, and red stars are coolest.
Spectral classes from hottest to coolest: O, B, A, F, G, K, M (memory aid: Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy, Kiss Me). The Sun is class G.
The Hertzsprung–Russell (H–R) diagram plots luminosity (brightness) against surface temperature; temperature increases to the LEFT.
Main sequence: a diagonal band from hot, bright stars (upper left) to cool, dim stars (lower right); about 90% of stars are on it.
Red giants and supergiants: upper right (cool but very bright because they are huge).
White dwarfs: lower left (hot but dim because they are small).
Apparent brightness depends on distance; absolute magnitude/luminosity is the true brightness.

A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity. Main types: spiral, elliptical and irregular.
The Milky Way, our galaxy, is a barred spiral galaxy containing hundreds of billions of stars; the solar system is about 26,000 light-years from its centre, in one of the spiral arms.
The nearest large galaxy is Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years away.
The universe began with the Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.
Evidence: distant galaxies are moving away from us, faster the farther they are (redshift, Hubble's law); the cosmic microwave background radiation, the afterglow of the early universe; the observed amounts of hydrogen and helium.
